## Florence 2026: The Complete Guide — Uffizi, Duomo, David, Oltrarno & the Secrets Most Visitors Never Find

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/city-breaks/florence-complete-guide-2026
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** city-breaks
**Publicat:** 2026-07-31
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-31

**Descriere:** Florence 2026 complete guide. Uffizi and David tickets, Duomo dome booking, best neighbourhoods, budget tips and what to skip in the most-visited city in Italy.

**Rezumat rapid:** Florence (Firenze) is the city where the Renaissance was born and where more great art is concentrated per square kilometre than anywhere else on Earth. The historic centre is UNESCO World Heritage. Essential must-sees: Uffizi Gallery (Botticelli, Leonardo, Raphael — €25, book weeks ahead), Brunelleschi's Dome climb (463 steps, world's largest masonry dome — €30 Brunelleschi Pass, book in advance), Michelangelo's David at the Accademia (€16), and the Bargello (Italy's greatest Renaissance sculpture collection, almost no queue). Best kept secret: the Oltrarno neighbourhood across the Arno — artisan workshops, Brancacci Chapel, Bardini Garden — where Florentines actually live. Best time: April–June and September–October.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How many days do you need in Florence?**
R: Two full days is the absolute minimum to cover the Uffizi, the Duomo dome climb, Michelangelo's David, and the Ponte Vecchio. Three to four days lets you add the Oltrarno, the Bargello, Brancacci Chapel, Boboli Gardens, and a day trip to Siena, Pisa, or the Chianti countryside. A week allows you to genuinely understand the city. One day is enough for a single highlight — but not enough to understand what makes Florence extraordinary.

**Î: How far in advance should I book Florence museums?**
R: For July–August: Uffizi and Brunelleschi Dome climb should be booked 4–6 weeks ahead. The Dome sells out first — book the moment your dates are confirmed. David at the Accademia: 2–3 weeks ahead in peak season. For April–June and September–October: 2 weeks ahead for Uffizi and Dome, 1 week for Accademia. The Bargello almost never sells out — walk in any morning.

**Î: What is the Brunelleschi Pass and is it worth it?**
R: The Brunelleschi Pass (€30, valid 72 hours) covers the dome climb, Baptistery, Bell Tower, Crypt of Santa Reparata, and the Museo dell'Opera del Duomo. It is worth it — the Opera del Duomo museum alone (Ghiberti's original Gates of Paradise, Michelangelo's Pietà Bandini) would justify €15 on its own. The Giotto Pass (€20, excludes the dome) is worth it only if heights aren't your thing. The cathedral itself is free.

**Î: What is the Bargello and why do most tourists miss it?**
R: The Bargello Museum (Via del Proconsolo 4) is Italy's greatest Renaissance sculpture museum — and Florence's most underrated major site. It houses Donatello's bronze David (the first life-size nude sculpture since antiquity, 1440s), a second David by Michelangelo (Tondo Pitti), works by Verrocchio (Leonardo's teacher), Cellini's Perseus model, and extraordinary bronze reliefs by both Ghiberti and Brunelleschi from the 1401 Baptistery door competition. Entry: €10. It opens at 08:15 and is almost always quiet in the morning — the opposite of the Uffizi.

**Î: What is the Oltrarno and why should I go?**
R: The Oltrarno ('beyond the Arno') is the neighbourhood south of the Arno river, separated from the historic centre by the Ponte Vecchio and other bridges. It's where Florentines actually live — artisan workshops producing leather, bookbinding, goldsmithy, and furniture restoration; local wine bars; Palazzo Pitti with five museums and Boboli Gardens; the Brancacci Chapel (Masaccio's frescoes, the 'Sistine Chapel of the early Renaissance'); Bardini Garden (the best view of the Duomo in the city); and San Miniato al Monte. Cross the Arno and spend an afternoon here.

**Î: What is lampredotto and should I try it?**
R: Lampredotto is Florence's quintessential working-class street food — the fourth stomach of a cow (the abomasum), slow-braised until tender, sliced thin, and served in a crusty roll (semelle) with salsa verde (parsley, capers, anchovies) and optional spicy sauce. It's been sold from trippaio carts in Florence for centuries. It costs €4–5. Most visitors are apprehensive; most who try it are surprised. Find it at carts near Mercato Centrale, Mercato Sant'Ambrogio, and Piazza dei Cimatori.

**Î: What is Bistecca alla Fiorentina?**
R: A T-bone steak (minimum 1 kg, usually 1.2–1.5 kg) from Chianina IGP cattle — the large white breed of the Val di Chiana — grilled over hardwood embers and served rare, finished with coarse salt, pepper, and Tuscan olive oil. It is always priced by weight (approximately €50–65/kg in 2026) and intended for two people to share. If you ask for it well-done, the chef will refuse. This is not rudeness — it is the definition of the dish.

**Î: What are Florence's best hidden viewpoints?**
R: Three better than Piazzale Michelangelo (where every tour bus goes): the Bardini Garden terrace (€10 garden entry, views of the Duomo and Arno without crowds); the Caffetteria delle Oblate rooftop (a café inside the Oblate public library, free to enter, extraordinary Duomo view from the terrace, €3 for coffee); and San Miniato al Monte (a 12th-century Romanesque church 30 minutes' walk uphill from the Arno, free entry, most peaceful elevated view in the city — arrive for Vespers at 17:30 if you can).

## Formula 1 in Europe 2026: How to Attend a Grand Prix — Tickets, Budget & Best Races

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/city-breaks/formula-1-europe-grand-prix-2026
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** city-breaks
**Publicat:** 2026-07-31
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-31
**Traducere a:** [formula-1-europa-2026-grand-prix](https://plecari.com/ro/city-breaks/formula-1-europa-2026-grand-prix)

**Descriere:** How to attend a European F1 Grand Prix in 2026. Best races, ticket prices, real budget, accommodation strategy and what to expect at your first GP weekend.

**Rezumat rapid:** The most accessible European Grand Prix for fans in Central and Eastern Europe is the Hungarian Grand Prix at Hungaroring (Budapest) — 1h20 by flight or 8h by car from Bucharest, with General Admission weekend tickets from €100–150. Other accessible European races: Italian GP at Monza (from €120 GA), Spanish GP at Barcelona (from €150), Austrian GP at Red Bull Ring (from €180). Total weekend budget (ticket + travel + accommodation): €400–1,200 per person depending on race and ticket category. The 2026 season introduces the first major technical regulation change since 2022 — new hybrid power units, active aerodynamics, and lighter cars that make every race unpredictable.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How much do Formula 1 tickets cost?**
R: General Admission (GA, no fixed seat): €100–200 for a full weekend (Friday–Sunday) at most European races. Grandstand seats: €200–600. Premium grandstands (pit straight, Turn 1): €400–1,200. Paddock Club (hospitality, track access): €3,000–6,000. Monaco is the most expensive (no GA, grandstands from €500). Hungaroring and Red Bull Ring are among the most affordable on the calendar.

**Î: Where do I buy official F1 tickets?**
R: Directly from formula1.com or the individual circuit websites (hungaroring.hu, monzanet.it, circuitcat.com, formula1.at for Red Bull Ring). Do NOT buy from unauthorised resale sites — fake tickets are common at major GPs and you will be refused entry. Formula 1 now uses digital tickets with unique QR codes verified against your name at the gate.

**Î: General Admission or grandstand — which is better?**
R: GA is excellent at circuits with natural geography — Hungaroring and Red Bull Ring have hills from which you can see 60–70% of the track without a fixed seat, and the atmosphere is festival-like. At Monza and Barcelona, grandstands are worth the premium as the flat circuit layout limits GA viewing. For your first GP, Hungaroring GA is the best introduction: cheap, social, great sightlines from the hills.

**Î: What is the best European Grand Prix for a first-time attendee?**
R: Hungarian GP (Hungaroring, Budapest): closest to Central/Eastern Europe, most affordable tickets, compact circuit where you see a large percentage of the race, and you can combine it with a Budapest city break. Monza (Italian GP) has the most intense atmosphere — if Ferrari scores points, the tifosi create an experience unlike anything else in sport. Barcelona is good but hotter and more expensive.

**Î: What changed in F1 for the 2026 season?**
R: 2026 introduces the largest technical regulation change since 2022. New power units with a 50/50 split between internal combustion and electric motor (previously ~80/20). Active aerodynamics — deployable front and rear wings that adjust automatically. Lighter cars overall. The result: a complete reset of the competitive order, with teams that struggled in 2023–2025 potentially competitive and vice versa. Every race in 2026 has an element of genuine unpredictability that multi-year regulations eliminate.

**Î: How far in advance should I buy F1 tickets?**
R: Monaco: 6–12 months ahead (sells out almost immediately). Silverstone, Monza, Spa: 4–6 months ahead for preferred grandstands. Hungaroring, Red Bull Ring, Barcelona: 2–3 months ahead is usually fine for GA. For 2026, with the new regulations creating unusual interest, buying 3–4 months ahead for any race is the safe approach.

**Î: What should I bring to a Formula 1 race?**
R: Ear protection (essential — even the 2026 engines are very loud at close range), sunscreen SPF50+, refillable water bottle (free water at most circuits), comfortable walking shoes (you cover 5–10 km on race weekend), portable phone charger, lightweight rain poncho (mountain circuits like Red Bull Ring change weather quickly), and a cap or hat. Download the official F1 app before arriving — it streams race radio and live timing so you can follow strategy in real time.

## Gdańsk 2026: The Complete City Break Guide to Poland's Baltic Pearl

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/gdansk-complete-guide
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-08-08
**Actualizat:** 2026-08-08
**Traducere a:** [gdansk-ghid-complet](https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/gdansk-ghid-complet)

**Descriere:** Complete Gdańsk guide: Hanseatic Old Town, European Solidarity Centre, Museum of the Second World War, Baltic amber, Sopot beach resort and Malbork Castle — the world's largest castle. Real prices...

**Rezumat rapid:** Gdańsk is Poland's most important Baltic seaport, with a spectacular Hanseatic Old Town reconstructed after World War II, the birthplace of the Solidarity movement that contributed to the fall of communism, the world capital of amber, and the gateway to Malbork Castle — the world's largest castle. It is a completely different destination from Krakow or Warsaw. Direct flights from Bucharest from 40 EUR.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How do I get from Bucharest to Gdańsk?**
R: Wizz Air operates direct flights Bucharest (OTP) → Gdańsk (GDN). Duration: ~2h15. Prices: 40–100 EUR return with 3–6 weeks' advance booking. The airport is 15 km from the centre — bus 210 or B takes 35 minutes (~5 PLN/1.15 EUR), taxi/Bolt 20 minutes (35–50 PLN/8–12 EUR).

**Î: What is the European Solidarity Centre and why is it important?**
R: The European Solidarity Centre (ECS) documents the Solidarity movement — the Polish trade union founded in 1980 at Gdańsk by Lech Wałęsa and the shipyard workers, which decisively contributed to the fall of communism in Eastern Europe. It is a modern interactive museum built right next to the former Gate No. 2 of the shipyard — where everything started. Ticket: ~34 PLN (8 EUR). Free on Mondays.

**Î: What is Malbork Castle and is the excursion worth it?**
R: Malbork Castle is the world's largest castle by area — a medieval Teutonic Knights fortress built in the 13th–15th centuries, a UNESCO site. It is 45 minutes by train from Gdańsk (25–35 PLN/5.75–8 EUR return). Castle ticket: ~70–80 PLN (16–18 EUR) with audio guide. Plan 3–4 hours.

**Î: What is Goldwasser and is it worth trying?**
R: Goldwasser is Gdańsk's traditional liqueur — a herbal liqueur with 22-karat gold flakes in suspension, produced in Gdańsk since 1598. It is one of Europe's oldest liqueurs. Drink cold, neat. A bottle: 35–60 PLN (8–14 EUR) in local shops.

**Î: Is Sopot worth a visit from Gdańsk?**
R: Absolutely. Sopot is 15 minutes by SKM train (5–8 PLN return). It is the elegant Baltic seaside resort — with Europe's longest pier (511 m), fine sand beach and the Monte Cassino Street full of restaurants and bars. Perfect as a half-day or full day combined with Gdańsk.

**Î: What is Baltic amber and where do I buy it in Gdańsk?**
R: Baltic amber is fossilised tree resin from 40–50 million years ago, washed up on the Baltic shore. Gdańsk produces 70–90% of the world's amber. Mariacka Street is the best address for authentic jewellery — prices are negotiable starting from 50–60% of the asking price. Verify authenticity: real amber is light (floats in salt water) and becomes electrostatically charged when rubbed.

**Î: How much does a 3-day city break in Gdańsk cost?**
R: A 3-day/2-night city break costs 190–330 EUR per person (mid-range), including flights, accommodation, food and the Malbork excursion. Gdańsk is similarly priced to Krakow and Warsaw: local beer 3–5 EUR, mid-range lunch 8–15 EUR, mid-range accommodation 35–65 EUR per night.

**Î: What is the best time to visit Gdańsk?**
R: May–September: best for beaches (Sopot), Motława waterfront walks and street life. July–August: most lively, St Dominic's Fair (Poland's oldest and largest fair, since the 13th century). December: Christmas markets on Długi Targ. Avoid January–March if you don't handle Baltic cold well.

## Travel Insurance Guide 2026: What It Covers, What It Costs and 7 Mistakes to Avoid

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/asigurari/ghid-asigurare-calatorie
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** asigurari
**Publicat:** 2026-07-25
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-25
**Traducere a:** [ghid-asigurare-calatorie-2026](https://plecari.com/ro/asigurari/ghid-asigurare-calatorie-2026)

**Descriere:** Everything you need to know about travel insurance in 2026. What it covers, what it does not, real prices by destination, the difference from the EHIC, and the most common mistakes.

**Rezumat rapid:** A standard travel insurance policy for one week in Europe costs €12–25 per person (€30,000 medical cover, repatriation, baggage). For non-EU destinations (Turkey, UK, USA) prices rise to €20–70/week. The European Health Insurance Card is NOT a substitute — it covers only emergencies in public EU hospitals and does not cover repatriation, trip cancellation, or sports accidents. A single night of hospitalisation in Italy costs €500–3,000 without insurance.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How much does travel insurance cost?**
R: Prices vary by destination and duration. Europe 7 days: €12–25. Turkey 7 days: €15–30. USA 7 days: €35–70. Worldwide 14 days: €40–80. For frequent travellers, an annual multi-trip policy (€120–250/year) is more economical from 3+ trips per year.

**Î: Is the European Health Insurance Card enough?**
R: No. The EHIC covers emergency medical treatment in PUBLIC hospitals in EU countries only, under the same conditions as local residents. It does not cover: medical repatriation (which can cost €10,000–50,000), trip cancellation, lost baggage, winter sports, or private hospitals. It is a useful supplement, not a complete insurance solution.

**Î: What does standard travel insurance NOT cover?**
R: The most common exclusions: undeclared pre-existing conditions, accidents under the influence of alcohol or drugs, extreme sports (without a specific add-on), planned medical treatment abroad, travel to conflict zones, and pandemics (with some insurers). Always read the general conditions before purchasing.

**Î: Can I buy travel insurance after I have already left home?**
R: Yes, but with restrictions. Most insurers apply a waiting period of 3–7 days after purchase before the policy is active. If you forgot to buy before departure, purchase immediately — but be aware you are not covered during those first days.

**Î: Do I need travel insurance for Turkey?**
R: Absolutely yes. Turkey is outside the EU, so the EHIC does not apply. Medical costs at Turkish private hospitals are surprisingly high (€500–2,000/night). Private travel insurance is the only protection you have.

**Î: Is travel insurance compulsory?**
R: Not legally for most destinations, but it is compulsory for a Schengen short-stay visa (minimum €30,000 medical cover required). For all other destinations it is optional but strongly recommended for any trip where medical costs abroad could be financially catastrophic.

**Î: Does credit card travel insurance count?**
R: Sometimes partially. Many premium credit cards (Gold, Platinum, Visa Infinite) include travel insurance as a benefit, but typically with lower coverage limits (€10,000–25,000), requirements to have paid the trip with that card, and exclusions for pre-existing conditions. Check your card's terms carefully — it may supplement but usually should not replace a dedicated policy.

## Mediterranean Cruise Guide 2026: Everything You Need to Know Before You Book

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/croaziere/ghid-croaziere-mediterana
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** croaziere
**Publicat:** 2026-07-25
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-25

**Descriere:** Complete Mediterranean cruise guide for 2026. Real costs, what is included, which cruise line to choose, West vs East Med, best ports, when to book and what to avoid.

**Rezumat rapid:** A 7-night Mediterranean cruise costs between €399 and €900 per person depending on the cruise line, cabin type and season. The price includes accommodation, main meals and onboard entertainment. It does NOT include: alcoholic drinks, shore excursions, the mandatory gratuity (~€10–15/person/day), Wi-Fi, or flights to the embarkation port. Total realistic cost for two people for a week: €1,700–3,500 including flights, gratuities and a few excursions.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: What does the cruise price include?**
R: Typically included: accommodation in your cabin, main meals (breakfast, lunch, dinner at the buffet and main dining room), onboard entertainment (shows, pools, activities) and port access fees. NOT included: alcoholic beverages, specialty restaurants, organised shore excursions, spa treatments, Wi-Fi, the mandatory service charge (€10–15/person/day), and flights to the embarkation port.

**Î: When is the best time to book a Mediterranean cruise?**
R: Early booking (8–12 months ahead) gives the best prices and widest cabin selection. Peak season (July–August) costs 30–50% more than May–June or September. Last-minute deals can be exceptional but you lose control over dates and cabin category.

**Î: Interior cabin or balcony — is the price difference worth it?**
R: Depends on how you use the cabin. If you are rarely in your room (eating, sleeping, that is all), an interior cabin is excellent — you save €150–300 per person for the same itinerary. If you want morning coffee watching the sea or are doing a longer cruise, the balcony is worth the investment.

**Î: Which is better — Western or Eastern Mediterranean?**
R: Western Med (Spain, France, Italy) is ideal for a first cruise — large cities, easy logistics, cultural variety. Eastern Med (Greece, Croatia, Turkey) is better if you have done the west — spectacular islands, dramatic scenery, more exotic ports. Both are excellent; the choice depends on what you have already seen.

**Î: Which cruise line is best for first-timers?**
R: MSC and Costa are the classic first-cruise choices — European style, competitive prices, embarkation from Italian ports (short flight from most of Europe). Norwegian is excellent if you want more freedom and do not mind spending 30–50% more. Royal Caribbean is best for families with teenagers who want activities and thrill rides.

**Î: Are cruise shore excursions worth it?**
R: Ship-organised excursions are convenient (the ship waits for you if the tour runs late) but expensive — typically 2–3x the price of independent alternatives. For relaxed ports like Santorini or Dubrovnik, you can easily explore independently. For complex destinations like Pompeii or Ephesus, a guided excursion adds context that is hard to replicate on your own.

**Î: What is the mandatory gratuity and can I avoid it?**
R: Most cruise lines automatically add a service charge to your onboard account: approximately €10–15 per person per day. On a 7-night cruise for two people, that is €140–210. It is technically possible to request removal at Guest Services, but it is considered poor practice as it comes directly from the wages of cabin stewards and restaurant staff. Factor it into your budget from the start.

**Î: Is travel insurance necessary for a cruise?**
R: Yes — more so than for any other type of holiday. Cruise cancellation policies are the harshest in the travel industry (up to 100% forfeiture within 2 weeks of sailing). Medical repatriation from a cruise ship can be exceptionally complex and expensive. Travel insurance specifically noting 'cruise cover' is strongly recommended.

## Greece 2026 Holiday Guide: Which Island, Real Costs, When to Go and What to Know

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/city-breaks/greece-2026-holiday-guide
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** city-breaks
**Publicat:** 2026-07-29
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-29
**Traducere a:** [grecia-2026-ghid-vacanta](https://plecari.com/ro/city-breaks/grecia-2026-ghid-vacanta)

**Descriere:** Complete guide to a Greece holiday in 2026. Which island suits you, real prices by destination, how to get there, best beaches, car rental tips, and why September beats August.

**Rezumat rapid:** Greece is Europe's most popular summer destination in 2026, with Crete, Rhodes, Corfu, Santorini and Mykonos leading bookings. A 7-night holiday for two costs €750–3,500 depending on island and season. The sweet spot: Crete or Rhodes in September — same excellent weather, 20–30% lower prices, far fewer crowds. EU citizens need no visa. No eSIM needed (EU free roaming applies). A rental car is essential on large islands like Crete and Rhodes.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Which Greek island is best for families with children?**
R: Crete is the best overall family destination — the largest island, varied beaches with safe shallow water, excellent all-inclusive options, good medical infrastructure, and plenty of non-beach activities (Minoan palaces, gorges, markets). Zakynthos and Rhodes are also strong family choices. Avoid Santorini and Mykonos with young children — the terrain is difficult, prices are extreme, and neither island is designed for family tourism.

**Î: Is September good for Greece?**
R: September is arguably the best month to visit Greece. Weather remains excellent (28–32°C air, 25°C sea temperature), the crowds reduce dramatically, prices drop 20–30% compared to August, and popular sites like Akrotiri in Santorini or the Palace of Knossos in Crete are actually enjoyable rather than overwhelming. The only downside: some seasonal restaurants and bars begin closing from mid-September.

**Î: Do I need a visa or eSIM for Greece?**
R: EU citizens need no visa — enter with a national ID card. Greece is in the EU, so free roaming applies — use your home mobile plan without extra charges. No eSIM needed for Greece specifically, though an eSIM is useful if your itinerary includes Turkey or other non-EU countries.

**Î: Is a rental car necessary in Greece?**
R: On large islands: essential. On Crete (250 km long) and Rhodes, the best beaches and villages are only reachable by car. On smaller islands (Mykonos, Paros, Zakynthos), ATVs or scooters are common alternatives. On Santorini and Hydra, cars are impractical or prohibited. See the full guide: car rental in Greece 2026.

**Î: What is the cheapest Greek island?**
R: For European travellers: Crete and Rhodes consistently offer the best value at the beach resort level — wide choice of all-inclusive hotels, direct flights from most European cities, and competitive prices. Lesbos, Samos, and Kos are cheaper but less frequently served. Santorini and Mykonos are in a category of their own — significantly more expensive than all other islands.

**Î: How much does a meal cost in Greece?**
R: A full meal at a local taverna (Greek salad + grilled fish or meat + wine) costs €15–25/person. Beach clubs and tourist-facing restaurants on Santorini, Mykonos, and the most popular resort areas charge €30–50/person. The best value: inland tavernas a few streets back from the main waterfront, particularly in Crete and Rhodes, where the food is better and the prices much lower.

**Î: Can I do a cruise of the Greek islands instead of staying on one island?**
R: Yes, and it is often excellent value. A 7-night Greek island cruise visits Santorini, Mykonos, Crete, and Rhodes or other islands — staying on the ship each night, spending 6–8 hours in each port. Costs: from €450/person for a cabin on MSC or Costa. For a comparison of cruising vs island stay, see the Mediterranean cruise guide.

## Greek Islands Cruise 2026: Santorini, Mykonos, Crete — Complete Guide with Real Prices

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/croaziere/greek-islands-cruise-2026

**Rezumat rapid:** A 7-night Greek islands cruise starts from €499–600 per person in an interior cabin (Costa or MSC), embarking from Athens (Piraeus), Bari or Ravenna. Classic itineraries visit Santorini, Mykonos, Crete (Heraklion), and Rhodes, with all main meals included. Add flights from your home country (€100–250 return), the mandatory service charge (~€70 per person for 7 nights), and optional shore excursions (€40–100 per port). **Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How much does a 7-night Greek islands cruise cost?**
R: Base cabin prices start from €499–600/person (interior cabin, Costa or MSC). Add: flights to the embarkation port (€100–250 return from most of Europe), mandatory service charge (€70/person for 7 nights at €10/day), optional drinks (€100–250 if not buying a package), shore excursions (€40–100 per port independently), and travel insurance (€25–50). Realistic all-in budget for two people: €1,700–2,800.

**Î: Which cruise line is best for Greek islands?**
R: MSC and Costa offer the best value for Greek island itineraries with the most departure options from Italian and Greek ports. Norwegian is better if you prioritise flexible dining. For a first cruise in the Greek islands, MSC from Civitavecchia (Rome) or Athens is the most accessible option. Celebrity Cruises offers premium Greek island itineraries with superior food quality.

**Î: Is Santorini still worth visiting on a cruise in 2026?**
R: Yes, but with caveats. Santorini has imposed daily limits on cruise passengers — some ships are now diverted in August. If your itinerary guarantees Santorini, the port stop is spectacular. If it says 'subject to availability', plan for the possibility of visiting Milos or Folegandros instead. September sailings have significantly fewer restrictions and a better experience.

**Î: Where do Greek island cruises embark?**
R: The most popular embarkation ports for Greek island cruises are Athens/Piraeus (closest to the islands, 1.5h direct flight from most European capitals), Bari (Southern Italy), Ravenna (near Venice), and Civitavecchia (Rome). Athens is the most convenient for itineraries focused on the eastern Mediterranean and Greek islands specifically.

**Î: Can I explore Greek islands independently without the cruise ship excursions?**
R: Yes, and it's significantly cheaper. At Santorini: cable car up and walk to Oia (free). At Mykonos: walk from the port into town and beach (free). At Crete: local bus to archaeological sites (€3–8 each way) plus €15–20 entrance. Ship excursions cost €50–120 per port for essentially the same content you can do independently for €15–25.

**Î: What is the best month for a Greek islands cruise?**
R: May–June is the best combination of weather, price, and experience. Sea temperatures reach 22–24°C (warm enough to swim), air temperatures 25–28°C, prices 15–25% lower than August, and crowds are manageable. September is equally excellent. July–August is peak season — hottest, most expensive, and most crowded, with Santorini restrictions in effect.

**Î: Do I need a visa or eSIM for a Greek islands cruise?**
R: EU citizens need no visa — Greece is an EU member state. The EHIC covers medical emergencies at Greek public hospitals. No eSIM needed within Greece. However, if your itinerary includes Turkey (Ephesus/Kusadasi), Turkey is non-EU — buy an eSIM before departure, as provider websites are blocked inside Turkey since 2025.

## Helsinki 2026: The Complete City Break Guide to Finland's Capital — Suomenlinna, Sauna and Nordic Design

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/helsinki-complete-guide
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-08-10
**Actualizat:** 2026-08-10
**Traducere a:** [helsinki-ghid-complet](https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/helsinki-ghid-complet)

**Descriere:** Complete Helsinki guide: Suomenlinna (UNESCO island fortress, ferry included in transport ticket), Senate Square Cathedral, Temppeliaukio Rock Church carved from solid stone, Design District, Löyly...

**Rezumat rapid:** Helsinki is Finland's capital and our most northerly city break — a compact, clean and fascinating city with the neoclassical Senate Square, UNESCO Suomenlinna island fortress (ferry included in the HSL 3.30 EUR transport ticket), Temppeliaukio Rock Church carved from solid granite, the Design District with Marimekko and Iittala, and the Finnish sauna ritual at Löyly. Less expensive than Oslo or Stockholm, and Finland uses the euro.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How do I get from Bucharest to Helsinki?**
R: Wizz Air operates direct flights Bucharest (OTP) → Helsinki Vantaa (HEL). Duration: ~3h30. Prices: 80–200 EUR return. The airport is 20 km from the centre — the I train (Airport Rail Link) takes 30 minutes (3.30 EUR with HSL ticket). Alternative: Finnair City Bus, 40 minutes, 7 EUR.

**Î: Does the Suomenlinna ferry cost extra?**
R: No — the HSL ferry to Suomenlinna is included in the normal public transport ticket. An HSL A/B ticket costs 3.30 EUR and includes 80 minutes of travel on all transport modes, including the Suomenlinna ferry. If you buy a day ticket (8–9 EUR) or 24h ticket, the ferry is automatically included. Entry to Suomenlinna island itself is free — you only pay for the specific museums on the island (8–12 EUR each).

**Î: What is Temppeliaukio (Rock Church) and how was it built?**
R: Temppeliaukio is a Lutheran church built in 1969 by carving directly into the solid granite of a hill in the Töölö neighbourhood. The walls are bare natural rock, the dome is circular copper and glass, and the acoustics are exceptional (used for concerts). Ticket: 8 EUR. It is one of the world's most unusual churches — it resembles no other European religious building.

**Î: Finnish sauna — what is Löyly and how do I book?**
R: Löyly is Helsinki's most popular modern public sauna — a wooden building on the Baltic Sea shore with three sauna types (smoke, high temperature, infrared), outdoor sea pools and a waterfront restaurant. Sauna ticket: 19–25 EUR. Mandatory online booking 2 days ahead — sells out quickly. More authentic and cheaper alternative: Yrjönkatu sauna (historic public bath from 1928, ~15 EUR).

**Î: What is Helsinki's Design District and is it worth visiting?**
R: Helsinki Design District is an area of 25+ streets in the city centre with Finnish design shops, galleries, cafés and studios. Marimekko (textiles with geometric patterns), Iittala (glass and ceramics), Arabia and many indie Finnish brands have flagship stores and factory outlets in the district. Entry to the area is free — shopping is optional. The best Nordic design shopping in Europe.

**Î: How much does a 3–4 day city break in Helsinki cost?**
R: Helsinki is more affordable than Oslo but similar to Stockholm. Daily budget: 68–100 EUR (budget-conscious). Mid-range: 120–180 EUR per day. Advantage over other Nordic capitals: many major attractions are free (Senate Square, parks, Cathedral, Suomenlinna island), the ferry is included in the transport ticket and there's a market scene with good food at fair prices.

**Î: What is Finnish salmon soup and where do I find it?**
R: Salmon soup (lohikeitto) is Finland's unofficial national dish — a creamy soup with fresh salmon, potatoes, onion, dill and sour cream. At Kauppatori Market Square or Vanha Kauppahalli (Old Market Hall), a warm portion costs 8–14 EUR. Essential on any Helsinki visit.

**Î: Helsinki or Stockholm — which is better for a city break?**
R: Stockholm: larger, more top attractions (Vasa Museum, ABBA Museum), more expensive, more touristy. Helsinki: more compact, more Nordic in identity, more authentic, slightly cheaper, excellent design and sauna scene. Both worth visiting. For a single Nordic: Stockholm if you want the big museums; Helsinki if you want the authentic Finnish experience.

## Hidden Holiday Fees 2026: Every Cost Nobody Tells You About Before You Book

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/zboruri/hidden-holiday-fees-2026
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** zboruri
**Publicat:** 2026-07-31
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-31
**Traducere a:** [taxe-ascunse-vacanta-2026](https://plecari.com/ro/zboruri/taxe-ascunse-vacanta-2026)

**Descriere:** The complete guide to hidden fees in European travel — low-cost airline surcharges, hotel tourist taxes, DCC at ATMs, resort fees, car rental extras, and how to avoid or budget for each one.

**Rezumat rapid:** Hidden costs can add €100–400 to a holiday budget you thought was settled. The main culprits: low-cost airline baggage supplements (€25–100 per direction), hotel tourist tax not shown on Booking.com (€2–7/night), Dynamic Currency Conversion at ATMs and card terminals (3–8% loss on every transaction), car rental counter extras (CDW excess, insurance upgrades: €70–175/week), data roaming outside the EU (€3–12/day), and service charges added automatically to restaurant bills. The rule: always add 15–20% above the headline price.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: What fees are NOT included in hotel prices on Booking.com?**
R: The local tourist tax (€2–7/night depending on city and hotel category) is NOT included in the displayed price on Booking.com. You pay it at check-in, in cash or by card. Barcelona, Amsterdam, Rome, Venice, Paris, Lisbon — all have compulsory tourist taxes that appear only in the fine print or at check-in. Some hotels also charge resort fees (especially in Turkey and Egypt) at check-in that weren't visible at booking.

**Î: How do I avoid losing money at ATMs abroad?**
R: Always choose to pay in the LOCAL CURRENCY, never in your home currency. Dynamic Currency Conversion (DCC) is a mechanism where the ATM or payment terminal makes the conversion at an exchange rate 3–8% worse than your bank's rate. If the screen asks 'pay in pounds or euros?' — choose euros. If it asks 'conversion by ATM or your bank?' — choose your bank.

**Î: Why is my actual holiday spend always more than what I planned?**
R: Because headline prices exclude most of the real costs: the Ryanair 'from €25' doesn't include your bag; the hotel 'from €60' doesn't include the tourist tax; the 'free' city WiFi doesn't cover your roaming in Turkey; and that nice restaurant lunch came with a 12.5% service charge and a €2/person cover charge. Adding 15–20% to every headline price before booking gives a realistic picture.

**Î: How much does Dynamic Currency Conversion actually cost?**
R: 3–8% on every transaction where you choose your home currency instead of the local one. On a holiday with €800 of card spending, DCC costs €24–64. On €2,000 (a family holiday), it's €60–160. Use Revolut or Wise (0% exchange fee) and always choose local currency, and this cost drops to zero.

**Î: What car rental fees appear at the counter that aren't in the online price?**
R: The most common surprise fees at the rental counter: CDW excess reduction (€10–15/day, sometimes mandatory), additional driver fee (€5–15/day), young driver surcharge (under 25), airport collection surcharge (€5–20), fuel policy pre-purchase (often non-refundable), tyre/glass/roof protection (€3–8/day each). Total: €70–175 for a 7-day rental. Buy comprehensive insurance when booking online — it's cheaper and prevents most of this.

**Î: What tourist taxes are applied in Europe's top destinations in 2026?**
R: The biggest tourist taxes in 2026: Amsterdam (16% on room rate — the highest), Barcelona (€4–6.75/night), Rome (€3.50–7/night), Venice (€5–10/day for day visitors plus per-night hotel tax), Paris (€1–5/night), Lisbon (€2/night), Dubrovnik (€2/night). These are all mandatory, non-avoidable, and frequently not shown on Booking.com at search time.

**Î: Is the 'airport tax' included in flight prices shown on comparison engines?**
R: Usually yes — EU regulations require that the final price including taxes and charges be shown in search results. But 'optional' charges (baggage, seat selection, priority boarding) are added separately. The advertised base fare and the realistic all-in price for a passenger with a bag can differ by €50–150 per direction on low-cost airlines.

## How to Find Cheap Accommodation in 2026: 12 Strategies That Actually Work

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/cazari/how-to-find-cheap-accommodation
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** cazari
**Publicat:** 2026-07-30
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-30
**Traducere a:** [cum-gasesti-cazare-ieftina](https://plecari.com/ro/cazari/cum-gasesti-cazare-ieftina)

**Descriere:** How to find cheap accommodation: when to book, which platforms to compare, the zone strategy that saves 30–50%, hidden costs to check before confirming, and how to read reviews.

**Rezumat rapid:** The most effective strategies for cheap accommodation: book early with free cancellation and re-book if the price drops; compare at least 3 sources (Booking, the hotel's own website, and one alternative platform); stay in zone 2–3 of the city (30–50% cheaper with identical experience); choose apartments with kitchens for groups or stays over 5 nights; avoid peak season. On a 5-night trip for two people, these adjustments save €100–250 compared to booking impulsively on the first platform that appears.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Is it cheaper to book directly with the hotel or through Booking.com?**
R: It depends. Booking.com charges hotels a 15–25% commission. Many independent hotels pass some of this back to direct bookers as a 5–15% discount on their own website. Large chains (Marriott, Hilton, IHG) typically have identical prices everywhere. The practical rule: always check the hotel's own website after checking Booking — 2 minutes that can save €10–25/night.

**Î: Should I book accommodation early or last-minute?**
R: For popular destinations in peak season (Mediterranean in July–August, ski resorts in February): book early with free cancellation, then set a price alert and rebook if it drops. Last-minute works for off-season travel or less popular destinations where hotels prefer partial revenue to empty rooms. Never wait last-minute for Greece in August or Dubrovnik in July.

**Î: When does an apartment make more sense than a hotel?**
R: For groups of 3 or more (cost splits across everyone), for stays of 5+ nights (kitchen saves €15–30/day on meals), and for families with children (space and flexibility). For 1–2 people on a 2–3 night city break, a budget hotel is typically comparable or cheaper with less logistical complexity.

**Î: What hidden costs should I check before confirming accommodation?**
R: Always check: local tourist tax (€1–10+/person/night — not shown in displayed price on all platforms), resort/city fee (€5–25/night at resort hotels), parking (€10–30/night at central hotels), breakfast if not included (€10–20/person), and Airbnb cleaning fee (€30–80 per stay, not in the per-night price).

**Î: Is Airbnb still worth using in 2026?**
R: For apartments: yes, with caveats. In major European cities, stricter short-term rental regulations have reduced supply and pushed prices up. Booking.com Apartments and Vrbo often list the same properties without the cleaning fee surprise. Always compare the total price (nightly rate × nights + cleaning fee) rather than the per-night headline price.

**Î: What is a good Booking.com score and how reliable are reviews?**
R: 8.0+ is generally reliable; 8.5+ for confidence; 9.0+ is excellent. But always sort by 'Most Recent' — a hotel with an 8.7 overall but recent reviews of 6.0 has degraded since the score was built. Look for specific mentions of cleanliness, noise, Wi-Fi, and whether the location matches what the map shows.

**Î: What is the Booking.com Genius programme?**
R: Genius is Booking.com's free loyalty programme. Level 1 (2 completed bookings): 10% discount at participating properties. Level 2 (5 bookings): 15% discount plus early check-in and late check-out. Levels do not expire. If you book 2+ hotels per year, Genius adds 10–15% savings at no cost.

**Î: Are hostels worth it for adults, not just students?**
R: Private rooms in well-rated social hostels are excellent value at any age: €25–50/night with communal areas (bar, kitchen, organised events) that make solo travel less isolating. Dormitory beds (€8–20/night) are the cheapest accommodation available. Key threshold: 8.5+ on Hostelworld consistently means adequate cleanliness and a reasonable atmosphere.

## How to Install an eSIM on iPhone or Android: Step-by-Step Guide 2026

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/esim-roaming/how-to-install-esim
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** esim-roaming
**Publicat:** 2026-07-29
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-29
**Traducere a:** [cum-instalezi-esim](https://plecari.com/ro/esim-roaming/cum-instalezi-esim)

**Descriere:** Exact steps to install an eSIM on iPhone and Android, which phones support it, common errors and fixes, and how to set up dual SIM so you keep your regular number while using local data.

**Rezumat rapid:** Installing an eSIM takes 2–3 minutes: buy a plan from a provider like Airalo or Saily, receive a QR code by email, go to your phone's SIM or mobile data settings, select 'Add eSIM', scan the QR code, and the profile downloads automatically. Do this at home on a stable Wi-Fi connection before your trip. The eSIM sits dormant until you land and activate it — your regular SIM stays active for calls and SMS the entire time.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Does my phone support eSIM?**
R: iPhone: XS, XR and all newer models (from 2018). iPhone 6, 7, 8, and X do not have eSIM. Samsung: Galaxy S20 and newer, Z Fold/Flip series. Google Pixel: 3 and newer. Quick check: dial *#06# — if an 'EID' code appears in the list, your phone supports eSIM. On iPhone: Settings → General → About → look for 'EID'. On Android: Settings → Connections or Network → if 'Add eSIM' appears, you have support.

**Î: Do I need Wi-Fi to install an eSIM?**
R: Yes. The phone downloads the eSIM profile from the provider's servers, which requires an internet connection. Install at home on your own Wi-Fi before the trip. If you are already abroad without data, you can install via a hotel or café Wi-Fi, but it is much simpler to do it in advance.

**Î: Can the QR code be scanned more than once?**
R: No. Most eSIM QR codes are single-use — once scanned and the profile installed, the code is deactivated. If you scan it and the installation fails (poor Wi-Fi, phone restart mid-process), contact the provider. Most will issue a new code for free for genuine installation failures.

**Î: How do I activate the eSIM when I land?**
R: The eSIM profile is installed but inactive until you turn it on. When you land: go to Settings → Mobile Data (iPhone) or Connections → SIM Manager (Android) → select your eSIM profile → enable it as the data SIM. Also ensure 'Data Roaming' is enabled on the eSIM profile — without this, the eSIM connects to partner networks but no data flows.

**Î: Can I keep my regular number while using an eSIM?**
R: Yes — that is the primary advantage of eSIM. Your physical SIM stays active for calls, SMS, and bank verification codes. The eSIM handles data. Both work simultaneously with dual SIM. Set data to the eSIM, calls and SMS to your physical SIM, and you have the best of both: local data rates and your regular number.

**Î: What if my phone is carrier-locked?**
R: A carrier-locked phone cannot use SIM cards from other operators, including eSIM profiles. eSIM support and being carrier-unlocked are separate requirements — you need both. Contact your carrier to unlock the phone (usually free after the contract period ends). Note: this does not apply to carrier-locked eSIM functionality — if your carrier has locked eSIM access, it needs to be unlocked separately.

**Î: Can I use an eSIM in Turkey?**
R: Yes, but you must buy and install it BEFORE arriving in Turkey. Since 2025, Turkish authorities block access to major eSIM provider websites (Airalo, Saily) from within Turkey. The eSIM profile installed at home works normally once you land in Istanbul or Antalya.

**Î: How long does an eSIM plan last?**
R: Plans are typically sold with a fixed data allowance and a validity period: for example, 5 GB valid for 30 days from activation. The plan expires when you use all the data OR when the validity period ends — whichever comes first. Some providers offer 'top up' options if you run out of data before the period ends.

## Iași 2026: Complete City Break Guide — Palace of Culture, Eminescu and Saint Parascheva

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/iasi-complete-guide
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-08-08
**Actualizat:** 2026-08-08
**Traducere a:** [iasi-ghid-complet](https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/iasi-ghid-complet)

**Descriere:** Complete Iași guide: Palace of Culture (4 museums in one neo-Gothic building), Three Hierarchs Church, Metropolitan Cathedral with Saint Parascheva's relics, Copou Park with Eminescu's linden tree...

**Rezumat rapid:** Iași is the historic capital of Moldova and Romania's most important cultural and spiritual centre in the east — with the Palace of Culture (an impressive neo-Gothic building with 4 museums), the Three Hierarchs Church (stone carvings unrivalled in Romania), the Metropolitan Cathedral with Saint Parascheva's relics, Copou Park with Mihai Eminescu's linden tree and a vibrant university life with 60,000+ students. It was Moldova's first capital and the place where modern Romanian cultural identity was forged.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How do I get from Bucharest to Iași?**
R: Direct flight: Blue Air, Wizz Air operate OTP → IAS. Duration: ~1 hour. Prices: 50–120 EUR return. By train: InterCity/InterRegio Bucharest Nord → Iași, ~4–5 hours, 80–130 RON. By car: ~380 km on A2 + DN28, ~4.5 hours. Iași Airport (IAS) is 8 km from the centre — Bolt: 20–35 RON, taxi: 30–50 RON.

**Î: What is the Palace of Culture and how many museums does it have?**
R: The Palace of Culture is Iași's symbol — a spectacular neo-Gothic building constructed between 1906 and 1925 on the site of Stefan the Great's former princely court. It houses 4 museums: the Art Museum (European and Romanian paintings), the Museum of Moldovan History, the Polytechnic Museum and the Ethnographic Museum. Combined ticket: ~30–50 RON. The palace's clock tower is visible from across the central area.

**Î: Who is Saint Parascheva and why is she important in Iași?**
R: Saint Parascheva (Saint Cuvioasa Parascheva) is the patron saint of Moldova. Her relics are kept at Iași's Metropolitan Cathedral and represent one of Orthodoxy's most important relics. On 14 October (her feast day), hundreds of thousands of pilgrims come to Iași from across Romania and the diaspora — Romania's largest pilgrimage, with 1+ million faithful at peak days.

**Î: What is the connection between Iași and Mihai Eminescu?**
R: Mihai Eminescu, Romania's greatest poet, lived and created in Iași for much of his life. Copou Park houses the famous 'Eminescu's linden tree' — an ancient linden under whose shade the poet is said to have rested and found inspiration. The Junimea literary society, of which Eminescu was a member and which published his first poems, also operated in Iași.

**Î: How much does a 2–3 day city break in Iași cost?**
R: Iași is one of Romania's most affordable destinations: restaurant lunch 30–60 RON, dinner 50–100 RON per person, mid-range accommodation 150–280 RON per night. A 3-day/2-night city break costs 120–250 EUR per person including flights.

**Î: The Saint Parascheva pilgrimage — is 14 October worth going?**
R: Depends what you're looking for. 14 October in Iași is a unique experience in Romania — hundreds of thousands of pilgrims, tents along the boulevard, solemn procession. If you're interested in Orthodox culture and mass social phenomena, absolutely worth it. If you want to visit peacefully, avoid this period — accommodation sells out, traffic is chaotic.

**Î: What are the Bukovina Monasteries and how do I visit them from Iași?**
R: The Bukovina Monasteries (Voroneț, Sucevița, Moldovița, Humor) are UNESCO sites with unique polychrome exterior frescoes — painted in the 15th–16th centuries, having survived 500 years of weather. They are 130–170 km from Iași (1.5–2 hours). You can do a day trip from Iași by car or guided tour.

**Î: What is the best time to visit Iași?**
R: May–June: ideal — Copou Park in bloom, pleasant temperatures, active university life. September: International Theatre Festival (FIT). October: Saint Parascheva pilgrimage (if interested). Winter: cold (-10°C possible) but intense cultural vibes.

## Car Rental in Greece 2026: Documents, Prices, Rules and Island-by-Island Guide

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/inchirieri-auto/inchiriere-masina-grecia-2026
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** inchirieri-auto
**Publicat:** 2026-07-25
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-25

**Descriere:** Everything you need to know before renting a car in Greece: required documents, 2026 traffic law changes, real prices by season, which islands need a car and which traps to avoid.

**Rezumat rapid:** EU citizens can rent a car in Greece with their EU driving licence — no international permit required. Minimum age is 21, with a young driver surcharge for under-25s. A credit card is required for the deposit. Key 2026 change: speed limits in urban areas have dropped to 30 km/h with stricter enforcement and higher fines. On large islands (Crete, Rhodes), a rental car is practically essential to reach the best beaches and villages.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Do I need an international driving permit for Greece?**
R: No, if you hold an EU driving licence. EU licences are recognised directly across all member states. An international driving permit is only required for drivers from outside the EU (USA, UK, Australia, etc.) or when the licence is not written in Latin characters.

**Î: What credit cards do Greek rental companies accept?**
R: Typically Visa or Mastercard credit cards in the driver's name, used for the security deposit hold. Debit cards are accepted less frequently and with additional conditions. Revolut can work if you have the credit card version (not prepaid or debit). Always verify before booking — especially with small local companies on smaller islands, which sometimes insist on a traditional credit card.

**Î: Should I bring my own car or rent locally?**
R: Depends on the destination. For Halkidiki or Thassos (reachable by road), your own car works well. For Crete, Rhodes, Corfu, or Zakynthos (reached by flight), rent locally — it is far cheaper and simpler than paying €100–200 each way to ship your car on a ferry.

**Î: What is the average car rental price in Greece in peak season?**
R: A small hatchback (Hyundai i10, VW Polo) costs €35–70/day in July–August on the islands. Prices drop 20–30% in May–June and September. Booking 4–6 weeks ahead typically saves 25–40% compared to walk-up prices at the island airport.

**Î: What happens if I scratch the car?**
R: If CDW (Collision Damage Waiver) is included, the company covers the damage minus the excess (which can be €500–1,500). If you have not reduced the excess to zero, you pay that amount. Always photograph the car thoroughly at collection — every existing scratch, on all four sides, roof included — and email the photos to yourself immediately as timestamped proof.

**Î: Can I drive between Greek islands with a rental car?**
R: No. Rental contracts in Greece are almost always restricted to the island or region where you collected the car. Taking the vehicle on a ferry to another island is specifically prohibited by most rental agreements. If you want to visit multiple islands, you return the car, take a ferry or flight, and rent again at the next island.

**Î: Is a GPS or a phone sufficient for navigation in Greece?**
R: Your phone with Google Maps is completely sufficient. Download the offline map for the island before departure. The counter GPS (€8–15/day) is an unnecessary expense. Road signs in Greece are bilingual (Greek and Latin alphabet) on main roads, so navigation is manageable even without a device — but GPS helps on the narrow backroads of Crete or Corfu.

## Interrail 2026: The Complete Guide to Train Travel Across Europe

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/zboruri/interrail-europe-2026-complete-guide
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** zboruri
**Publicat:** 2026-07-14
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-14

**Descriere:** Everything you need to know about Interrail in 2026. Pass prices, best routes, night trains, seat reservations, and whether a rail pass actually saves you money.

**Rezumat rapid:** An Interrail Global Pass in 2026 starts at €212 (youth, 4 days/1 month) or €330 (adult). A full month of unlimited travel: €522 adults. The pass covers 33 European countries. Night trains (Nightjet: Vienna-Rome, Munich-Amsterdam) save hotel nights. Key caveat: high-speed trains (TGV, Frecciarossa, AVE) require paid seat reservations (€10-34 per segment) on top of the pass. Best value: 5+ cities in 2-4 weeks, youth pass, shoulder season.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How much does an Interrail Global Pass cost in 2026?**
R: 2nd class prices — Youth (12-27): 4 days/1 month = €212, 7 days = €268, 1 month continuous = €522. Adult (28-59): 4 days = €330, 7 days = €414, 1 month = €713. Senior (60+): ~10% discount. Children under 12: FREE with a paying adult (max 2 children).

**Î: Do I need seat reservations with Interrail?**
R: Depends on the train. Regional trains (Germany, Austria, Czech Republic, Switzerland): NO, just board. High-speed trains: YES, mandatory — TGV France (€10-20), Frecciarossa Italy (€13), AVE Spain, Eurostar (€34). Night trains (Nightjet): YES — seats from €14, couchettes from €34. Book at interrail.eu or at the station.

**Î: Is Interrail cheaper than flying?**
R: For 2-3 fixed cities: usually not — budget flights are cheaper. For 5+ cities with flexibility: Interrail wins, especially for under-27s (€212 for 4 travel days = ~€53/day). Plus: no baggage fees, you arrive in city centres (not airports 30-80 km away), and the scenery is spectacular.

**Î: Can I use Interrail on night trains?**
R: Yes, but you must pay a compulsory berth or seat reservation. Nightjet (ÖBB) is the main operator: Vienna-Rome, Vienna-Venice, Munich-Amsterdam, Zurich-Hamburg, Vienna-Paris. Reservations: seats from ~€14, couchettes from ~€34, private sleepers higher. Book the moment reservations open (typically 3-6 months ahead) — cheap berths sell out in days on popular routes.

## Is Romania Expensive? Real Travel Costs in 2026

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/city-breaks/is-romania-expensive
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** city-breaks
**Publicat:** 2026-07-09
**Traducere a:** [romania-scumpa-ghid](https://plecari.com/ro/city-breaks/romania-scumpa-ghid)

**Descriere:** An honest cost breakdown for visiting Romania in 2026 — meals, hotels, transport, and activities with actual prices from someone who lives here.

**Rezumat rapid:** Romania is one of the most affordable countries in the EU. A comfortable mid-range day in Bucharest costs around €60–80 per person (hotel, meals, transport, one activity). Budget travelers can manage on €30–40/day. Outside the capital, costs drop further — a pension in Transylvania with breakfast runs €25–40 per night for a double room.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How much does a meal cost in Romania?**
R: A full meal at a local restaurant costs €6–10. A coffee is €1.50–2.50. A three-course dinner at a mid-range restaurant runs €15–25 per person. Fast food is €4–6. Street food like covrigi (pretzels) costs under €1.

**Î: Is Bucharest cheaper than other European capitals?**
R: Significantly. Bucharest is roughly 40–50% cheaper than Prague, 50–60% cheaper than Vienna, and about half the cost of Barcelona or Rome for equivalent experiences. Only Sofia and Belgrade are comparably cheap among European capitals.

**Î: Do I need cash or can I pay by card?**
R: Card payments are widely accepted in cities — restaurants, supermarkets, taxis, and most attractions take Visa and Mastercard. In rural areas and small villages, carry some cash (Romanian leu, RON). ATMs are everywhere in cities.

**Î: How much should I budget per day in Romania?**
R: Budget: €30–40/day (hostel, local food, public transport). Mid-range: €60–80/day (3-star hotel, restaurants, occasional taxi). Comfort: €100–150/day (4-star hotel, car rental, guided tours). These are per-person estimates.

**Î: Is it cheaper to visit Romania in winter?**
R: Accommodation outside ski resorts is cheaper in the off-season (November–March, excluding Christmas/New Year). However, Romania's best value is actually in spring (April–June) and early autumn (September–October) — pleasant weather, fewer tourists, and no peak-season surcharges.

**Î: How much does a rental car cost in Romania?**
R: A compact car rents for €20–35 per day including basic insurance. Fuel costs around €1.50–1.70 per liter. Renting a car is the best way to explore Transylvania, Maramureș, and the Danube Delta at your own pace.

## Istanbul City Break 2026: 3-Day Itinerary, Real Costs and Everything You Need to Know

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/city-breaks/istanbul-city-break-guide
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** city-breaks
**Publicat:** 2026-07-29
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-29
**Traducere a:** [istanbul-city-break-ghid](https://plecari.com/ro/city-breaks/istanbul-city-break-ghid)

**Descriere:** Complete Istanbul city break guide for 2026. Hagia Sophia, Grand Bazaar, Bosphorus cruise, Turkish hammam, best neighbourhoods, real budget, and the eSIM you must buy before you fly.

**Rezumat rapid:** A 3-night Istanbul city break costs €250–550 per person all-in (flight + hotel + food + sites). Istanbul is one of Europe's most affordable city break destinations: a full meal costs €5–10, a Bosphorus ferry €1–2, and most major mosques are free. Essential to know before travelling: Turkey is not in the EU, so roaming applies — buy an eSIM before you fly (provider websites are blocked inside Turkey since 2025). Travel insurance is mandatory — the EHIC does not work in Turkey.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How many days do you need in Istanbul?**
R: 3 days covers the essentials: Day 1 for Sultanahmet (Hagia Sophia, Blue Mosque, Topkapi Palace, Basilica Cistern), Day 2 for the Grand Bazaar, Galata district and Bosphorus, Day 3 for Kadıköy on the Asian side and a Turkish hammam. 4–5 days lets you add the Prince's Islands, Balat neighbourhood, and more food exploration. Even 2 full days produces a rewarding trip if you prioritise ruthlessly.

**Î: Is Istanbul safe for tourists in 2026?**
R: Yes. Istanbul is a safe city for tourists. Standard urban precautions apply: watch for pickpockets at the Grand Bazaar and on the T1 tram, use Bolt or Uber rather than unlicensed taxis, and be wary of unsolicited invitations to 'my friend's bar' (a well-documented scam where the bill arrives at €100–200+). The tourist police in Sultanahmet are responsive and helpful.

**Î: Do I need a visa for Istanbul?**
R: Most Western nationalities (UK, US, Canada, Australia, most EU countries) can enter Turkey without a visa for up to 90 days — but check your specific nationality at the Turkish Ministry of Foreign Affairs website, as requirements vary. Your passport must be valid for at least 6 months from your entry date. National ID cards are NOT accepted in Turkey.

**Î: Do I need an eSIM for Istanbul?**
R: Yes, strongly recommended — and buy it before you fly. Turkey is not in the EU, so free roaming does not apply. Carrier roaming costs €10–15/GB. A 5 GB Turkey eSIM costs approximately $10–15 on Airalo. Critical: since 2025, Turkish authorities block access to eSIM provider websites from within Turkey. You cannot purchase after arrival — the websites simply do not load.

**Î: What is the Museum Pass Istanbul and is it worth it?**
R: The Museum Pass Istanbul (approximately €55–65 for 5 days) covers 12 major sites including Topkapi Palace, Hagia Sophia Museum section, Chora Church, Dolmabahçe Palace, and several others. If you plan to visit Topkapi (€20) + Hagia Sophia Museum (entry charges for non-prayer access) + Dolmabahçe (€25+), the pass pays for itself. Valid for 5 consecutive days.

**Î: What currency should I use in Istanbul?**
R: Turkish lira (TRY). In tourist areas and large restaurants, euros and US dollars are sometimes accepted but at poor rates. Withdraw TRY from ATMs (not at the airport — rates are poor there). Use Revolut or Wise for card payments to avoid foreign transaction fees. Always refuse DCC (Dynamic Currency Conversion) — choose Turkish lira at every terminal. For the full payment guide: how to pay abroad without fees.

**Î: What is a Turkish hammam and which one should I choose?**
R: A Turkish hammam (bath house) involves a steam room, exfoliating scrub (kese), and soap massage. The experience typically takes 45–90 minutes. For a first visit: Çemberlitaş Hamamı (€40–80, open since 1584, central location), Süleymaniye Hamamı (€30–50, more local atmosphere), or Kılıç Ali Paşa Hamamı (€80–120, the most beautifully restored). Book online to guarantee a slot.

## Karlovy Vary 2026: The Complete City Break Guide to Europe's Most Beautiful Spa Town

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/karlovy-vary-complete-guide
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-08-07
**Actualizat:** 2026-08-07
**Traducere a:** [karlovy-vary-ghid-complet](https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/karlovy-vary-ghid-complet)

**Descriere:** Everything you need to know about Karlovy Vary: thermal springs, colonnades, Becherovka, real prices, accommodation and how to get there from Bucharest. UNESCO since 2021.

**Rezumat rapid:** Karlovy Vary is Central Europe's most famous spa resort town, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2021. Also known as Carlsbad, it offers 15 mineral thermal springs, spectacular Belle Époque architecture, Becherovka — the local liqueur dubbed 'the 13th spring' — and a unique atmosphere along the Teplá River. Distance from Prague: 120 km, approximately 1.5 hours by car or coach.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How do I get from Bucharest to Karlovy Vary?**
R: The fastest option is flying Bucharest (OTP) → Prague (PRG), then taking a coach or driving 1.5 hours to Karlovy Vary. There are no direct flights to Karlovy Vary Airport (KLV). Bucharest–Prague tickets start from 50–120 EUR return if booked 4–6 weeks in advance.

**Î: How much does a 3-day city break in Karlovy Vary cost?**
R: A 3-day/2-night city break costs 300–500 EUR per person (mid-range), including flights, accommodation and meals. The resort is more affordable than Prague: a restaurant lunch costs 10–20 EUR, a central hotel room starts from 60–80 EUR per night, and basic spa treatments start from 40–80 EUR per session.

**Î: What are the colonnades in Karlovy Vary?**
R: The colonnades are elegant covered galleries, built in neo-baroque and Art Nouveau styles, housing the thermal springs. There are 5 main colonnades: Mill Colonnade (the largest), Market Colonnade, Hot Spring Colonnade, Garden Colonnade and Castle Colonnade. Access to the springs is free — you only need a special spa cup.

**Î: What do the thermal springs in Karlovy Vary taste like? Do I have to drink them?**
R: The springs have a strong sulphurous and mineral flavour — salty, slightly eggy, and warmer than you'd expect. Drinking them is not mandatory, but it's part of the authentic experience. The Vřídlo spring (the main geyser) is 72°C and rises 12 metres high — you can watch it, not drink it. The easiest springs to drink from are no. 3 or no. 5.

**Î: What is Becherovka and where can I buy it?**
R: Becherovka is an herbal liqueur (38% ABV), created in 1807 by Jan Becher in Karlovy Vary. It is nicknamed locally 'the 13th spring'. You can buy it at any supermarket or souvenir shop, but the Jan Becher Museum in the centre is worth visiting (entry ~7 EUR). A 0.5-litre bottle costs 10–15 EUR.

**Î: Is it worth visiting Loket Castle on a day trip?**
R: Absolutely. Loket is just 12 km from Karlovy Vary and can easily be visited in half a day. It's a medieval castle on a granite rock surrounded by the Ohře River — one of the most photogenic spots in the Czech Republic and a filming location for James Bond Casino Royale (2006). The bus costs ~2 EUR, castle entry ~8 EUR.

**Î: What is the best time to visit Karlovy Vary?**
R: May–June and September–October are the ideal periods: pleasant temperatures (15–22°C), fewer tourists than in July, and prices 20–30% lower. Avoid the first week of July — the Karlovy Vary International Film Festival takes place and accommodation prices skyrocket. Winter has its own charm, but some colonnades have reduced hours.

**Î: Do I need a visa for the Czech Republic as a Romanian citizen?**
R: No. The Czech Republic is part of the European Union and the Schengen Area. As a Romanian citizen with a valid ID card or passport, you can enter freely. The currency is the Czech Crown (CZK) — 1 EUR ≈ 25 CZK in 2026. Bank cards are accepted almost everywhere.

## Kotor 2026: The Complete City Break Guide to Montenegro's UNESCO Jewel

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/kotor-complete-guide
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-08-07
**Actualizat:** 2026-08-07
**Traducere a:** [kotor-ghid-complet](https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/kotor-ghid-complet)

**Descriere:** Complete Kotor guide: medieval Old Town, 1,350-step fortress walls, Bay of Kotor, Our Lady of the Rocks and baroque Perast. Real prices, the cruise ship warning and when to go for peace and quiet.

**Rezumat rapid:** Kotor is the best-preserved medieval town on the Adriatic — a labyrinth of narrow streets enclosed by fortress walls that climb the rock face behind the city, all sheltered within the deepest bay in the Mediterranean. UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1979. Direct access from Romania: flight OTP → Tivat (TIV) with Wizz Air, 1h30, or flight to Dubrovnik and a 2-hour transfer through Montenegro.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How do I get from Bucharest to Kotor?**
R: The most direct option: flight OTP → Tivat (TIV) with Wizz Air (seasonal, May–September), then 30 minutes by taxi or bus to Kotor. Alternative: flight OTP → Dubrovnik (DBV) with Wizz Air or Ryanair (year-round), then 2 hours by bus or 1.5 hours by car through Montenegro. Third option: flight to Belgrade + overnight bus Belgrade–Kotor (7–8 hours, 20–30 EUR).

**Î: How much does it cost to climb Kotor's City Walls?**
R: The standard ticket for the City Walls and San Giovanni Fortress is 8–10 EUR in 2026. There's a trick: if you leave before 08:00, you can climb for free — the ticket booths aren't open and there's no barrier. The climb has 1,350 steps and takes 45–90 minutes depending on pace and photo stops.

**Î: What currency does Montenegro use?**
R: Montenegro uses the euro (EUR) despite not being an EU member. No currency exchange needed. Cards are accepted at hotels and larger restaurants, but many small local places and stalls are cash-only.

**Î: When is the best time to visit Kotor?**
R: May–June and September–October are the ideal periods: pleasant temperatures (20–28°C), warm water for swimming, prices 20–30% lower than July–August and, most importantly, no cruise ships overwhelming the town. July–August: hot (35°C+), crowded, 5–7 ships per day each with 2,000–4,000 passengers.

**Î: What's the difference between Kotor and Perast, and is Perast worth visiting?**
R: Perast is a tiny baroque village 12 km from Kotor, with restored Venetian palaces, a few restaurants and access to the boat for Our Lady of the Rocks island church. It's completely different from Kotor — quieter, more elegant, more photogenic at sunset. Worth at least a half-day. Bus Kotor–Perast: 1.50 EUR, 20 minutes.

**Î: What is Our Lady of the Rocks?**
R: Our Lady of the Rocks (Gospa od Škrpjela) is an artificial island in the middle of the Bay of Kotor, near Perast, which local sailors built over several centuries by repeatedly sinking boats and stones. On the island stands a church from 1630 with an impressive collection of votive paintings. Boat from Perast to the island: 5–6 EUR.

**Î: The cats of Kotor — myth or reality?**
R: Absolute reality. Kotor is one of the world's most famous cat cities — dozens of semi-wild cats live in the Old Town, fed by locals. There is even a Cat Museum in the town centre. Cats are considered Kotor's symbol — defenders of the city in local legends.

**Î: Can I visit Kotor as a day trip from Dubrovnik?**
R: Yes, it's one of the most popular day trips from Dubrovnik. Distance: approximately 90 km (2 hours by car or 2.5 hours by bus). Bus Dubrovnik–Kotor: 10–15 EUR return. In one day you can see the Old Town, partly climb the walls and visit Perast. But if you want to fully climb San Giovanni Fortress and do the boat tour, you need at least 2 nights in Kotor.

## Krakow 2026: The Complete City Break Guide to Poland's Former Royal Capital

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/krakow-complete-guide
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-08-08
**Actualizat:** 2026-08-08
**Traducere a:** [cracovia-ghid-complet](https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/cracovia-ghid-complet)

**Descriere:** Complete Krakow guide: medieval Main Square, Wawel Castle, Kazimierz Jewish quarter, Auschwitz-Birkenau and Wieliczka Salt Mine. Polish zloty, real prices and why Krakow is Central Europe's best va...

**Rezumat rapid:** Krakow (Kraków) is Poland's former royal capital and the best-preserved medieval centre in Central Europe — a city with a 40,000 m² Main Square, a royal castle above the Vistula, an authentic Jewish quarter and the world's most important Holocaust memorial site 70 km away. It is also one of Europe's most affordable destinations: average budget 40–60 EUR/day. Direct flights from Bucharest from 35 EUR.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How do I get from Bucharest to Krakow?**
R: Wizz Air and Ryanair operate direct flights Bucharest (OTP) → Krakow (KRK). Duration: ~2 hours. Prices: 35–100 EUR return with 3–6 weeks' advance booking. The airport is 15 km from the centre — bus 292 takes 40 minutes (5 PLN/1.15 EUR), taxi/Bolt 20 minutes (40–60 PLN/9–14 EUR).

**Î: What currency does Poland use? Can I pay in euros?**
R: Poland uses the Polish Złoty (PLN). 1 EUR = 4.33 PLN in 2026. Euros are rarely accepted and at an unfavourable rate. Always pay in PLN. Best exchange rate: PKO BP, Pekao or ING ATMs. Avoid Euronet (high fees) and airport exchange.

**Î: Do I need to book Auschwitz tickets in advance?**
R: Yes — advance booking is essential. Auschwitz-Birkenau requires mandatory booking for guided tours. Tickets sell out 4–6 weeks ahead in peak season. The guided tour is mandatory (unguided entry is only available early morning). Book via GetYourGuide or directly on the official Auschwitz memorial website.

**Î: How much does a 3-day city break in Krakow cost?**
R: A 3-day/2-night city break costs 200–350 EUR per person (mid-range), including flights, accommodation, food and the Auschwitz tour. Krakow is one of Europe's most affordable cultural capitals: pierogi 3–5 EUR a portion, local beer 1 EUR, full lunch 5–10 EUR, mid-range accommodation 35–60 EUR per night.

**Î: What is Kazimierz and is it worth visiting?**
R: Kazimierz is Krakow's former Jewish quarter, separated from the Old Town by the Wisła River. It was the centre of Polish Jewish life until the Holocaust, with 7 functioning synagogues and a distinct culture. Today it is Krakow's most vibrant neighbourhood — restaurants, bars, art galleries, and Plac Nowy with zapiekanki (baguette pizza) at 2–4 EUR.

**Î: Is the Wieliczka Salt Mine worth it?**
R: Yes — Wieliczka is 15 km from Krakow, a UNESCO site with 300 km of underground galleries sculpted in salt, with chapels, underground lakes and statues. Guided tour ticket: ~30 EUR. Visit duration: 2–2.5 hours. It's the main alternative to Auschwitz if you want a lighter day emotionally.

**Î: What is the best time to visit Krakow?**
R: May–June and September–October: pleasant temperatures (14–22°C), fewer tourists than summer, prices 20–30% lower. July–August: lively and warm, but crowded. December: Christmas markets on the Main Square and in Kazimierz — magical atmosphere with seasonal prices.

**Î: Is Krakow safe for tourists?**
R: Yes, Krakow is a safe city. The Old Town and Kazimierz are safe day and night. Watch out for: taxis without meters (use Bolt), street currency exchange scams (counterfeit notes given for EUR/USD) and inflated prices at restaurants directly on the Main Square.
