## How to Pay Abroad Without Fees in 2026: Revolut, Wise, Cash and the DCC Trap

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/city-breaks/pay-abroad-no-fees
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** city-breaks
**Publicat:** 2026-07-29
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-29
**Traducere a:** [cum-platesti-strainatate-fara-comisioane](https://plecari.com/ro/city-breaks/cum-platesti-strainatate-fara-comisioane)

**Descriere:** The best payment methods for travel: when to use Revolut, when to use cash, how to avoid Dynamic Currency Conversion, and which ATMs to use to avoid skimming.

**Rezumat rapid:** The best setup for paying abroad: Revolut or Wise as your primary card (zero foreign exchange fees, interbank rate), your regular bank card as a backup, and €100–200 in local cash for markets, small restaurants and taxis. Always refuse Dynamic Currency Conversion (DCC) — when an ATM or card terminal offers to charge you 'in your home currency,' always choose local currency instead. DCC costs 3–8% more than your card's conversion rate. On a €1,000 holiday spend, that is €30–80 wasted.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Is Revolut safe to use abroad?**
R: Yes. Revolut is regulated as an electronic money institution in the EU and UK. For travel spending, it is one of the best tools available — interbank rate conversion with no markup, instant notifications, instant card freeze if lost, and spending analytics. Be aware of the free plan's limits: free ATM withdrawals up to €200/month (2% fee after that), and a small weekend markup on some currencies.

**Î: What is Dynamic Currency Conversion (DCC) and why should I always refuse it?**
R: DCC occurs when a card terminal or ATM offers to convert your transaction into your home currency — 'so you know exactly what you're paying.' It sounds helpful but the exchange rate applied is 3–8% worse than your card's rate. Always choose 'pay in local currency' regardless of what the terminal says. Your card (especially Revolut or Wise) does the conversion at a far better rate.

**Î: How much cash should I take on holiday?**
R: For EU destinations (France, Spain, Italy, Greece): €100–150 for a week is sufficient if you pay by card at restaurants and hotels. For non-EU destinations with more cash-based economies (Turkey, Morocco, Southeast Asia): €200–400 equivalent in local currency. Always withdraw from local ATMs rather than exchanging at the airport — airport exchange rates are consistently 8–12% worse than ATM rates.

**Î: Which ATMs are safe to use abroad?**
R: ATMs located inside bank branches are the safest — card skimming devices are almost never fitted on ATMs inside a bank. Avoid standalone ATMs on tourist streets, in bars, or near major attractions. Always cover the keypad with your hand when entering your PIN. If the card slot feels loose or has anything attached over it, use a different machine.

**Î: Can I use my regular bank card abroad?**
R: Yes, your Visa or Mastercard bank card works in virtually every country. The cost: typically 1–3% foreign transaction fee plus a currency conversion fee of 1–2%, charged by your bank. On a €1,500 holiday, that adds €30–75 in fees. Revolut or Wise costs €0–5 for the same spending. The bank card is best kept as a backup rather than a primary payment method.

**Î: Does contactless payment work everywhere in Europe?**
R: Almost everywhere in Western and Northern Europe (UK, France, Germany, Netherlands, Scandinavia), contactless is universal. In Southern and Eastern Europe, smaller restaurants, markets, and local taxis may be cash-only. In Turkey, major tourist areas accept cards widely; bazaars and local transport are often cash. Keep €50–100 local currency for these situations.

**Î: What is the best way to get foreign currency before travelling?**
R: Do not exchange money before you travel — airport exchange bureaux at your departure airport and bank branches at home offer poor rates. The best rates consistently come from withdrawing local currency at ATMs at your destination, using Revolut or Wise (which hold or convert at interbank rates). If you must have cash before departure, order it online through a specialist currency provider (Wise, moneycorp) rather than walking into a bank or airport counter.

**Î: What EU261 compensation can I claim on flights from Bucharest?**

This applies to Wizz Air, Ryanair, and all carriers operating from Romanian airports.

**Î: Is it worth using Wizz Discount Club?**

## Portugal Holiday Guide 2026: Lisbon, Porto and the Algarve — Complete with Real Costs

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/city-breaks/portugal-holiday-guide-2026
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** city-breaks
**Publicat:** 2026-07-30
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-30
**Traducere a:** [vacanta-portugalia-2026-lisabona-porto-algarve](https://plecari.com/ro/city-breaks/vacanta-portugalia-2026-lisabona-porto-algarve)

**Descriere:** Portugal holiday guide 2026: Lisbon, Porto and the Algarve. Real budgets, a 10-day itinerary, best beaches, hidden sea caves and what nobody tells you before you go.

**Rezumat rapid:** Portugal is the best value destination in Western Europe in 2026. Daily budget: €55–80 (versus €90–120 for equivalent experiences in Spain or Italy). Lisbon: tram 28 through historic neighbourhoods, pastéis de nata at €1.20, Alfama and free viewpoints, Sintra 40 minutes away by train. Porto: Port wine cellars with tasting from €10, UNESCO Ribeira waterfront, Francesinha, the best grilled fish in Europe. The Algarve: golden limestone cliffs, Benagil Sea Cave, Praia da Marinha, Ponta da Piedade. Flights from most of Europe from €60–120. A rental car is essential for the Algarve.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How many days do you need in Portugal?**
R: Minimum 5 days for Lisbon + Sintra + Porto. Ideally 10 days for the full experience: 3 days Lisbon + 1 day Sintra + 3 days Porto + 3 days Algarve. For a single long weekend: choose Lisbon OR Porto — not both in 3 days, the rush diminishes the experience of both.

**Î: Is Lisbon or Porto better?**
R: Lisbon: larger, more cosmopolitan, beach access 30 minutes by train (Cascais), more intense nightlife. Porto: smaller, more authentic, 20–30% cheaper, better food, Port wine cellars with Douro river views. If you can: do both — the high-speed train takes 2h30 and costs €25.

**Î: Is Portugal cheaper than Spain?**
R: Yes, significantly — especially Porto versus Barcelona or Madrid. Coffee: €0.80–1.20 (vs €2–3 in Spain). Full meal: €8–14 (vs €12–18). 3-star hotel: €50–90/night (vs €80–130). Daily budget in Porto: €45–65 vs €70–100 in Barcelona.

**Î: When is the best time to visit Portugal?**
R: May–June and September–October: excellent weather (22–28°C), minimal queues, reasonable prices. July–August: hot (28–35°C in the Algarve), crowded and slightly more expensive — but still below other Mediterranean destinations. Winter: Lisbon and Porto are pleasant (15–18°C), the Algarve becomes quiet and very affordable.

**Î: Do you need a rental car in Portugal?**
R: Depends on your itinerary. Lisbon: no — metro, tram and walking cover everything. Porto: no — metro and walking. Sintra: no — train from Rossio station (€4.70, 40 minutes). The Algarve: absolutely yes. The beaches are spread along 150 km of coastline with minimal public transport between them.

**Î: Is Portugal safe for tourists?**
R: Portugal consistently ranks in the top 5 safest countries in the world (Global Peace Index). The main risk: pickpocketing on tram 28 and in crowded areas of Alfama. Use a crossbody bag, keep your phone in a front pocket. Otherwise: relaxed, welcoming, no significant issues.

**Î: What should you eat in Portugal?**
R: Pastéis de nata (€1.20 at Pastéis de Belém or Manteigaria), Francesinha in Porto (beer sauce, melted cheese, layers of meat — €8–10), grilled fish at Matosinhos (€12–18), bacalhau à Brás (salt cod with eggs and crispy potatoes — €8–12), ginjinha cherry liqueur served in a chocolate cup (€1.50 at Rossio Square stands).

**Î: Do I need an eSIM or special insurance for Portugal?**
R: Portugal is in the EU — free roaming applies with any EU mobile plan, and the EHIC covers emergency treatment at public hospitals. No eSIM needed. A full travel insurance policy (€15/week) adds repatriation, cancellation and baggage cover — recommended but not as critical as for non-EU destinations like Turkey or the UK.

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/riga-complete-guide

**Publicat:** 2026-08-07

**Rezumat rapid:** Riga is the capital of Latvia and the largest city in the Baltics, home to the world's densest Art Nouveau district — over 800 buildings — and a medieval UNESCO Old Town. It is one of Europe's most affordable capitals: average mid-range budget 60–80 EUR/day. Direct flights from Bucharest (Wizz Air/Ryanair) from 40–90 EUR return.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How do I get from Bucharest to Riga?**
R: Direct flights operate from Bucharest (OTP) to Riga (RIX) with Wizz Air and Ryanair. Flight time: approximately 2h15. Prices: 40–100 EUR return if booked 3–6 weeks in advance. Riga Airport is 13 km from the centre — bus no. 22 takes 30 minutes for 1.50 EUR.

**Î: What currency does Latvia use? Is it in the Eurozone?**
R: Yes, Latvia adopted the euro in 2014. You pay in EUR just like any other Eurozone country. Bank cards are accepted almost everywhere, including markets and public transport with the Rīgas Satiksme card.

**Î: What is Black Balsam and is it worth trying?**
R: Riga Black Balsam (Rīgas Melnais Balzāms) is a black herbal liqueur made from 24 plants and roots, at 45% ABV. It has an intense, bittersweet taste with notes of mint and wormwood. Traditionally drunk in coffee (Balsam Coffee) or mixed with blackcurrant juice to soften the intensity. A 0.5-litre bottle costs 8–12 EUR at a supermarket.

**Î: How safe is Riga for tourists?**
R: Riga is generally safe. The Old Town and Art Nouveau district are safe day and night. Watch out for: the bar scam in the Old Town (friendly locals invite you for a drink, then present a bill for hundreds of euros), unmarked taxis at the airport (use Bolt), and pickpockets in crowded areas. Avoid peripheral neighbourhoods at night.

**Î: How much does a 3-day city break in Riga cost?**
R: A 3-day/2-night city break costs 250–400 EUR per person (mid-range), including flights, accommodation and meals. Riga is among Europe's most affordable capitals: a restaurant lunch 10–15 EUR, local beer 2–4 EUR, public transport 1.50 EUR per journey. Mid-range accommodation starts from 50–80 EUR per night.

**Î: Is the excursion to Rundale Palace worth it?**
R: Absolutely — Rundale is the most impressive Baroque palace in the Baltic states, nicknamed 'the Versailles of Latvia', 80 km south of Riga. Built between 1736–1768 to plans by architect Bartolomeo Rastrelli (who also designed the Winter Palace in St Petersburg). Entry costs 10–14 EUR, guided minibus tour from Riga ~35–50 EUR.

**Î: What is the best time to visit Riga?**
R: June–August: very long days (light until 10:30 PM), active terraces, festivals. May and September: pleasant temperatures, fewer tourists, prices 20–30% lower. December: renowned Christmas markets, magical atmosphere but cold. Avoid January–February: extreme cold, some attractions have reduced hours.

**Î: Are there direct flights from Bucharest to Riga?**
R: Yes. Wizz Air operates direct flights OTP–RIX several times a week. Ryanair also in season. Prices start from 40 EUR return on offer, up to 120–150 EUR at peak season. Flight time: 2h10–2h20.

## Germany's Romantic Road: Complete 2026 Guide — Castles, Mad King Ludwig & Medieval Towns

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/romantic-road-germany-castles-ludwig
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-08-06
**Actualizat:** 2026-08-06
**Traducere a:** [drumul-romantic-germania-castele-ludwig](https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/drumul-romantic-germania-castele-ludwig)

**Descriere:** Guide to Germany's Romantic Road — from Würzburg to Neuschwanstein. King Ludwig II's castles (UNESCO 2025), Rothenburg ob der Tauber, Harburg, real 2026 prices, 1–7 day itineraries.

**Rezumat rapid:** Germany's Romantic Road (Romantische Straße) runs 460 km from Würzburg to Füssen and is Germany's most popular holiday route. King Ludwig II's castles — Neuschwanstein (€21 + €2.50 booking fee, UNESCO since 2025), Hohenschwangau (€21), Linderhof (€10), Herrenchiemsee (€11) — are the highlight. Rothenburg ob der Tauber is Europe's best-preserved medieval town. The full route takes 5–7 days by car, or can be sampled from Munich as day trips.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How long does the Romantic Road take?**
R: The full Würzburg–Füssen route covers 460 km and can technically be driven in one day — but that means stopping nowhere. Realistically: 5–7 days for the complete route with major stops. 3 days if you choose selectively (Rothenburg + Nördlingen + Neuschwanstein). 1 day from Munich if you only want Neuschwanstein + Hohenschwangau.

**Î: Are King Ludwig II's castles UNESCO World Heritage Sites?**
R: Yes — since 2025. The four palaces of King Ludwig II (Neuschwanstein, Linderhof, Herrenchiemsee, and the King's House on Schachen) were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2025 as a serial property, recognized for 'the romantic and eclectic spirit of the era' and their perfect integration into the Bavarian Alpine landscape.

**Î: How far in advance should I book Neuschwanstein?**
R: Book 2–3 months ahead for July–August visits. The castle receives 6,000+ visitors per day in peak season and tickets sell out. Book at hohenschwangau.de with a €2.50 online booking fee per ticket. Without an online reservation you can buy at the Ticket Center on the day of your visit — but availability is not guaranteed in summer.

**Î: Can I do the Romantic Road without a car?**
R: Partially. The Romantic Road Coach runs May–September, Sundays only, on the northern route (Frankfurt–Rothenburg). Regional trains connect the major cities (Würzburg, Augsburg, Füssen). But many castles and small villages (Harburg, Weikersheim, Creglingen) are practically inaccessible without a car. Recommended: rent a car at Frankfurt or Munich, drive the route, and return it at the other end.

**Î: What is the difference between Neuschwanstein and Hohenschwangau?**
R: Neuschwanstein is Ludwig II's built castle — Neo-Romanesque, unfinished, the most photographed. Hohenschwangau is the castle where Ludwig II grew up, built by his father Maximilian II — older (12th century, rebuilt 1833), more authentically medieval, less photographed. Both are worth visiting: Hohenschwangau explains why Ludwig built Neuschwanstein. Identical prices: €21 each.

**Î: What is the Bayern Ticket and how does it help on the Romantic Road?**
R: Bayern Ticket costs €29 for 1–5 people and covers all regional trains in Bavaria for one full day (weekdays after 9:00 AM, all day weekends). Perfect for Munich–Füssen (Neuschwanstein) or Munich–Augsburg. Does not cover ICE/IC express trains. The most cost-effective ticket for day trips from Munich on the Romantic Road.

## Saily eSIM Review 2026: Prices, VPN, and How It Compares

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/esim-roaming/saily-esim-review

**Publicat:** 2026-07-29

**Descriere:** Detailed Saily eSIM review with real 2026 prices per destination, built-in VPN breakdown, and honest comparison with Airalo and Yesim.

**Rezumat rapid:** Saily is NordVPN's eSIM product — available in 150+ countries with competitive prices, a built-in VPN (with ad blocker and web protection), and the most generous unlimited data threshold at 5 GB/day at full speed. Compared to Airalo (the largest aggregator with 200+ countries and maximum plan variety) and Yesim (virtual phone numbers and simple regional plans), Saily wins on unlimited plans and security features, while Airalo wins on fixed-data plan prices and exotic destinations. For most travellers, the right choice depends on destination: compare all three before buying. All three must be purchased before arriving in Turkey, where provider websites are blocked.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Is Saily eSIM legitimate and safe?**
R: Yes. Saily is developed by Nord Security (the company behind NordVPN), which has been operating since 2012 with tens of millions of subscribers globally. It is not a new or unknown startup — it benefits from Nord's established infrastructure, security expertise, and regulatory compliance across EU and UK markets. Data plans are provided through local network partners in each country. It holds a 4.7★ rating on Trustpilot with over 97,000 reviews.

**Î: Does Saily include a real VPN?**
R: Saily includes a VPN that encrypts your connection on any network (not just public Wi-Fi), plus a built-in ad blocker and web protection against malicious domains. It is not the full NordVPN product — it lacks some advanced features like Threat Protection, dedicated IP, obfuscated servers, and split tunnelling. For travel purposes (securing public Wi-Fi, blocking ads to save data), the Saily VPN layer is sufficient for most users.

**Î: Is Saily cheaper than Airalo?**
R: Varies by destination and plan type. For fixed-data plans (5-10 GB), Airalo is often slightly cheaper per gigabyte. But Saily's unlimited plans are significantly better value — $23.99 for 7 days of unlimited data (5 GB/day at full speed) vs $27.00 at Airalo (3 GB/day at full speed). Check both for your specific destination — the difference on standard plans is usually $1-3.

**Î: Can I use Saily for multiple countries in one trip?**
R: Yes — Saily offers regional plans covering multiple countries simultaneously. The Europe plan covers 35+ European countries under a single plan, eliminating the need to buy separately for each destination. If your trip spans France, Italy, and Croatia, one European plan covers all three. Regional plans are slightly more expensive per GB than country-specific ones but save time and hassle on multi-country trips.

**Î: Can I install Saily and Airalo on the same phone?**
R: Yes, if your phone supports multiple eSIM profiles (most modern phones do). You can install profiles from different providers for different destinations and activate them individually. Many frequent travellers maintain separate eSIM profiles for their regular destinations and activate the relevant one before each trip.

**Î: Does Saily work in Turkey?**
R: Yes — but you must purchase and install before arriving. Since 2025, Turkish authorities block access to eSIM provider websites (including Saily, Airalo, and Yesim) from within Turkey. If you try to buy after landing in Istanbul or Antalya, the website will not load. Install the eSIM at home, and it activates automatically when you land.

**Î: What phones support eSIM for Saily?**
R: Saily works on any eSIM-compatible phone: iPhone XS or newer (2018+), Samsung Galaxy S20 series and newer, Google Pixel 3 and newer, and most Android phones released from 2021 onwards. Check by dialling *#06# on your phone — if an EID number appears, your phone supports eSIM.

**Î: What happens when I run out of data on Saily?**
R: When your fixed plan's data runs out, you can buy an additional plan directly in the app — it activates immediately without needing a new QR code. On unlimited plans, after exceeding 5 GB in a day, speed drops to ~1 Mbps (sufficient for messaging and basic browsing, but not for video streaming). Full speed resets the next day.

**Î: Is Saily Ultra worth it?**
R: Saily Ultra is a monthly subscription that bundles eSIM data + NordVPN + NordPass + ClassPass. The Premium plan ($59.99/month) includes 30 GB at full speed, then unlimited at ~1 Mbps, plus all Nord products. It's worth it if you already need NordVPN and travel frequently — otherwise, individual per-trip plans are more cost-effective.

## Santorini 2026: Complete Guide — Oia, Fira, Caldera, Volcanic Beaches, Real Budget and What Other Guides Don't Tell You

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/city-breaks/santorini-complete-guide-2026
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** city-breaks
**Publicat:** 2026-08-19
**Traducere a:** [santorini-ghid-complet-2026](https://plecari.com/ro/city-breaks/santorini-ghid-complet-2026)

**Descriere:** Complete Santorini guide 2026. Oia vs Fira, the real sunset, volcanic beaches, caldera cruise, Assyrtiko wines, Akrotiri, real prices and local tips.

**Rezumat rapid:** Santorini is a volcanic arc in the Aegean Sea, 200 km southeast of Athens, famous for its white-washed houses with blue domes, the Oia sunset, and its caldera — the flooded crater of a volcano that erupted around 1600 BC (the explosion that contributed to the fall of Minoan civilization). Best time to visit: May–June or September–October (25–30°C, manageable crowds, prices 30–50% below July–August peak). Recommended base: Fira (central, best transport connections, nightlife, reasonable prices) or Imerovigli (quiet, caldera panorama, walkable to Fira). Real budget: 5 nights for 2 people costs €1,200–2,500 (non-luxury), including flights, accommodation, food and experiences.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: When is the best time to visit Santorini?**
R: May–June and September–early October are optimal: temperatures of 25–30°C, moderate meltemi wind, prices 30–50% lower than July–August, and significantly fewer crowds. July–August brings 35°C+ heat, strong wind that can cancel ferries, and peak prices (a caldera-view room can reach €600–1,000/night). April is beautiful but the sea is cold (18°C) and some restaurants/bars are still closed. November: quiet but rainy, many venues closed.

**Î: How do I get to Santorini?**
R: Direct flights operate seasonally (May–October) from many European cities to Thira airport (JTR). Alternatively: fly to Athens (year-round, budget airlines) then take a ferry from Piraeus port (5–8 hours conventional ferry at €35–45, or 2–2.5 hours speed ferry at €60–80; operators: Blue Star Ferries, SeaJets, Golden Star). The overnight ferry is a budget-smart option: depart Piraeus 19:00–21:00, arrive Santorini 05:00–07:00 — saves one night of accommodation.

**Î: Oia or Fira — where is it better to stay?**
R: Fira: best as a base — island's transport hub, most restaurants and bars, prices 30–40% lower than Oia, excellent caldera panorama. Oia: most photogenic spot, most famous sunset, but also most expensive and crowded — accommodation is the island's priciest, and at sunset the Byzantine Castle area is packed with hundreds of people. Imerovigli: the perfect compromise — quiet, panoramic, 25-minute walk to Fira along the caldera rim trail.

**Î: How much does a 5-night Santorini trip cost?**
R: Average budget for 2 people (5 nights): flights €160–360, accommodation €350–800 (3-star in Fira/Kamari; infinity pool caldera hotels start at €250/night), food €250–400, local transport €50–80 (bus + ATV or car for 2 days), experiences (caldera boat tour, wine tasting) €80–160. Total: €890–1,800 for 2 people or €445–900 per person. Oia cave hotel on the caldera: add 50–100%.

**Î: Is the caldera boat tour worth it?**
R: Yes — it's the definitive Santorini experience. A 5–6 hour catamaran tour includes sailing the caldera, a stop at volcanic hot springs (warm sulfurous water with a rust color), hiking to the active crater on Nea Kameni island, snorkeling in crystal-clear water, and often a sunset dinner with seafood and local wine on board. Prices: €50–80/person for group tours, €150–300 for private. Book 3–5 days ahead in season — popular tours fill up fast.

**Î: What are the best beaches in Santorini?**
R: Santorini doesn't have classic white-sand beaches — its beaches are volcanic: black, red, or pebble. Red Beach (Kokkini Paralia): visually spectacular (red cliff, reddish sand), but small and crowded. Perivolos/Perissa: the longest beaches (black sand), ideal for families, with sun loungers and beachfront restaurants. Kamari: organized with a promenade and open-air cinema. Vlychada: lunar landscape with wind-sculpted cliffs, very photogenic, less crowded. White Beach: accessible only by boat from Red Beach.

**Î: What are Assyrtiko wines and why do they matter?**
R: Assyrtiko is Santorini's signature grape — a dry white wine with vibrant acidity, intense minerality, and notes of citrus and sea salt, grown on volcanic soil at 300+ m altitude. Vines are trained in the traditional 'kouloura' shape (a circular crown close to the ground) to protect grapes from meltemi wind. Wineries to visit: Santo Wines (caldera panorama, tasting €15–25), Venetsanos (in a 1947 cave winery), Gavalas (oldest winemaking family, since 1888). Vinsanto — the local dessert wine from sun-dried grapes — is exceptional.

**Î: How do you get around the island without a car?**
R: KTEL bus covers main routes: Fira–Oia (20 min, €1.80), Fira–Kamari (15 min, €1.80), Fira–Perissa (20 min, €2.40), Fira–Akrotiri (20 min, €1.80). Summer frequency: every 20–40 minutes on popular routes. ATV/quadbikes (€25–45/day) are popular but dangerous — Santorini has one of Greece's highest ATV accident rates. Rental car (€35–60/day) is safer and more comfortable. Taxis: fewer than 30 on the entire island, 30–60 minute waits in season.

## Sarajevo 2026: The Complete City Break Guide to the Jerusalem of Europe

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/sarajevo-complete-guide
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-08-08
**Actualizat:** 2026-08-08
**Traducere a:** [sarajevo-ghid-complet](https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/sarajevo-ghid-complet)

**Descriere:** Complete Sarajevo guide: Baščaršija, the Latin Bridge (Franz Ferdinand assassination), the Tunnel of Hope and the siege history. Europe's cheapest capital — full budget from 25 EUR/day, the KM curr...

**Rezumat rapid:** Sarajevo is the capital of Bosnia and Herzegovina and one of Europe's most fascinating and moving cities — the place where the Ottoman East meets the Austro-Hungarian West, where a mosque and a cathedral stand 100 metres apart, and where 20th-century history (the Franz Ferdinand assassination in 1914, the siege of 1992–1996) is physically present in the city streets. It is also Europe's most affordable capital: daily budget of 25–50 EUR.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How do I get from Bucharest to Sarajevo?**
R: Wizz Air operates direct flights Bucharest (OTP) → Sarajevo (SJJ) several times a week. Duration: approximately 1h30. Prices: 40–100 EUR return. Alternative: fly to Belgrade (45 min, 30 EUR) + coach Belgrade–Sarajevo (7 hours, 20–25 EUR). By car: ~700 km, 7–8 hours through Serbia or Bulgaria.

**Î: What currency does Bosnia and Herzegovina use?**
R: Bosnia uses the Convertible Mark (BAM or KM). 1 EUR = 1.96 KM — practically 2 KM to 1 EUR, easy calculation. Euros are sometimes informally accepted but at an unfavourable rate. Pay in KM. Best exchange rate: local BBI or Raiffeisen ATMs. Avoid Euronet (high fees) and airport exchange.

**Î: Is Sarajevo safe for tourists?**
R: Yes, Sarajevo is a safe city for tourists. The Old Town (Baščaršija) and the Austro-Hungarian zone are safe day and night. Caution: outside the city, in the mountains, there may be uncleared landmines from the war — never leave marked paths. Inside the city, this risk does not exist.

**Î: What is the Tunnel of Hope and is it worth visiting?**
R: The Tunnel of Hope (Tunel Spasa) is an 800-metre tunnel hand-dug under the airport runway in 1993, the only connection between besieged Sarajevo and the outside world. Food, weapons and people passed through it for almost 3 years. Today it's a museum — you visit a preserved section of the tunnel and the siege exhibition. Ticket: ~8 EUR. It is probably the most important experience in Sarajevo.

**Î: How much does food cost in Sarajevo?**
R: Sarajevo is Europe's most affordable capital for food. Ćevapi (10 pieces with bread): 5–7 EUR. Burek at a local bakery: 1.50–2.50 EUR. Full lunch at a traditional restaurant: 7–12 EUR. Dinner with drinks: 10–18 EUR. Bosnian coffee: 0.80–1.50 EUR — the cheapest in Europe.

**Î: What is Bosnian coffee and how is it drunk?**
R: Bosnian coffee is served in a džezva (small copper pot), with a glass of water and a cube of Turkish delight (rahat). Don't stir sugar into the coffee — hold the rahat in your mouth and sip the coffee over it. The ritual is slow, social, almost ceremonial. Don't rush it — it's a form of hospitality.

**Î: Is the day trip to Mostar from Sarajevo worth it?**
R: Absolutely — Mostar is 2.5 hours by coach (10–12 EUR return) and is one of the most spectacular cities in the Balkans, with the reconstructed Old Bridge (Stari Most), the Ottoman bazaar Kujundziluk and Blagaj (the source of the Buna River with a dervish tekke). Works as a day trip, but an overnight stay is worthwhile.

**Î: What is the best time to visit Sarajevo?**
R: April–June and September–October: pleasant temperatures (14–22°C), fewer tourists, normal prices. July–August: warm (25–30°C), more lively. December–January: cold (-5°C), possible snow, but authentic atmosphere in wood-heated cafés. Sarajevo works well year-round — it has no bad season.

## Sibiu 2026: The Complete City Break Guide to Transylvania's Cultural Capital

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/sibiu-complete-guide
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-08-08
**Actualizat:** 2026-08-08
**Traducere a:** [sibiu-ghid-complet](https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/sibiu-ghid-complet)

**Descriere:** Complete Sibiu guide: medieval Piața Mare, the Bridge of Lies, the ASTRA Museum (Europe's largest open-air museum), Brukenthal Palace, the Transfăgărășan Highway and Romania's best Christmas market...

**Rezumat rapid:** Sibiu (Hermannstadt in German) is Romania's best-preserved medieval centre and one of Central Europe's most complete destinations — with three interconnected medieval squares, Europe's largest open-air museum (ASTRA Museum), Brukenthal Palace, the houses with eyes and direct access to the Transfăgărășan Highway. It was European Capital of Culture in 2007 and has Romania's most beautiful Christmas market. Direct flights from Bucharest with Blue Air and TAROM.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How do I get from Bucharest to Sibiu?**
R: Direct flight: Blue Air and TAROM operate OTP → SBZ flights. Duration: ~1 hour. Prices: 50–120 EUR return. By car: ~280 km via Pitești–Râmnicu Vâlcea–Sibiu (A1 motorway + DN1), ~3 hours. By train: InterCity Bucharest–Sibiu, ~4–5 hours, 80–120 RON. By coach: Flixbus or local operators, ~5–6 hours, 50–80 RON.

**Î: What are the 'eyes of the houses' in Sibiu?**
R: The old houses in Sibiu's Historic Centre have attic windows shaped like eyes that look down at the street — a unique architectural feature that inspired the city's nickname 'City of Eyes'. The mansard windows with outward-opening shutters resemble blinking eyelids. They are visible on any street in the Old Town and are Sibiu's most photographed architectural element.

**Î: What is the Bridge of Lies and why is it called that?**
R: The Bridge of Lies (1859) is Romania's first cast-iron bridge and one of the first in Europe. Legend says the bridge creaked when someone told a lie on it — which is why young lovers avoided making false declarations of love there. Other versions say the 'liars' were merchants who exaggerated prices in the small market below. Crossing is free and it is one of Sibiu's most photographed sights.

**Î: Does the ASTRA Museum deserve a full day?**
R: Yes — the ASTRA Museum is Europe's largest open-air museum, with 96 hectares in Dumbrava Forest and 400+ traditional structures from across Romania (water and wind mills, houses, wooden churches, workshops). A complete route needs 3–4 hours. Adult ticket: 35 RON (~7 EUR). Free on Mondays. Best if you're interested in Romanian rural architecture and civilisation.

**Î: How much does a 2–3 day city break in Sibiu cost?**
R: A 3-day/2-night city break costs 200–350 EUR per person (mid-range), including flights from Bucharest, accommodation and food. Sibiu is an affordable destination: a restaurant dinner 50–100 RON per person (~10–20 EUR), mid-range accommodation 200–350 RON per night (~40–70 EUR), most central attractions almost free.

**Î: Is Sibiu's Christmas market really Romania's best?**
R: Yes — Sibiu Christmas Market (held on Piața Mare in November–December) is consistently rated Romania's best and one of Central Europe's most beautiful. The medieval Piața Mare with lights, traditional product stalls, mulled wine and music creates an atmosphere that rivals Vienna or Prague. Book accommodation 2–3 months ahead if going during this period.

**Î: Does the Transfăgărășan start from Sibiu?**
R: The Transfăgărășan (DN7C) starts near Sibiu (Cartișoara/Avrig, ~30 km away) and climbs to Bâlea Lake (2,034 m). The road is fully open in summer (July–October). From Sibiu you can do a day trip to Bâlea Lake by car or guided tour. BBC Top Gear called it 'the world's greatest road' in 2009.

**Î: What is the best time to visit Sibiu?**
R: Spring (May–June) and autumn (September–October) are ideal — pleasant temperatures, fewer tourists, Transfăgărășan open in October. Summer (July–August): lively, International Theatre Festival (FITS), but warmer and more touristy. December: Christmas Market — the legendary experience. Winter (January–March): low prices, snow on rooftops, Păltiniș ski resort 30 km away.

## Sicily 2026: The Complete Guide — Palermo, Etna, Taormina, Agrigento & Everything You Need to Know

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/city-breaks/sicily-complete-guide-2026
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** city-breaks
**Publicat:** 2026-07-31
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-31

**Descriere:** Sicily 2026 complete guide. Palermo vs Catania, Mount Etna, Valley of Temples, Taormina, real budget breakdown, when to go and how to get around by car.

**Rezumat rapid:** Sicily is the Mediterranean's largest island and one of the world's richest concentrations of history, food, and natural drama — 2,800 years of successive civilisations (Greeks, Romans, Arabs, Normans, Spanish) layered into a landscape dominated by Europe's largest active volcano. In 2026, Etna is active (summit cable car operating, guided hikes to ~2,850 m; check INGV daily status). Best bases: Palermo (west) and Catania/Taormina (east). A car is essential for anything beyond the main cities. Best time: April–June and September–October. July–August: beach holiday viable but archaeological sites punishingly hot (40°C+).

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Do I need a car in Sicily?**
R: Yes, for anything beyond Palermo or Catania city limits. Public transport in Sicily is slow and infrequent outside the main cities. Without a car, you cannot visit the Valley of the Temples on your own schedule, reach most beaches, explore the rural interior, or visit the Baroque towns of the Val di Noto efficiently. Book a car online before arriving — on the spot in summer it tends to be expensive and sold out. Watch the insurance: the base rental price often excludes full cover. Pay extra for zero-excess cover or bring your own excess insurance.

**Î: Is Mount Etna safe to visit in 2026?**
R: Yes. Etna is one of the world's most monitored volcanoes and is accessible to visitors year-round. The volcano was active in early 2026 (flank eruption in Valle del Bove, January 2026; Northeast Crater reactivation December 2025; eruptive episode 5-6 July 2026 that briefly closed Catania airport). This is normal Etna behaviour. The cable car operates to 2,500 m; guided tours go to approximately 2,850–3,000 m depending on daily conditions. Summit treks above 2,800 m require a licensed guide. Check INGV (ingv.it) or etnaexplore.com the morning of your visit for current altitude limits.

**Î: How many days do you need in Sicily?**
R: At minimum: 5–7 days covers Palermo, Etna, and either Taormina or Agrigento. 10–14 days covers the whole island properly: Palermo, Monreale, Cefalù, Etna, Taormina, Siracusa and Ortigia, Noto, Agrigento, plus some beach time. Sicily is large (25,000 km² — comparable to Wales or Maryland) and distances are greater than they look on a map.

**Î: What is the best airport to fly into for Sicily?**
R: Catania Fontanarossa (CTA) for the east: Taormina 50 km, Etna 30 km, Siracusa 60 km. Palermo Falcone-Borsellino (PMO) for the west: Palermo city 35 km, Cefalù 70 km, Agrigento 130 km. For a full-island itinerary, fly into one and out of the other — eliminating backtracking entirely.

**Î: What is the best time to visit Sicily?**
R: April–June and September–October. May is arguably the best single month: wildflowers on the hillsides, temperatures 20–26°C, sea warm enough for brave swimmers, archaeological sites without summer heat exhaustion (40°C+), and accommodation prices 30–40% below peak. September: warmest sea (25–27°C), visible crowds reduction after mid-month, grape harvest on Etna slopes.

**Î: What is Palermo's Arab-Norman architecture?**
R: From 827 AD to 1072 AD, Sicily was ruled by Arab emirs who transformed Palermo into one of the most sophisticated cities in the Mediterranean world. When the Norman Roger II conquered Sicily in 1072, rather than erasing what the Arabs had built, he incorporated their craftsmen and their aesthetic — Byzantine mosaics, Arab geometric decoration, and Norman stone architecture — into a unique synthesis. The result: Cappella Palatina (Palatine Chapel), the Cathedral of Monreale, the Church of San Giovanni degli Eremiti, and the Church of La Martorana — buildings that exist nowhere else on Earth and were inscribed as UNESCO World Heritage in 2015.

**Î: What is the difference between arancini and arancine?**
R: A critical Sicilian linguistic battle: in Catania and eastern Sicily, the rice ball is 'arancino' (masculine, cone-shaped like the Etna volcano). In Palermo and western Sicily, it's 'arancina' (feminine, round like the orange it resembles — arancia). Ordering the wrong version in the wrong city is a guaranteed conversation starter. The rice ball itself: fried arborio rice encasing a filling of ragù (meat sauce) or butter and mozzarella, coated in breadcrumbs. €2–3 each.

## Sighișoara 2026: The Complete Guide to Europe's Only Permanently Inhabited Medieval Citadel

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/sighisoara-complete-guide
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-08-08
**Actualizat:** 2026-08-08
**Traducere a:** [sighisoara-ghid-complet](https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/sighisoara-ghid-complet)

**Descriere:** Complete Sighișoara guide: Clock Tower (64m), Covered Scholars' Staircase with 175 steps, Vlad Dracula's birthplace, Church on the Hill and the Medieval Festival. UNESCO 1999, real prices and why S...

**Rezumat rapid:** Sighișoara is the only permanently inhabited medieval citadel in Europe and one of the world's best-preserved medieval towns — inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1999. With approximately 2,000 residents who live today in the medieval houses, it has the 13th-century Clock Tower (the city's symbol), the covered Scholars' Staircase from 1642 and the birthplace of Vlad Drăculea (Vlad the Impaler — Dracula's inspiration). It is the smallest but most authentic medieval town in the Transylvanian series.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How do I get to Sighișoara from Bucharest or Brașov?**
R: From Brașov: direct train Brașov → Sighișoara, 1–1.5 hours, 20–40 RON. By car: 130 km, ~1.5 hours. From Bucharest: direct train ~4–5 hours or via Brașov. By car: ~280 km, ~3 hours. Sighișoara has no airport — the nearest are Brașov-Ghimbav (GHV, ~130 km) or Cluj (CLJ, ~110 km).

**Î: What is the Clock Tower and how much does it cost?**
R: The Clock Tower (Turnul Sfatului) is Sighișoara's symbol — a 64-metre tower built in the 13th century, today housing a history museum. Climb to the upper level for a complete panoramic view of the citadel. Ticket: ~20–25 RON (~4–5 EUR). Hours: Tuesday–Sunday 10:00–17:30.

**Î: Is Sighișoara truly Vlad Dracula's birthplace?**
R: Yes — according to historical documents, Vlad Dracul (Vlad II, father of Vlad the Impaler) lived in Sighișoara's citadel and Vlad the Impaler was born around 1431 in this house. The house at no. 5 in Citadel Square is today a themed restaurant and museum. The 'Dracula's room' ticket: ~15–20 RON (~3–4 EUR), including a costumed actor.

**Î: What is the Scholars' Staircase and why is it special?**
R: The Scholars' Staircase (Scara Acoperită) is a covered wooden staircase with 175 steps, built in 1642 to protect students and churchgoers from the weather on their daily journey to the School on the Hill and the Church on the Hill. It is unique in Romania and one of the few remaining covered medieval staircases in Europe. Access is free.

**Î: How long do I need for a visit to Sighișoara?**
R: The citadel can be visited completely in 3–4 hours: Clock Tower, Citadel Square, Vlad Dracula's House, Scholars' Staircase, Church on the Hill. Including the Lower Town and surroundings, a full day. Sighișoara works excellently as a day trip from Brașov (1.5 hours) or Sibiu (1.5 hours).

**Î: Sighișoara Medieval Festival — when does it take place and is it worth it?**
R: Sighișoara's Medieval Festival takes place every year in the last week of July (in 2026: 24–27 July). It is Romania's largest medieval festival, with knight tournaments, craftsmen in period costume, period music, pyrotechnics and open-air performances. The citadel becomes a living medieval stage. Book accommodation 3–4 months ahead.

**Î: Is Biertan worth visiting combined with Sighișoara?**
R: Yes — Biertan is 30 km from Sighișoara and is another UNESCO site — a Saxon village with an impressive fortified church, with three rings of defensive walls. The Sighișoara + Biertan combination in one day is one of Transylvania's best circuits. Biertan ticket: ~15 RON (~3 EUR).

**Î: What is the best time to visit Sighișoara?**
R: May–June and September: ideal — few tourists, pleasant temperatures, citadel just as spectacular. July (last week): Medieval Festival — lively and unique but crowded. Evening (after 18:00): the citadel empties of day tourists and becomes authentic and almost eerie — one of the best experiences.

## Sinaia 2026: The Complete Guide to the Pearl of the Carpathians — Peleș Castle and the Bucegi Mountains

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/sinaia-complete-guide
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-08-08
**Actualizat:** 2026-08-08
**Traducere a:** [sinaia-ghid-complet](https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/sinaia-ghid-complet)

**Descriere:** Complete Sinaia guide: Peleș Castle (online booking mandatory), Pelișor Castle, Sinaia Monastery (1695), cable car to 2,000m and Bucegi hiking trails. Real prices, how to book Peleș tickets and why...

**Rezumat rapid:** Sinaia is Romania's most elegant mountain resort — nicknamed the 'Pearl of the Carpathians' — with Peleș Castle (King Carol I's summer residence, considered one of the world's most beautiful castles), Sinaia Monastery from 1695, a cable car to the Bucegi Mountains at 2,000m and belle époque villas among pine forests. 1h45 from Bucharest and 40 minutes from Brașov by train.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How do I buy tickets for Peleș Castle — are there walk-up tickets?**
R: NO — Peleș Castle tickets are purchased EXCLUSIVELY online, in advance, for a specific time slot. No walk-up tickets since 2023. Available slots: Wednesdays 10:00–12:45, Thursday–Sunday 9:15–11:00. Maximum capacity: 500 people per slot. Book at peles.ro or GetYourGuide. Prices: 60–100 RON (~12–20 EUR) depending on tour type. Book at least 1–2 weeks ahead in season.

**Î: How do I get from Bucharest to Sinaia?**
R: Train: InterRegio/Rapid Bucharest Nord → Sinaia, ~1h45–2h, 30–60 RON (~6–12 EUR). Most practical — Sinaia station is 15 minutes' walk from the Monastery and 25–30 minutes from Peleș Castle (or direct taxi, ~20 RON). By car: ~130 km on A3 + DN1, ~1h30–2h (watch out for weekend traffic). Bus: less comfortable, ~2–3 hours.

**Î: Is the Sinaia cable car to Cota 2000 worth it?**
R: Absolutely — the cable car ascends in two stages: Sinaia → Cota 1400 → Cota 2000. From Cota 2000, the panoramic view of the Bucegi Mountains is exceptional. Summer: starting point for hiking trails to Babele, Heroes' Cross, Ialomița Cave. Winter: ski station. Return ticket: ~50–80 RON (~10–16 EUR). Note: the cable car has variable hours and sometimes closes for wind or technical issues — check on the day of your visit.

**Î: What is Pelișor Castle and how does it differ from Peleș?**
R: Pelișor is the smaller castle built next to Peleș for Crown Prince Ferdinand and his wife Queen Maria. Art Nouveau rather than Neo-Renaissance. Separate ticket (~30 RON). Less visited, more authentic — Queen Maria's Gold Room is remarkable. Accessible on foot from Peleș (5 minutes).

**Î: Is Sinaia Monastery worth visiting?**
R: Yes — Sinaia Monastery (1695) is located halfway between the station and Peleș, on a forest footpath. It is one of the oldest and most important monasteries in the southern Carpathians, with two churches (the Old one from 1695 and the Great one from 1846), remarkable frescoes and a museum with the first Bible printed in Romanian (1688). Free entry to the monastery; museum: ~10 RON.

**Î: Can Sinaia be done as a day trip from Bucharest?**
R: Yes, but with caveats. A day from Bucharest allows visiting Peleș Castle + Sinaia Monastery + a short stroll through the resort. Not enough time for cable car + hiking + Pelișor. If you want to explore fully, stay overnight. Warning: DN1 weekend traffic can turn 2 hours into 3.5–4 hours.

**Î: What is the best season for Sinaia?**
R: Spring (May–June) and autumn (September–October): ideal — forests in colour, temperatures 12–20°C, fewer tourists, Bucegi excellent for hiking. Summer (July–August): most lively but most crowded — book Peleș months ahead. Winter (December–March): Cota 1400 and 2000 with snow — active ski resort, winter mountain atmosphere.

**Î: Sinaia or Predeal — which is better for skiing?**
R: Sinaia has more cultural and historical attractions (Peleș, Monastery). Predeal (18 km north) is more ski-oriented — more slopes, cheaper. Bușteni (10 km north) has the Heroes' Cross on the Bucegi plateau. Sinaia offers the best balance of tourism + skiing.

## Ski Travel Insurance 2026: What Is Covered, What Is Not, and How to Choose

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/asigurari/ski-travel-insurance
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** asigurari
**Publicat:** 2026-07-30
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-30
**Traducere a:** [asigurare-schi-munte](https://plecari.com/ro/asigurari/asigurare-schi-munte)

**Descriere:** Complete guide to ski and winter sports travel insurance in 2026. Piste rescue costs, off-piste cover, equipment insurance, trip cancellation, and the clauses that catch skiers out every season.

**Rezumat rapid:** Standard travel insurance does NOT cover skiing — it must explicitly state 'winter sports' or 'ski cover' to be valid on the slopes. The most important coverage: piste rescue and mountain rescue (helicopter evacuation costs €3,000–15,000 in the Alps), emergency medical treatment for ski injuries (knee ligament surgery: €15,000–40,000), and piste closure cover. Off-piste skiing requires explicit endorsement — without it, any injury off a marked run invalidates the entire medical claim. Buy ski insurance before departure; purchasing on the mountain after an injury has occurred is not possible.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Does standard travel insurance cover skiing?**
R: Almost never. Standard travel insurance treats skiing as a hazardous activity and excludes it from medical and accident coverage unless winter sports cover is explicitly added or the policy specifically states it includes skiing. Always verify before purchase — look for 'winter sports,' 'ski cover,' or 'hazardous activities including skiing' in the policy wording.

**Î: How much does mountain rescue cost in the Alps?**
R: Helicopter rescue in the French, Swiss, Austrian, and Italian Alps costs €3,000–15,000 depending on complexity, duration, and whether a doctor flies with the rescue team. In some Alpine countries (France, Austria), rescue costs are partially covered by the piste operator's levy (already included in your lift pass). In Switzerland, costs can be higher. Without insurance, rescue is billed to the individual — payable within 30 days in most cases.

**Î: Is off-piste skiing covered?**
R: Only with an explicit off-piste endorsement. Most ski insurance policies distinguish between on-piste (marked runs within the ski area boundary) and off-piste (unmarked terrain, backcountry). An injury sustained off-piste on a policy without off-piste cover invalidates the medical claim entirely. If you ski off-piste at any point, even briefly, confirm your policy explicitly covers it.

**Î: What is piste closure insurance and is it worth it?**
R: Piste closure insurance pays a daily cash benefit (typically €30–50/day) when the ski area closes due to insufficient snow, extreme weather, or other causes outside your control. It does NOT refund your lift pass or accommodation — it pays a fixed sum per day of closure. Worth considering for peak-season bookings in lower-altitude resorts susceptible to snow shortages.

**Î: Does ski insurance cover equipment theft?**
R: Only if the equipment cover is explicitly included. Most ski policies offer optional equipment cover for skis, boots, poles, and helmet up to a stated limit (typically €500–1,500). Equipment must be properly secured when not in use — left unattended on a ski rack outside a restaurant is often excluded. Hired equipment is usually covered differently from owned equipment.

**Î: Can I buy ski insurance after I arrive at the resort?**
R: No legitimate insurer will sell you ski insurance after you have already started skiing — the insurable risk has already materialised. Buy before departure. If you are already at the resort and realise you are not covered: stop skiing until you have purchased coverage, then purchase online for the remaining days. Some insurers exclude the first 24 hours after purchase for this reason.

**Î: What happens if I am injured and cannot return on my original flight?**
R: Ski insurance covers the cost of extending your accommodation and rebooking your flight if a medical situation prevents you from travelling on the original date. This requires a medical certificate from the treating doctor stating that you are not fit to travel. The insurer typically requires pre-authorisation before booking a new flight.

**Î: Does ski insurance cover ski lessons?**
R: Injury during ski school lessons is covered under standard ski insurance — lessons on marked runs with a qualified instructor are treated as normal on-piste skiing. The exception: any lesson conducted off-piste requires the off-piste endorsement.

## Skopje 2026: The Complete City Break Guide to Europe's Most Controversial Capital

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/skopje-complete-guide
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-08-08
**Actualizat:** 2026-08-08
**Traducere a:** [skopje-ghid-complet](https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/skopje-ghid-complet)

**Descriere:** Complete Skopje guide: the Skopje 2014 project explained, Old Ottoman Bazaar, Kale Fortress, Matka Canyon and why North Macedonia is the most affordable destination in the Balkans. Macedonian denar...

**Rezumat rapid:** Skopje is the capital of North Macedonia and one of Europe's most bizarre, most fascinating and most affordable capitals. The city centre was reconstructed between 2006 and 2014 with 130+ colossal statues, neoclassical arcades and a pirate ship moored on the Vardar River — all in a landlocked country. Next to this modern architectural extravagance lies one of the most authentic Ottoman bazaars in the Balkans. And 17 km from the centre — Matka Canyon, the most dramatic natural landscape in the region.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How do I get from Bucharest to Skopje?**
R: Wizz Air operates direct flights Bucharest (OTP) → Skopje (SKP). Duration: ~1h45. Prices: 30–80 EUR return. The airport is 25 km from the centre — the public bus takes 40 minutes (~80 MKD/~1.30 EUR), taxi 15–20 EUR. Alternative: train or bus from Belgrade (5–6 hours, 20–30 EUR) or from Sofia (3–4 hours, 15–25 EUR).

**Î: What currency does North Macedonia use?**
R: North Macedonia uses the Macedonian Denar (MKD). 1 EUR ≈ 61.5 MKD in 2026. Quick calculation: divide the denar amount by 61.5. Euros are informally accepted in some places, but pay in MKD for the best rate. City centre ATMs charge small fees — avoid Euronet.

**Î: What is the Skopje 2014 project and why is it controversial?**
R: Skopje 2014 was an ambitious urban project by the Macedonian government (2006–2014) that transformed the capital's centre with 130+ colossal statues, arcades and neoclassical façades applied over brutalist communist buildings, plus a 21-metre triumphal arch. The project cost approximately 500 million EUR — enormous sums for one of Europe's poorest countries. Criticised as grandiose kitsch and nationalist-identity propaganda, appreciated by others as an affirmation of national identity. A unique spectacle found nowhere else.

**Î: Is the Matka Canyon day trip worth it?**
R: Absolutely — Matka is 17 km from Skopje's centre and is one of the most spectacular natural destinations in the Balkans. A dramatic gorge with emerald lakes, medieval monasteries clinging to cliffs, the Vrelo Cave (with underwater stalactites) and hiking trails. Boat tour through the canyon: ~200 MKD (3.25 EUR). Guided excursion from Skopje with boat included: 20–35 EUR.

**Î: How much does a city break in Skopje cost?**
R: Skopje is one of Europe's cheapest capitals: a coffee 1–2 EUR, a full restaurant meal rarely over 5–7 EUR, mid-range accommodation 25–50 EUR per night. A 3-day/2-night city break costs 130–250 EUR per person including flights. North Macedonia is 50–60% cheaper than Greece or Croatia.

**Î: Is Skopje safe to visit?**
R: Yes, Skopje is a safe capital for tourists. The Old Town (Bazaar) and Macedonia Square are safe day and night. Standard pickpocket precautions in crowded areas. Inter-ethnic relations (Macedonians and Albanians) are generally peaceful in 2026.

**Î: Is the Mother Teresa Memorial House worth visiting?**
R: Yes — Mother Teresa (Agnes Gonxha Bojaxhiu) was born in Skopje on 26 August 1910. The Memorial House on Macedonia Boulevard houses an exhibition about her life and missionary work. Free entry, 30–45 minutes. One of the few places in the world directly linked to her birthplace.

**Î: What is the best time to visit Skopje?**
R: April–June and September–October: pleasant temperatures (15–24°C), authentic atmosphere, low prices. July–August: hot (30–36°C) and lively. December: Christmas markets on Macedonia Square. Avoid heatwave periods if heat-sensitive — summer city centre can exceed 38°C.

## Split 2026: Complete Guide — Diocletian's Palace, Hvar & Brač Islands, Beaches, Budget & Insider Tips

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/city-breaks/split-complete-guide-2026
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** city-breaks
**Publicat:** 2026-08-19
**Traducere a:** [split-ghid-complet-2026](https://plecari.com/ro/city-breaks/split-ghid-complet-2026)

**Descriere:** Complete Split guide 2026. Diocletian's Palace, Riva, Marjan, Hvar and Brač islands, beaches, Dalmatian cuisine, real prices and local tips.

**Rezumat rapid:** Split is Croatia's second city and the gateway to the Dalmatian islands, built literally in and around Diocletian's Palace — a 4th-century Roman fortress that became a living city, with 3,000 people residing today within the palace walls. Best time to visit: May–June and September–October (24–30°C, warm sea, without July–August crowds). Recommended base: the old town (Grad) or Bačvice (urban beach, 10 min from centre). Real budget: a 4-night city break for 2 people costs €600–1,400, including flights, accommodation, food and experiences. Split is ideal as a base for day trips to Hvar, Brač, Vis, and Trogir.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: When is the best time to visit Split?**
R: May–June and September–October are optimal: temperatures of 24–30°C, sea temperature 22–26°C, and prices 25–35% below peak season. July–August: 35°C+, the old town overcrowded (cruise ships disgorge 5,000–10,000 passengers daily), and peak prices. April is beautiful but the sea is cold (17°C). September is the perfect month: sea at its warmest (26°C), tourists thin out, and locals reclaim the Riva.

**Î: How do I get to Split?**
R: Budget airlines fly direct from many European cities. Split Airport (SPU) is 25 km from the centre — bus 37 (€5, 30–40 min) or taxi/transfer (€35–45). Alternatively, Split is a major stop on a Dalmatian coast road trip.

**Î: What is Diocletian's Palace and why is it special?**
R: Diocletian's Palace is a Roman fortress built between 295–305 AD as the retirement residence of Roman Emperor Diocletian (the only emperor to voluntarily abdicate). What makes it unique: it's not a ruin you visit — it's a living city. 3,000 people reside today within the palace walls. The Roman basement halls (Podrumi) are the world's best-preserved. The Cathedral of St Domnius is built directly into Diocletian's mausoleum. The Peristyle — the central courtyard with Corinthian granite columns — hosts performances and cafés. UNESCO since 1979.

**Î: Are the Hvar and Brač islands worth visiting from Split?**
R: Yes, both are perfect day trips. Hvar (1–2 hours by catamaran/ferry): Hvar town is the 'Saint-Tropez of the Adriatic' — Spanish fortress, Venetian harbour, lavender fields, excellent restaurants, lively nightlife. Visit the Pakleni Islands by boat. Brač (50 min by catamaran): has Zlatni Rat (Golden Horn) — a horn-shaped beach that shifts with currents, one of Croatia's most photographed. Both accessible by ferry from Split port — Jadrolinija (slow ferry, cheaper, takes cars) or Krilo/TP Line (fast catamaran, passengers only).

**Î: How much does a 4-night Split city break cost?**
R: Average budget for 2 people (4 nights): flights €120–280, accommodation €200–600 (central apartment or 3-star hotel), food €180–380 (konobe, markets, pekare), local transport €30–50 (bus + one ferry day), experiences (palace tour, Hvar excursion, Marjan) €50–120. Total: €580–1,430 for 2 or €290–715 per person. Split is 20–30% more affordable than Dubrovnik.

**Î: What are the best beaches in and near Split?**
R: Bačvice (10 min from centre): urban sandy beach, shallow water, perfect for picigin (the traditional Split ball game played in knee-deep water). Kašjuni (below Marjan): small pebble beach among pines, crystal water, beach bar, relaxed atmosphere — locals' favourite. Žnjan (east): long pebble beach, organised, with beach bars and water sports. Stobreč (8 km east): village near Split with beach and camping. The islands Čiovo (Trogir bridge) and Šolta (30 min ferry) have wilder beaches.

**Î: How do ferries work from Split to the islands?**
R: Split port is Dalmatia's main ferry hub. Companies: Jadrolinija (classic ferries, takes cars, slower, cheaper) and Krilo/TP Line (fast catamarans, passengers only, pricier). Direct destinations: Hvar (1–2 hours, €8–15/person catamaran), Brač/Supetar (50 min, €5–8), Vis (2.5 hours, €10–15), Korčula (3.5 hours), Dubrovnik (4 hours catamaran). Tickets: online at jadrolinija.hr or bookaway.com (recommended in summer — catamarans sell out!), or at port kiosks (risky in summer). In summer, book at least 2–3 days ahead for popular catamarans (Split–Hvar, Split–Vis).

**Î: Is Split safe for tourists?**
R: Yes, very safe. Split is a relaxed city with very low crime. Only concerns: pickpockets in the old town at peak season (as in any tourist destination) and inflated prices at Riva restaurants (the harbour promenade) — locals eat on the back streets. At night, the centre is lively and safe — Croatian going-out culture is strong, streets are full until 02:00–03:00.

## Stockholm 2026: The Complete City Break Guide to Scandinavia's Capital — Vasa Museum, Gamla Stan and the Archipelago

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/stockholm-complete-guide
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-08-10
**Actualizat:** 2026-08-10
**Traducere a:** [stockholm-ghid-complet](https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/stockholm-ghid-complet)

**Descriere:** Complete Stockholm guide: medieval Gamla Stan on its island, the Vasa Museum (17th-century warship), ABBA Museum, Skansen, Royal Palace, free Monteliusvägen panorama and the 30,000-island archipela...

**Rezumat rapid:** Stockholm is Sweden's capital and one of Europe's most beautiful cities — built on 14 islands connected by bridges, with medieval Gamla Stan on the original island, the Vasa Museum (the world's only intact 17th-century warship), ABBA Museum and a 30,000-island archipelago at the city's doorstep. Expensive by Nordic standards, but with 10 permanently free museums and spectacular panoramas completely free of charge.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How do I get from Bucharest to Stockholm?**
R: Wizz Air operates direct flights Bucharest (OTP) → Stockholm Arlanda (ARN). Duration: ~3h15. Prices: 80–200 EUR return. Arlanda Airport is 45 km from the centre — the Arlanda Express train takes 18 minutes (299 SEK ~27 EUR). Alternative: Flybussen coach, 40 minutes, 99–149 SEK (~9–14 EUR).

**Î: What currency does Sweden use and what is the exchange rate?**
R: Sweden uses the Swedish Krona (SEK). 1 EUR ≈ 11.20 SEK in 2026. Sweden is virtually cashless — cards are accepted everywhere, including street food stalls. Cash is rarely needed. Revolut or Wise cards are recommended to avoid conversion fees on SEK transactions.

**Î: What is the Vasa Museum and why is it worth it?**
R: The Vasa Museum houses the world's only completely intact 17th-century warship — a Swedish battleship that sank in 1628 just 1,300 metres from Stockholm harbour on its maiden voyage, salvaged in 1961 and restored over 30 years. Adult ticket: 240 SEK (~21 EUR) in summer (May–Sept), 195 SEK (~17 EUR) other months. Children under 18 enter free. It is the most visited museum in Scandinavia.

**Î: Is the ABBA Museum worth the high price?**
R: ABBA The Museum is among Europe's most interactive museums — original costumes, gold records, Mamma Mia props and installations where you can 'perform' with ABBA digitally. Ticket: 329 SEK (~29 EUR). Not included in the Stockholm Card. Worth it if you're an ABBA or Swedish pop fan. Book online in advance — sells out at peak season.

**Î: What are Stockholm's 10 free museums?**
R: Among the permanently free museums: Nationalmuseum (European art, Rembrandt, Rubens, Renoir), Moderna Museet (modern and contemporary art, Picasso, Dalí, Warhol), Arkitekturmuseet, Historiska Museet, Medelhavsmuseet. These rival major museums in other European capitals — a remarkable advantage over London or Paris.

**Î: Is the Stockholm Card (949 SEK/day) worth it?**
R: Only if you visit 3–4 paid museums in a single day. It includes 69+ attractions, but the ABBA Museum is not included. Quick calculation: Vasa (240) + Skansen (250) + Royal Palace (190) = 680 SEK. Stockholm Card 1 day: 949 SEK — not worth it for these three alone. For 2+ days with multiple museums, it may be advantageous. Calculate exactly based on your plan.

**Î: What is Monteliusvägen and why is it Stockholm's best free viewpoint?**
R: Monteliusvägen is a 500-metre pedestrian path along Södermalm's clifftop, with unobstructed views of Gamla Stan, City Hall and Riddarfjärden bay — one of the best panoramic views in Scandinavia, completely free at any hour. It is also Stockholm's most romantic sunset spot.

**Î: How do I visit the Stockholm Archipelago?**
R: The Stockholm Archipelago covers 30,000 islands and rocks in the Baltic Sea. Day boat tours depart from central Strömkajen pier (facing City Hall). 2–3 hour tour: 200–350 SEK (~18–31 EUR). Day trip to Vaxholm (fortress island) by public ferry: 75–100 SEK (~7–9 EUR) return — the best value option.

## Tallinn 2026: The Complete City Break Guide to Europe's Best-Preserved Medieval City

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/tallinn-complete-guide
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-08-08
**Actualizat:** 2026-08-08
**Traducere a:** [tallinn-ghid-complet](https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/tallinn-ghid-complet)

**Descriere:** Complete Tallinn guide: UNESCO medieval Old Town, Toompea, the KGB Museum at Hotel Viru, Telliskivi, Kadriorg Park and the ferry to Helsinki. Real prices, cruise ship tips and the complete Baltic t...

**Rezumat rapid:** Tallinn is the capital of Estonia and the best-preserved medieval centre in Europe — a fairytale city with Gothic towers, intact medieval walls and 15th-century merchant squares, UNESCO-listed since 1997. It is simultaneously one of the world's most digitalised and most modern cities. Direct flights from Bucharest with Wizz Air from 40 EUR return.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How do I get from Bucharest to Tallinn?**
R: Wizz Air operates direct flights Bucharest (OTP) → Tallinn (TLL) several times a week. Duration: approximately 2h30. Prices: 40–110 EUR return with 3–6 weeks' advance booking. The airport is 4 km from the centre — tram no. 4 takes 15 minutes (2 EUR), taxi/Bolt 10 minutes (7–12 EUR).

**Î: What currency does Estonia use?**
R: Estonia has used the euro (EUR) since 2011 — one of the first former Soviet republics to adopt the single currency. No currency exchange needed. Tallinn is one of the most cashless cities in Europe — cards are accepted even at small kiosks and markets.

**Î: What is the KGB Museum at Hotel Viru and is it worth visiting?**
R: The KGB Museum is on the 23rd floor of Hotel Viru — the secret floor, built by the Soviets in 1972 as a surveillance zone. The KGB installed listening equipment in rooms and monitored all Western guests. Today it's a guided museum (15 EUR, tour lasts 45 min, advance booking recommended). It is one of Tallinn's most fascinating experiences.

**Î: How much does it cost to enter Tallinn's Old Town?**
R: Access to the Old Town (Vanalinn) is completely free — there is no entry ticket. Some individual attractions have fees: St Olaf's Church Tower (8 EUR, panoramic view), Kiek in de Kök + Bastion Tunnels (14 EUR), Town Hall (7 EUR, seasonal), Alexander Nevsky Cathedral (free).

**Î: Is the ferry to Helsinki from Tallinn worth it?**
R: Absolutely. The Tallinn–Helsinki fast ferry takes 2 hours (Tallink Silja, Viking Line). Price: 20–45 EUR return. Helsinki + Tallinn in the same 4–5 day city break is one of the most popular Nordic combinations. Alternatively, Helsinki as a day trip (depart in the morning, return in the evening).

**Î: What is Telliskivi and is it worth visiting?**
R: Telliskivi Creative City is a converted industrial district turned cultural space, with independent cafés, restaurants, art galleries, vintage shops and weekend markets. It's the bohemian alternative to touristy Old Town — prices 20–30% lower and a more authentic atmosphere. A 10-minute walk from the Old Town.

**Î: What is the best time to visit Tallinn?**
R: June–August: extremely long days (sun sets after 10:30 PM around the solstice), active terraces, festivals. May and September: pleasant temperatures (12–18°C), fewer tourists, prices 20–25% lower. December: Christmas markets on Raekoja plats — one of the most beautiful in Europe. Avoid January–March: extreme cold, some reduced hours.

**Î: Is the Tallinn Card worth buying?**
R: The Tallinn Card (28 EUR/24h, 38 EUR/48h) includes: free entry to 50+ museums, unlimited public transport and restaurant discounts. Worth it if you visit 4+ paid museums in a day. If your itinerary is mostly Old Town (largely free) and Telliskivi, you may not recoup the cost.

## Hidden Fees in Car Rental: How to Avoid Paying Double

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/inchirieri-auto/taxe-ascunse-inchiriere-auto
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** inchirieri-auto
**Publicat:** 2026-07-09

**Descriere:** CDW, excess, fuel policy, airport surcharges, GPS fees — what awaits you at the counter and how to avoid every extra cost. A practical guide with real numbers.

**Rezumat rapid:** The most common hidden fees in car rental are: the excess on CDW insurance (you may pay €500–2,000 if you damage the car, even with basic insurance included), the airport surcharge (10–15% added when collecting from an airport), the young driver fee (under 25 years), overpriced GPS (€10–15/day) and the fuel policy trap ('full-to-empty' versus 'full-to-full'). You avoid them by reading the terms before booking and refusing add-ons at the collection counter.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: What is the CDW excess and why does it matter?**
R: CDW (Collision Damage Waiver) is the basic insurance included in the price, but it comes with an excess — the amount you pay out of pocket if you damage the car. The excess can be €500–2,000, blocked on your card as a deposit at collection. You can reduce the excess to zero with a third-party excess insurance (far cheaper than what the counter offers).

**Î: Is the extra insurance at the counter worth it?**
R: Almost never. Counter insurance costs €15–30 per day and is the rental industry's biggest upsell. A third-party excess waiver from a specialist (e.g. insurance4carhire, iCarhireinsurance, RentalCover) costs 3–5 times less for the same cover and the same period.

**Î: What is the 'full-to-full' fuel policy?**
R: You collect the car with a full tank and return it full. It is the fairest option — you pay only for what you use, at petrol station prices. The alternative 'pre-purchase fuel' means you pay for a full tank at collection (at the company's price, higher than a petrol station) and return the car empty — but you never manage to empty it exactly, so you always lose paid fuel.

**Î: Why is collecting at the airport more expensive?**
R: Airports charge rental companies a concession fee for access to the terminal, parking and counter space. Companies pass this cost directly to you — as an 'airport surcharge' of 10–15% added to the total. Collecting from a city-centre location avoids the surcharge, but you need to get there from the airport.

**Î: What does a one-way fee mean?**
R: A one-way fee applies when you collect the car in one city and return it in another. It can be anywhere from €30 to over €100, depending on the company and distance. Some companies include one-way within the same country for free — check at booking, not at the counter.

**Î: Can I use my credit card insurance instead of buying CDW cover?**
R: Some premium credit cards (Visa Signature, Mastercard World Elite, Amex Gold) include car rental insurance as a benefit. However, you typically need to pay the full rental on that card, decline the rental company's CDW, and the cover is secondary (it kicks in after other insurance). Check your card's terms carefully — exclusions vary and not all rental companies accept card insurance.

## Thassos 2026: Complete Guide — Golden Beach, Marble Beach, Giola, Villages, Budget & Insider Tips

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/city-breaks/thassos-complete-guide-2026
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** city-breaks
**Publicat:** 2026-08-19
**Traducere a:** [thassos-ghid-complet-2026](https://plecari.com/ro/city-breaks/thassos-ghid-complet-2026)

**Descriere:** Complete Thassos guide 2026. Golden Beach, Marble Beach, Giola natural pool, island road trip, Cretan cuisine, ferry, real prices and local tips.

**Rezumat rapid:** Thassos is Greece's northernmost island, covered in pine forests that reach the waterline, with spectacular beaches (Golden Beach, Marble Beach, Paradise), the unique Giola natural rock pool, picturesque mountain villages, spit-roasted lamb, pine honey you won't find anywhere else, and prices 30–40% lower than the Cyclades or Crete. Best time to visit: June and September (25–30°C, quiet beaches). Recommended base: Limenas (capital, ferry access), Potos/Pefkari (south, beaches, nightlife), or Golden Beach (east, the island's finest beach). Real budget: 7 nights for 2 people costs €800–1,800.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How do I get to Thassos?**
R: Thassos has no airport — access is by ferry from the mainland. Two options: Keramoti ferry (30 min, every 30–60 min in summer, ~€5/person + ~€30–35/car) or Kavala ferry (1.5 hours, 4–6/day, to Skala Prinos on the west coast). The nearest airport is Kavala (KVA, also called Megas Alexandros), with seasonal flights from various European cities; from the airport, Keramoti port is 30 min by car. Alternatively, fly to Thessaloniki (SKG, year-round) and drive 2.5 hours to Keramoti. Many visitors from the Balkans and Central Europe drive to Keramoti with their own cars.

**Î: Do I need a car in Thassos?**
R: Strongly recommended. The island is small (~100 km circumference) with a fully paved coastal road, but the most beautiful beaches and mountain villages require a car. KTEL buses exist but run infrequently (3–5 services/day on main routes). Car rental: €25–45/day. Scooter: €15–20/day (sufficient for the coastal road but not mountain detours). The round-island drive is one of Thassos's best experiences — doable in a single day with beach stops.

**Î: When is the best time to visit Thassos?**
R: June and September are ideal: 25–30°C, sea temperature 23–26°C, quiet beaches, reasonable prices. July–August: 33–36°C, popular beaches crowded (especially Golden Beach and Marble Beach on weekends), prices 20–30% higher. May: beautiful, wildflowers, but the sea can still be cool (20°C). October: quiet, sea still warm (22°C), but some tavernas close by mid-month. Thassos is greener and cooler than the Cyclades or Dodecanese — the pine forests provide natural shade on many beaches.

**Î: What are the best beaches in Thassos?**
R: Golden Beach (east): 2 km of golden sand, crystal water, gentle entry — the island's best family beach. Marble Beach/Saliara (east): white marble sand with unreal turquoise water — the most photogenic. Paradise Beach (east): fine sand, crystal water, beach bar, youthful vibe. Aliki (south): twin bays flanking an archaeological site — beach + ruins + taverna. Porto Vathy (southwest): hidden emerald cove, excellent snorkelling. Giola (south): a natural seawater pool carved into rock — unique in Greece.

**Î: What is Giola and how do I get there?**
R: Giola is a natural circular pool (~20 m diameter) carved by the sea into the rock at Thassos's southern tip, near Astris village. Ocean water flows through an opening in the rock, forming a sheltered basin with emerald-green water warmer than the open sea. Access: drive to a roadside parking area (follow the 'Giola' sign), then walk 15–20 minutes down a rocky path — uneven, no guardrails, not suitable for small children. No facilities: bring water, sunscreen, and grippy footwear. Best time: early morning (08:00–10:00) when you'll have it to yourself.

**Î: Is the round-island drive worth it?**
R: Absolutely — it's one of Thassos's best experiences. The island is ~100 km around with a fully paved coastal road. In one day, you can complete the circuit with stops at beaches, mountain villages, and tavernas. Recommended route: Limenas → Golden Beach → Paradise Beach → Aliki → Giola/Astris → Potos → Limenaria → Skala Maries → Skala Prinos → Limenas. Must-stop detours: Marble Beach (5-min turn off the main road), Theologos (mountain village, spit-roasted lamb), and Kastro (abandoned hilltop village, 15-min hike). Total with stops: 6–8 hours.

**Î: What should I eat in Thassos?**
R: Spit-roasted lamb (souvla/kontosouvli) is the island speciality — whole lamb or large cuts slow-roasted over charcoal for hours, best at mountain tavernas in Theologos. Fresh fish at coastal tavernas (Skala Maries, Skala Potamias) comes straight off the boat — grilled sea bream or sea bass €10–14, grilled sardines €6–8. Pine honey (meli peuko) is Thassos's unique product — dark, dense, caramel-flavoured honey from bees feeding on pine resin, found nowhere else. Buy from roadside producers (€10–15/jar). Thassos olive oil is delicate and fruity. Raki (tsipouro) is offered free after every meal.

**Î: Is Thassos expensive?**
R: No — Thassos is one of Greece's most affordable islands. Average taverna prices: Greek salad €6–8, grilled fish €10–16, gyros €3.50–4, 500ml beer €3–4, frappé €2.50–3.50. Full meal at a local taverna: €12–20/person. Accommodation: €40–70/night for a studio, €70–130 for a 3-star hotel. Significantly cheaper than Santorini, Mykonos, or Crete. Supermarkets are pricier than mainland Greece but reasonable.

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/things-to-do-amsterdam

**Descriere:** Complete Amsterdam guide for 2026. Rijksmuseum, Anne Frank House, canal boats, coffee shops, cycling, and how to avoid the 16% tourist tax surprise.

**Rezumat rapid:** Amsterdam essentials: Rijksmuseum (€22, Rembrandt's Night Watch), Anne Frank House (€16, book 6–8 weeks ahead — it always sells out), Van Gogh Museum (€22), canal boat tour (€15–20), Jordaan neighbourhood (free, the most beautiful in the city), and a rented bicycle (€12/day). Daily budget: €80–120 — Amsterdam is expensive but worth it. Key warning: the tourist tax is 16% of your room rate and is NOT included in the Booking.com price shown.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How many days do you need in Amsterdam?**
R: 2–3 days covers the essentials: Rijksmuseum, Van Gogh Museum, Anne Frank House, a canal boat, and Jordaan. 4–5 days lets you add NDSM Wharf, Zaanse Schans windmills, Keukenhof (spring only), and deeper neighbourhood exploration. A long weekend works if you prioritise ruthlessly.

**Î: Is Amsterdam expensive?**
R: Yes, one of Europe's pricier cities. Beer at a bar: €5–6. A sit-down meal: €18–30. 3-star hotel: €120–200/night PLUS the 16% tourist tax. Daily budget: €80–120. Money-saving tricks: eat at Albert Heijn supermarket, get the I Amsterdam City Card (€65/24h, includes transport + museums), and avoid restaurants on Damrak and Leidseplein.

**Î: Are coffee shops legal in Amsterdam?**
R: Cannabis consumption is tolerated (not strictly legal — an important Dutch legal distinction) in licensed coffee shops. Rules: maximum 5g per person, consumption inside only, no mixing with alcohol (most coffee shops don't serve alcohol anyway), and you must be 18+. Smoking outdoors in most central areas has been restricted since 2023. Possession on the street remains technically illegal.

**Î: Do I need to book Anne Frank House in advance?**
R: Yes, absolutely, and as early as possible — 6–8 weeks ahead minimum in summer. The Anne Frank House sells out completely and there are no walk-up tickets. Book directly on annefrank.org. Tickets: €16 adults, €7 children (10–17), free under 10.

**Î: What is the tourist tax in Amsterdam?**
R: Amsterdam charges 16% of the room rate as a tourist tax — the highest in Europe. On a €150/night hotel for 3 nights, that's €72 extra. This is charged at check-in and is not visible in the Booking.com or Airbnb listed price. Always factor it into your accommodation budget.

**Î: Is Amsterdam safe?**
R: Yes, it is one of Europe's safest capitals. The main risks are: bicycle theft (always use a good lock), pickpockets in crowded tourist areas (Damrak, Central Station), and traffic — cyclists have absolute right of way and will not stop for pedestrians. Stay aware on bike lanes, which look like pavements but aren't.

**Î: What is the best way to get around Amsterdam?**
R: Bicycle. The city is completely flat, has 800km of dedicated bike lanes, and cycling is how locals actually move. Rent from MacBike or Donkey Republic (€12–15/day). Alternatively: trams (€4/single, GVB day pass €9.50), ferries (free across the IJ river), and walking for the centre. Avoid cars — parking is €7.50/hour in the centre and the streets are narrow.
