**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/things-to-do-athens

**Verticală:** experiente

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How many days do you need in Athens?**
R: 2-3 days for the city itself. Day 1: Acropolis + Acropolis Museum + Plaka sunset walk. Day 2: Ancient Agora + Monastiraki + food tour. Day 3: day trip (Meteora, Delphi, or Saronic islands cruise). With 4-5 days, add Cape Sounion at sunset, the National Archaeological Museum, the Athens Riviera beaches, and an evening in Psyrri or Exarchia.

**Î: Is the combined ticket for archaeological sites worth it?**

In peak season, the Acropolis alone costs €30, so the combined ticket gives you 6 extra sites for free. It's the best deal in Athens.

**Î: What's the best experience from Piraeus port (cruise passengers)?**

**Î: Is Athens safe?**

Standard big-city precautions: watch for pickpockets on the metro and crowded Monastiraki streets. Omonia Square can be rough late at night. Use Bolt/Uber instead of unlicensed taxis — they're cheaper and safer.

**Î: When is the best time to visit Athens?**
R: April-June and September-October — pleasant temperatures (20-28°C), lower prices, short queues at attractions. Avoid July-August: 38-42°C on the shadeless Acropolis is brutal. Winter (November-March) offers half-price tickets at sites, but some terrace restaurants close. Sweet spot: early October — perfect weather, few tourists, off-peak prices.

**Î: Which neighbourhood is best for accommodation in Athens?**
R: Plaka: most central and picturesque, but pricier (€80-150/night). Monastiraki: close to everything, vibrant, good value (€60-120). Koukaki: local favourite, 10 min from Acropolis, excellent authentic food (€50-100). Syntagma: best for metro/airport access, but lacks character (€70-140). Psyrri: best for nightlife (€55-110). Pangrati: authentic and quiet, near the Panathenaic Stadium (€45-90).

**Descriere:** Complete Barcelona guide 2026 — Sagrada Familia, Park Güell, Gothic Quarter, Barceloneta beach, authentic tapas, transport, tourist tax, realistic budget and insider tips.

**Rezumat rapid:** Barcelona must-dos 2026: Sagrada Familia (€26 standard, €40 with towers — booking essential 2-3 weeks ahead, no walk-up entry), Park Güell (€18 adult), Casa Batlló (€29+), Gothic Quarter (free), Barceloneta beach (free). **Î: How much does a 3-day city break in Barcelona cost?**

**Î: What is Barcelona's tourist tax in 2026?**

Charged at check-in, NOT shown on Booking.com. For a couple, 3 nights at a 4★ hotel = €50 extra. It's a significant amount that must be factored into your budget.

**Î: What's the best neighbourhood to stay in Barcelona?**
R: Eixample — best compromise: central, safe, well-connected, Gaudí on every corner (Sagrada Familia, Casa Batlló, Casa Milà). El Born — bohemian, wine bars, vintage shops, near the beach. Gràcia — village atmosphere, lower prices, Park Güell 15 minutes away. Barceloneta — beach, but can be noisy at night. Gothic Quarter — atmospheric but less safe at night in some areas.

**Î: Is Barcelona safe?**
R: Barcelona is generally safe, but has Europe's highest concentration of pickpockets. Risk zones: La Rambla, the metro (especially L3 and L1), Barceloneta beach, Gothic Quarter at night. Rules: phone and wallet in front pockets, backpack on your chest on the metro, don't put anything on the table/chair at restaurants, don't leave anything on your beach towel unattended.

**Descriere:** Complete Berlin 2026 guide — Brandenburg Gate, Reichstag dome, Holocaust Memorial, East Side Gallery, Checkpoint Charlie, Topography of Terror, Museum Island, Berghain, Potsdam day trip.

**Rezumat rapid:** Berlin deserves 4–5 days. Top priorities: Brandenburg Gate (free), Reichstag glass dome (free, advance online booking required), Holocaust Memorial (free), East Side Gallery (free), Topography of Terror (free), Museum Island (€14–22/museum). Currywurst: €4–5.50. Döner: €6–8. Berlin is cheaper than London or Paris, with dozens of major historical attractions completely free.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Is Berlin expensive?**
R: Berlin is one of the most accessible major capitals in Western Europe. Currywurst: €4–5.50. Döner kebab: €6–8. Mittagstisch (weekday lunch special): €10–14. Dozens of major historical attractions are completely free. 3-star hotel: €80–140/night. Realistic daily budget: €80–120/person comfortably. Significantly cheaper than London, Paris, or Zürich.

**Î: Do I need to book the Reichstag in advance?**
R: Yes, mandatory. The Reichstag glass dome is free but must be booked online at bundestag.de at least 2–3 weeks ahead (sometimes more in summer). The booking requires passport or ID details for all group members. Without a reservation you cannot enter — no matter how long you queue.

**Î: What is a Späti and why does it matter?**
R: Späti (Spätverkauf = late-night shop) is Berlin's neighbourhood convenience store open late or 24 hours — beer, drinks, snacks, cigarettes. Beer price at a Späti: €1–2 versus €4–6 at a bar. Locals pre-drink at the Späti before going out — it's a completely accepted cultural practice and part of the city's identity.

**Î: Is Museum Island worth doing in full?**
R: If you have 2–3 days, choose selectively. Pergamonmuseum (partial renovation in 2026 — check smb.museum for open sections), Neues Museum (Nefertiti bust), and Alte Nationalgalerie (19th-century German art) are the most powerful. Combined ticket for all 5 museums: ~€18–22.

**Î: How do I get into Berghain?**
R: Berghain is the world's most famous club and has one of the most selective doors. There is no guaranteed formula. What works better: come alone or in a very small group (2–3 people), don't dress in standard clubwear, don't photograph the queue, don't talk much at the door, be patient. €25+ entry if you get in. If you don't (it happens), don't take it personally — the door is the club's policy, not a verdict on you.

**Î: How much does a day in Bucharest cost?**
R: Budget (hostel + street food + public transport): 150-200 RON/day (€30-40). Mid-range (3★ hotel + restaurants + museums): 400-700 RON/day (€80-140). **Î: Is Bucharest safe for tourists?**

**Î: Is a guided tour worth it or should I explore on my own?**

**Î: Do card payments work everywhere?**
R: Yes, almost everywhere — restaurants, shops, public transport, museums. Exceptions: traditional markets (Obor, Amzei), some pretzel kiosks, and some taxis. Recommendation: carry 50-100 RON cash for these situations. Revolut and Wise work perfectly.

**Î: Which area should I stay in?**
R: For a first visit: near a metro station. Old Town / Universitate — ideal for nightlife and restaurants. Piata Victoriei — central, quick access to parks and museums. Piata Romana — perfect balance between centre and residential areas. Cotroceni — quiet, authentic, perfect for couples.

**Rezumat rapid:** Best things to do in Budapest 2026: Széchenyi Thermal Baths (13,200 HUF / ~€33 full-day locker), Parliament tour (7,000 HUF / ~€18 EU citizens, 14,000 HUF / ~€35 non-EU), Danube evening cruise (from €10-15), ruin bars in the Jewish Quarter (beer €2.50-4), Fisherman's Bastion (free lower terraces, 1,700 HUF upper tower), newly renovated Citadella (free park access, ~4,900 HUF exhibition), food tours (€40-65). **Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Széchenyi or Rudas — which is better in 2026?**
R: Széchenyi is Europe's largest medicinal bath, with spectacular outdoor pools and a social atmosphere — perfect for first-timers, especially in winter (warm water + steam). Rudas is more atmospheric, with Ottoman architecture from 1550, a star-lit dome, and a rooftop pool with Danube views — less touristy, ideal in the evening. Gellért is closed for renovation until 2028. Prices: Széchenyi 13,200 HUF (~€33), Rudas 12,000-15,000 HUF (~€30-38).

**Î: How many days do you need in Budapest?**

**Î: Is Budapest Card worth it in 2026?**
R: Depends on your style. Prices: 24h ~€40, 48h ~€55, 72h ~€65. Includes unlimited public transport, entry to 17+ museums, a Danube cruise, and 10-15% off baths. Worth it if you visit 4+ museums and use transport frequently. If your plan is thermal baths + food + ruin bars, you'll spend less without the card.

**Î: Is Budapest safe?**
R: Very safe. It's one of Europe's safest capitals. Only watch out for: pickpockets on the metro and in crowded tourist areas (Váci utca, Central Market), taxis off the street can overcharge — use Bolt or Főtaxi, and avoid restaurants on Váci utca that don't display prices.

**Î: What currency does Budapest use?**
R: Hungarian Forint (HUF). €1 ≈ 395-400 HUF (2026). Cards are accepted almost everywhere, including markets and kiosks. Revolut or Wise are ideal for real-rate conversion. Avoid street exchange offices — they have hidden fees. ATMs are fine, but always decline 'Dynamic Currency Conversion' (DCC) — let it charge in HUF.

**Î: How to get to Budapest?**
R: By air: direct flights from most European cities (1-3 hours). Budget airlines (Wizz Air, Ryanair) offer fares from €30-60 one-way. Airport to city: 100E bus (2,200 HUF / ~€5.50, 30-40 minutes to Deák Ferenc tér). By train: well connected to Vienna (2.5h), Prague (7h), Bratislava (2.5h). ## Things to Do in Dresden: Complete 2026 Guide with Prices, History & Insider Tips

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/things-to-do-dresden
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-08-06
**Actualizat:** 2026-08-06
**Traducere a:** [ce-sa-faci-in-dresda](https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/ce-sa-faci-in-dresda)

**Descriere:** Complete Dresden 2026 guide — Zwinger Palace, Frauenkirche rebuilt from rubble, Semperoper, Sistine Madonna, Saxon Switzerland day trip. The full story of the 1945 bombing and the reconstruction.

**Rezumat rapid:** Dresden deserves 2–3 days. Top priorities: Zwinger Palace courtyard (free) and Old Masters Gallery with Raphael's Sistine Madonna (~€14), Frauenkirche rebuilt from original stones (nave free, dome €10), Semperoper guided tour (€14) or opera performance, and the Saxon Switzerland day trip (30 min by train). Dresden is cheaper than Munich or Berlin, with a reconstruction story that exists nowhere else in Europe.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Why is Dresden called the 'Florence of the Elbe'?**
R: Dresden earned the nickname in the 18th century due to the Italian Baroque and Rococo architecture commissioned by Augustus the Strong — the Zwinger, Semperoper, Royal Palace, and Frauenkirche formed an architectural ensemble comparable to the finest in Europe. The historical irony: this very beauty attracted Allied attention in 1945, when Dresden was one of the few major German cities not yet bombed. It was attacked three months before the war ended.

**Î: What actually happened on the night of February 13, 1945?**
R: February 13–15, 1945: RAF (British) and USAAF (American) aircraft dropped over 3,900 tons of incendiary and high-explosive bombs on Dresden. The resulting firestorms reached 1,500°C and destroyed 1,600 acres of the city center. Approximately 25,000 people died, mostly civilians. The Frauenkirche collapsed the following morning. The debate about the military necessity of the attack continues — Dresden was not a major military target and the war was effectively already won.

**Î: How was the Frauenkirche rebuilt?**
R: The ruins stood in the city center throughout the Cold War as a deliberate memorial (an East German political decision). After reunification, reconstruction began in 1994, brick by brick, with original stones catalogued and reintegrated wherever possible. The dark, scorched stones are deliberately visible in the facade alongside lighter new sandstone — not a construction error, but an intentional design decision: a map of survival and renewal simultaneously. The reconsecration was held on October 30, 2005.

**Î: Is Dresden worth visiting compared to Berlin?**
R: They are different experiences. Berlin is the capital with Wall history, enormous free museums, and one of the world's best cultural scenes — it needs 4–5 days. Dresden is smaller, more Baroque, more intimate, with a unique reconstruction story and Saxon Switzerland 30 minutes away. 2 days are enough for Dresden, and it combines well with Berlin on a longer city break.

**Î: How do I get from Bucharest to Dresden?**
R: No direct flight. Most efficient: fly to Berlin (BER, 2h30 direct with Wizz Air) + train Berlin–Dresden (2h, €25–40). Or fly to Prague (2h direct) + train Prague–Dresden (2h15, €20–35). Alternatively, fly to Frankfurt or Munich + ICE train to Dresden (3–4h).

---

## Things to Do in Gdańsk: Complete 2026 Guide with Prices, Amber, Solidarity & Insider Tips

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/things-to-do-gdansk
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-08-05
**Actualizat:** 2026-08-05
**Traducere a:** [ce-sa-faci-in-gdansk](https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/ce-sa-faci-in-gdansk)

**Descriere:** Complete Gdańsk 2026 guide — Old Town, WWII Museum, European Solidarity Centre, Malbork Castle, amber on Mariacka Street, Sopot beach, Tricity day trips. The Baltic port where history changed Europe.

**Rezumat rapid:** Gdańsk deserves 3–4 days. Top priorities: Długi Targ and Old Town (free), Museum of the Second World War (~€8, free Tuesdays), European Solidarity Centre (~€8), amber shopping on Mariacka Street, day trip to Malbork Castle (45 min by train, world's largest Gothic castle). Sopot is 15 minutes by train with Europe's longest pier. Polish prices — pierogi €5–7, craft beer €2–3, 3-star hotel €40–70/night.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Why is Gdańsk historically significant?**
R: Gdańsk is where World War II began (September 1, 1939, the attack on Westerplatte) and where Communism began to unravel — in August 1980, Lech Wałęsa organized the strike at the Lenin Shipyard that created Solidarność, the first independent trade union in the Soviet bloc. This triggered the chain reaction that brought down Communist governments across Eastern Europe. The city's Hanseatic merchant architecture looks more like Amsterdam than Warsaw.

**Î: What is the amber from Gdańsk?**
R: The Polish Baltic coast produces 70–90% of the world's amber — fossilized tree resin 44 million years old, sometimes with perfectly preserved insects or plants inside. Gdańsk has been the center of the amber trade for at least 3,000 years. Mariacka Street is the commercial hub: jewelry, sculptures, and souvenirs, all in authentic amber. Buy from shops with certificates of authenticity, not from street stalls.

**Î: Is Malbork Castle worth the day trip?**
R: Absolutely. Malbork Castle (45 minutes by train from Gdańsk, ~€2 return) is the largest castle in the world by area and the most impressive Gothic castle complex in Central Europe — built by the Teutonic Knights from red brick in the 13th–15th centuries, UNESCO since 1997. Entry ~€25. Allow 3–4 hours. One of the most impressive day trips from any Central European city break.

**Î: What is Tricity (Trójmiasto)?**
R: Trójmiasto is the urban agglomeration of Gdańsk + Sopot + Gdynia. The SKM commuter train connects all three in 30–40 minutes total, with tickets at €1–2 per segment. Sopot is the resort town with Europe's longest wooden pier (511m), Monte Cassino (Poland's most animated pedestrian boulevard), and fine sandy beaches. Gdynia is a modern port city with an interesting naval museum. You can see all three in a single day.

**Î: When is the best time to visit Gdańsk?**
R: May–September: good weather, Sopot beaches open, cultural festivals. July–August: most animated, St. Dominic's Fair (Poland's oldest market, 750+ years). December: Christmas markets considered among Poland's most beautiful. Winter (Jan–Feb): minimum prices, quiet, but genuine Baltic cold (−5 to 5°C).

Budget: €45-70/day — incredibly affordable. Kebab meal: €5-8. Tea: €0.40. Ferry: ~€1. Museum Pass Istanbul: €105 (5 days, 13 museums). Non-EU visitors need an eSIM — roaming is expensive.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How many days do you need in Istanbul?**
R: Minimum 3 full days for the essentials: Day 1 — Sultanahmet (Hagia Sophia, Blue Mosque, Basilica Cistern, Topkapi). Day 2 — Bosphorus cruise + Grand Bazaar + Spice Bazaar. Day 3 — Asian side (Kadıköy, Moda) + hammam + shopping. With 4-5 days add Balat, Dolmabahçe Palace, Princes' Islands. With 7 days you explore everything — including day trips to Bursa or Cappadocia.

**Î: Do I need a visa for Istanbul?**
R: Most nationalities (US, UK, EU, Canada, Australia) can enter Turkey visa-free for up to 90 days. Passport must be valid for 6 months from entry date. National ID cards are NOT accepted — a common mistake.

**Î: Which is the best hammam in Istanbul?**
R: Depends on budget. Premium: Kılıç Ali Paşa Hamamı (from €90, spectacularly restored, luxury experience) or Ayasofya Hürrem Sultan (from €110, between Hagia Sophia and Blue Mosque). Budget: Mihrimah Sultan (from €25, most authentic, cash only) or Çinili Hamam Üsküdar (from €25, local atmosphere on the Asian side).

**Î: Is Istanbul safe for tourists?**
R: Yes, Istanbul is very safe for tourists. Tourist areas (Sultanahmet, Taksim, Kadıköy) are well-lit and populated. Standard precautions: watch for pickpockets at the Grand Bazaar and on tram T1, bargain on prices (first offer is 2-3x the real price), avoid taxis without meters (use BiTaksi or Bolt), and decline 'friendly' bar invitations — it's Istanbul's most famous scam (the bill arrives at €200+).

**Î: How do I get from Istanbul Airport (IST) to the city centre?**
R: Metro (M11 line): 30-40 TL (~€0.60), reach Sultanahmet with one transfer in ~60 minutes. Havaist (bus): 170-200 TL (~€3.50), 60-90 minutes to Taksim. Taxi/Bolt: 900-1,200 TL (€16-22), 45-90 minutes depending on traffic. Recommendation: the metro is fastest and cheapest.

**Î: What is Museum Pass Istanbul and is it worth it?**
R: Museum Pass Istanbul costs €105 and is valid for 5 days covering 13 museums/attractions, including Topkapi Palace with Harem and Galata Tower. It does NOT include Hagia Sophia (€25), Basilica Cistern (1,950 TL), or Dolmabahçe Palace (2,000 TL). Worth it if you visit 3+ included attractions — otherwise individual tickets are more economical.

**Î: Does my phone roaming work in Turkey?**
R: Turkey is NOT in the EU — free EU roaming does not apply. Your carrier will charge €3-15/day. An eSIM from Airalo costs €4-5 for 1GB/7 days — dramatically cheaper. Install before departure.

**Descriere:** Complete Krakow 2026 guide — Wawel Castle, Kazimierz Jewish Quarter, Wieliczka Salt Mine, Auschwitz-Birkenau, Polish food, what's free, and a realistic budget. Europe's cheapest city break.

**Rezumat rapid:** Krakow deserves 3–4 days. Top priorities: Wawel Castle (grounds free, exhibitions €10–18), Kazimierz Jewish Quarter, Wieliczka Salt Mine 15km away (€33, must book online), and the Auschwitz-Birkenau day trip (70km, free entry but guided tour strongly recommended). Krakow is Central Europe's most affordable city break — pierogi €6–8, craft beer €2–3, 3-star hotel €30–60/night. Direct flight from Bucharest with Wizz Air, ~2h.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How much does a 3-day city break in Krakow cost?**
R: Realistic budget per person: flights round-trip €60–120 (Wizz Air direct from Bucharest), 3 nights accommodation €90–180 (3-star hotel), attractions €80–100 (Wawel + Auschwitz + Wieliczka), food €40–60. Total: €270–460/person. Krakow is 40–50% cheaper than Prague or Vienna for equivalent experiences.

**Î: Do I need to book Auschwitz tickets in advance?**
R: Yes, mandatory in season (May–September). Entry to Auschwitz-Birkenau is free, but timed slots are limited and sell out 2–3 weeks ahead in summer. Book at auschwitz.org or via GetYourGuide. **Î: Is Wieliczka Salt Mine worth visiting?**
R: Absolutely. The Wieliczka Salt Mine (UNESCO, 14km from Krakow) is one of Europe's most impressive underground attractions — 22 chambers carved entirely in salt, including St. Kinga's Chapel at 101m depth with chandeliers and bas-reliefs all made from salt. Standard tour 2–3h, €33/adult. Book online — in peak season tickets sell out 3–5 days ahead.

**Î: What's the best neighborhood in Krakow to stay?**
R: Old Town (Stare Miasto, within the ring road) is ideal for a first visit — everything is walkable. Kazimierz (the Jewish Quarter) offers more atmosphere, better restaurants, and prices 20% lower — perfect if you've been to Krakow before. Avoid the area around the central train station — far from attractions and less pleasant at night.

**Î: What's the currency in Poland — do they use euros?**
R: Poland uses the Polish Złoty (PLN). 1 EUR ≈ 4.30 PLN. Most places accept cards, but cash is sometimes cheaper. Avoid airport exchange offices — Kantor (currency exchange) offices in Kazimierz offer better rates. Never exchange at banks — commissions are high.

## Things to Do in Lisbon: Complete 2026 Guide with Prices, Alfama, Sintra & Insider Tips

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/things-to-do-lisbon
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-08-06
**Actualizat:** 2026-08-06
**Traducere a:** [ce-sa-faci-in-lisabona](https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/ce-sa-faci-in-lisabona)

**Descriere:** Complete Lisbon 2026 guide — Alfama, Jerónimos Monastery, Belém, free miradouros, authentic fado, ginjinha, Sintra day trip. Important: Belém Tower closed for restoration in 2026.

**Rezumat rapid:** Lisbon deserves 3–4 days. Top priorities: Alfama and the historic neighborhoods (free, with fado in the evening), Jerónimos Monastery in Belém (~€18, book online), free miradouros at sunset, ginjinha at €1.50 a shot (mandatory), and the Sintra day trip (40 min by train, €2.45). Important 2026: Belém Tower is closed for restoration — photographable from outside but interior inaccessible. Lisbon is more expensive than Porto but offers unmatched neighborhood variety and energy.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Is the Belém Tower open in 2026?**
R: No — Belém Tower is closed for restoration under Portugal's Recovery and Resilience Plan, with reopening expected sometime mid-2026 (date unconfirmed at time of writing). You can photograph the tower from the riverside promenade and surrounding gardens. Jerónimos Monastery, 500 meters away, is open and justifies the Belém trip on its own.

**Î: Lisbon or Porto — which should I visit first?**
R: Lisbon is the first choice for a first visit to Portugal — larger, more diverse, with multiple distinct neighborhoods (Alfama, Chiado, Bairro Alto, Belém, Parque das Nações), more theatrical fado, and Sintra 40 minutes away. Porto is more authentic, 20–30% cheaper, and has Port wine at source. Ideally you visit both — they're 3 hours apart by train.

**Î: What is the couvert in Portuguese restaurants?**
R: When you sit down, the waiter automatically brings bread, butter, olives, sometimes cheese or fish paste. These are NOT free — they appear on your bill (€2–5 per person). If you don't want them, decline immediately: 'Não, obrigado.' It's completely normal to refuse.

**Î: Is Tram 28 worth it or is it just for tourists?**
R: Tram 28 is a real public transport line that crosses Alfama and connects the historic neighborhoods — not a tourist attraction, but the tram locals used for decades. Worth it for atmosphere and the route through steep neighborhoods, but in summer it's packed with tourists. The alternative: bus 737 does the same route faster, with no queue.

**Î: Is Sintra worth a day trip?**
R: Yes, unconditionally — it's one of the most beautiful day trips in southern Europe. Train from Rossio in 40 minutes (€2.45 return) takes you to Sintra, with Pena Palace (pink and yellow on the mountain, €17), the National Palace (in the town center, €10), the Moorish Castle with mountain walls (€10), and Cabo da Roca — the westernmost point of continental Europe. Book Pena Palace online — it sells out weeks in advance.

**Descriere:** Complete Ljubljana 2026 guide — Ljubljana Castle, Dragon Bridge, Metelkova, Lake Bled 1h away, Postojna Cave, Slovenian food, what's free. Europe's smallest and most surprising city break.

Top priorities: Ljubljana Castle (free walk up, funicular €6, excellent views), Dragon Bridge and Prešeren Square (free), Metelkova alternative art district (free during the day), Lake Bled day trip (1h15 by bus, €6) and Postojna Cave (1h, €28). **Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Is Lake Bled worth the day trip from Ljubljana?**
R: Yes, absolutely — it's one of the most photogenic views in Europe. 1h15 by bus from Ljubljana (€6 return), Lake Bled has a small island with a white church in the center, a medieval castle on a cliff above the water, and the Slovenian Alps as backdrop. The original kremšnita cream cake (since 1953) is mandatory. In summer it gets crowded — arrive early.

**Î: Is Ljubljana expensive?**

**Î: What is Metelkova and is it worth visiting?**
R: Metelkova is the former Yugoslav Army barracks, occupied in 1993 by artists and activists and transformed into the largest urban autonomous art zone in Europe. Buildings covered entirely with graffiti and art installations, alternative clubs, galleries, and a completely different energy from the tourist center. Daytime visit is free and interesting. Evenings (Thu–Sat) it becomes alternative nightlife. Not for everyone, but genuinely authentic.

**Î: How do I get from Bucharest to Ljubljana?**
R: No regular direct flight. The most efficient routes: fly to Venice (2h, Wizz Air/Ryanair) + bus or train to Ljubljana (2h30, ~€15–25). Or fly to Vienna (1h40) + Railjet train Vienna–Ljubljana (5h, €20–40). Or fly to Zagreb (1h) + bus Zagreb–Ljubljana (2h30, €8–15). Most accessible via Venice or Zagreb.

**Descriere:** Complete Munich 2026 guide — Marienplatz, English Garden with surfers, Nymphenburg Palace, Deutsches Museum, Bavarian beer gardens, Oktoberfest, and Neuschwanstein Castle day trip.

**Rezumat rapid:** Munich deserves 3–4 days. Top priorities: Marienplatz with the Glockenspiel (free), English Garden with the Eisbach surfers (free), Nymphenburg Palace (€15 full ticket), Deutsches Museum (€15), an evening at a local beer garden (€8–10 a litre), and the Neuschwanstein Castle day trip (€21 entry + train). Munich is expensive but has dozens of free attractions. Oktoberfest (September–October) transforms the city completely — book your hotel a year in advance.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Is Munich expensive?**
R: Yes — Munich is one of Germany's most expensive cities and among Europe's priciest. 3-star hotel: €100–180/night, beer at Hofbräuhaus: €12–13/litre, traditional meal: €20–35. But it has dozens of free attractions (English Garden, Marienplatz, Viktualienmarkt, state museums at €1 on Sundays) and beer gardens where you can bring your own food and only pay for drinks. Realistic budget: €100–150/person/day.

**Î: Is Oktoberfest worth it if you don't drink beer?**
R: Surprisingly yes. Oktoberfest is more than beer — it's a folk festival with carousels, live music, authentic Bavarian food (rotisserie chicken, pork knuckle, giant pretzels), and a globally unique atmosphere. Entry to the festival grounds is free. You only pay for food and drink inside the tents. Without beer, your daily budget drops to €25–40 versus €60–100+ with drinks.

**Î: How do I get to Neuschwanstein Castle from Munich?**
R: Regional train (Regionalbahn) Munich–Füssen: ~2h, €21 return, or €29 with Bayern Ticket (covers up to 5 people — best value for groups). From Füssen, bus 73/78 to the castle (€4–6). Castle ticket: €21 adults — online booking mandatory months in advance in summer. Alternatively, an organised tour from Munich with transport included: €50–70.

**Î: When is Oktoberfest 2026?**
R: Oktoberfest 2026: September 19 – October 4, 2026. Dates vary annually — the first Saturday after September 15 is always opening day. Munich hotels during this period cost 3–5x the normal rate (€200–600/night for a 3-star). Book accommodation at least 6–12 months in advance.

**Î: What is the Bayern Ticket and how do I use it?**
R: Bayern Ticket is a regional train pass for Bavaria, valid for one day for 1–5 people at the same fixed price: €29/group (€26 digital). Covers all regional trains (not ICE/IC) in Bavaria Monday–Friday after 9:00 AM, all day on weekends. Perfect for Neuschwanstein (Füssen), Salzburg (Austria), or anywhere in Bavaria. One person pays €29, but 5 people also pay €29 — extremely efficient for groups.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How many days do you need in Paris?**
R: 3-4 days for the highlights, 5 days for a complete experience. Day 1: Eiffel Tower + Seine cruise + Trocadéro. Day 2: Louvre (3-4h) + Tuileries + Champs-Élysées. **Î: Is Paris really that expensive?**
R: The sit-down terrace coffee that costs €5 makes headlines, but the same espresso at the bar counter is €1.50-2. A croissant from any boulangerie: €1.20. A crêpe from a street stand: €4-6. A full brasserie meal (steak-frites + wine): €15-20. Le Bouillon Chartier serves 3-course meals for €15-18 in a stunning Belle Époque dining room since 1896. Paris is expensive at tourist spots and surprisingly affordable everywhere else. The key: eat and drink where Parisians do.

**Î: Is the Paris Museum Pass worth it in 2026?**
R: Yes, if you visit 3+ museums. Paris Museum Pass 2026: 2-day €85, 4-day €105, 6-day €125. Includes Louvre (€32), Orsay (€16), Versailles (€21), Sainte-Chapelle (€22), Arc de Triomphe (€16), Orangerie (€12.50), Panthéon + 50 more. Does NOT include Eiffel Tower, Disneyland, Catacombs, or Seine cruises. Louvre + Orsay + Versailles + Sainte-Chapelle = €91 without pass — so from 3-4 museums in 2 days, the pass saves money plus skip-the-line.

**Î: How do I get from CDG airport to central Paris?**
R: RER B train is the best option: €11.45, 35 minutes, runs every 10-15 minutes. Roissybus: €16.60, 60-75 minutes to Opéra (better with bulky luggage). Taxi: fixed fare €55 (right bank) or €62 (left bank). Uber: €45-70 depending on demand. Never accept transport from people who approach you in the terminal — they're unlicensed and charge double.

**Î: What's the best neighbourhood for a hotel in Paris?**
R: Le Marais (3rd-4th arr.) — central, vibrant, close to Louvre and Notre-Dame. Saint-Germain (6th arr.) — elegant, literary, pricier. Montmartre (18th arr.) — atmospheric, cheaper, hilly. Bastille/Oberkampf (11th arr.) — local vibe, great restaurants, better prices. Avoid: Gare du Nord area at night, and the 1st arrondissement (ultra-touristy, double prices).

**Î: How far ahead should I book Eiffel Tower tickets?**
R: 60 days ahead minimum in summer for official tickets (they sell out within minutes of release). Guided tours with priority access via GetYourGuide are the practical alternative — tour operators have allocated quotas and can offer tickets even when the official site shows sold out. They cost more (€50-70) but include skip-the-line and a guide. Official 2026 prices: stairs to 2nd floor €14.80, elevator to summit €36.70.

## Things to Do in Porto: Complete 2026 Guide with Prices, Port Wine, Douro Valley & Tips

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/things-to-do-porto
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-08-05
**Actualizat:** 2026-08-05
**Traducere a:** [ce-sa-faci-in-porto](https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/ce-sa-faci-in-porto)

**Descriere:** Complete Porto 2026 guide — Ribeira UNESCO, Livraria Lello, Dom Luís Bridge, Port wine cellars in Gaia, francesinha, Douro Valley day trip. Porto is better than Lisbon and 30% cheaper.

**Rezumat rapid:** Porto deserves 3–4 days. Top priorities: Ribeira and Dom Luís I Bridge (free), Livraria Lello (€8, redeemable against a book), Port wine cellars in Vila Nova de Gaia (€15–25 with tasting), Clérigos Tower (€8), and the Douro Valley day trip (€50–80 guided). Francesinha is the mandatory meal. Porto is 30% cheaper than Lisbon and far more authentic — locals haven't left yet.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Porto or Lisbon — which is better?**
R: It depends what you're looking for. Lisbon is larger, more cosmopolitan, easier to reach. Porto is more authentic, more compact, with a stronger identity, Port wine at the source, and prices 20–30% lower for accommodation and food. Francesinha doesn't exist in Lisbon. If it's your first time in Portugal, Lisbon comes first. If you've already been — Porto is the revelation.

**Î: Is Livraria Lello worth it and how do I avoid the queue?**
R: Yes, it's worth it — it's one of the most beautiful bookshops in the world, with a polychrome carved wooden spiral staircase that inspired the (unconfirmed) rumor that J.K. Rowling, who lived in Porto in 1991–1993 as an English teacher, drew on it for Hogwarts. Entry costs €8, redeemable against any purchase. The queue is long 11:00–15:00. Arrive at opening (9:30 AM) or book online with a timed entry slot — you avoid 45+ minutes of waiting.

**Î: What is a francesinha and why is it mandatory?**
R: Francesinha is Porto's iconic sandwich — layers of cured ham, linguiça sausage, and steak between slices of bread, covered with melted cheese and a fried egg, flooded with a spicy beer-and-tomato sauce. It's a complete meal (€8–12), served with chips. It doesn't exist in Lisbon or anywhere else in Portugal — it's specific to Porto. Café Santiago is considered the benchmark.

**Î: What is Vila Nova de Gaia and why should I go?**
R: Vila Nova de Gaia is the city on the south bank of the Douro, directly across from Porto. All the major Port wine houses (Taylor's, Sandeman, Graham's, Calem) have their lodges there — on the hillside above the riverbank, with views across to Porto and the Ribeira. A tour with tasting costs €15–25. Cable car to the riverside: €5–7. It's the 2–3 hour excursion that justifies a flight to Porto on its own.

**Î: What is the couvert in Portuguese restaurants?**
R: When you sit down in a Portuguese restaurant, the waiter automatically brings bread, olive oil, butter, olives, sometimes cheese. They are NOT free — they appear on the bill. If you don't want to pay €2–4 extra, politely decline: 'Não, obrigado.' This is standard practice across Portugal, not a scam.

## Things to Do in Prague 2026: Castle, Beer Culture, Hidden Gems & Real Prices

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/things-to-do-prague
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-07-15
**Actualizat:** 2026-08-23
**Traducere a:** [ce-sa-faci-in-praga](https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/ce-sa-faci-in-praga)

**Descriere:** Complete Prague guide for 2026 with real prices in CZK and EUR, day-by-day itineraries, best beer halls, authentic Czech food, local neighbourhoods, day trips, and tested practical tips.

**Rezumat rapid:** Prague essentials 2026: Prague Castle — world's largest castle complex (Main Circuit ~450 CZK/~€18), Charles Bridge at dawn (free, go at 6 AM), Old Town Square + Astronomical Clock (free, hourly show), Czech beer at a local hospoda (55-80 CZK/€2-3 for the best lager on Earth), Vltava cruise (from 350 CZK), Jewish Quarter Josefov (~600 CZK full ticket), and day trip to Český Krumlov (UNESCO). Budget: €50-70/day (budget) or €100-150 (mid-range). 1 EUR ≈ 24.2 CZK (2026).

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How many days do you need in Prague?**
R: 3-4 days is ideal. Day 1: Old Town — Old Town Square, Astronomical Clock, Charles Bridge, Clementinum. Day 2: Prague Castle + Malá Strana + Petřín Hill. Day 3: Jewish Quarter (Josefov) + Vyšehrad + beer tasting. Day 4 (optional): day trip to Český Krumlov or Kutná Hora. With 2 days you can cover the essentials if you start early.

**Î: Is Prague Card worth it in 2026?**
R: Prague Card 2026 (2 days: ~€67, 3 days: ~€77, 4 days: ~€87) includes public transport + 60+ attractions + river cruise. Worth it if you visit 4+ museums/attractions per day. If your plan is mostly walking + food + beer + 2-3 major sights, it's cheaper without the card. Prague Castle alone costs ~450 CZK (~€18), and Josefov ~600 CZK (~€24).

**Î: What Czech beer should I try in Prague?**
R: Pilsner Urquell (the original pilsner from 1842, brewed in Plzeň), Budějovický Budvar (the real Czech Budweiser), Staropramen (brewed in Prague's Smíchov district), Kozel (excellent dark lager), Bernard (unpasteurised premium), and craft beers from BeerGeek or Bad Flash. A beer tasting tour (4-6 beers, €35-60) takes you to pubs you'd never find on Google. Beer at a local hospoda costs 55-80 CZK (€2.30-3.30) — the cheapest in Europe.

**Î: What's the best time to visit Prague?**
R: Spring (April-May) is ideal: gardens blooming, 15-22°C, moderate tourists. Autumn (September-October): spectacular colours, pleasant temperatures. Summer (July-August): hot (25-35°C) and crowded, but terraces and festivals. Winter (December-February): Prague Christmas markets are among Europe's finest, but it's cold (-5 to 3°C) and extremely crowded in the centre. November and March: cheapest but grey.

**Î: Is Prague safe for tourists?**
R: Prague is one of Europe's safest capitals. The only real issues: pickpockets on Charles Bridge, in metro A, and at the Astronomical Clock (use inside pockets); dishonest taxi drivers (use Bolt/Uber only); and tourist-area exchange offices that hide 15-20% commissions (use bank ATMs or pay by card). Violent crime is extremely rare.

**Î: Should I exchange money or pay by card in Prague?**
R: Pay by card wherever you can — acceptance is nearly universal. When paying by card abroad, ALWAYS refuse the POS conversion (DCC — Dynamic Currency Conversion) and choose to pay in CZK, otherwise you'll pay a hidden 3-7% fee. For cash (markets, kiosks), withdraw from bank ATMs (Komerční banka, ČSOB, Česká spořitelna). NEVER exchange at the tourist-street exchange offices — commissions reach 15-20%.

**Descriere:** Complete Seville 2026 guide — Real Alcázar, Cathedral, Plaza de España, authentic flamenco, cheap tapas, what's free, and day trips to Córdoba and Ronda. Real prices, insider tips, direct booking.

**Rezumat rapid:** Seville deserves 3–4 days. Top priorities: Real Alcázar (€15.50, mandatory nominative booking), Cathedral and Giralda Tower (€13 online), Plaza de España (free), and flamenco at an authentic tablao (€20–45). Summer is extreme — 40°C in July-August. Best time to visit: March–May or October–November. Cheap tapas, a unique atmosphere, and the finest Mudéjar architecture in the world.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: When is the best time to visit Seville?**
R: March–May and October–November are ideal: 20–26°C, orange blossom in spring, reduced crowds compared to summer. Summer (July–August) is brutal — 38–42°C at noon, asphalt surface temperatures exceeding 50°C. If you go in summer, plan all activities before 1 PM and after 6 PM. Winter (December–February) is cool (12–16°C) but perfectly functional with minimum prices.

**Î: Do I need to book Alcázar tickets in advance?**
R: Yes, it is mandatory. The Real Alcázar ticket is nominative — you must provide your name, ID or passport number, and nationality at booking. Entry is only permitted within a 30-minute slot. In peak season, tickets sell out days or weeks in advance. Book at alcazarsevilla.org at least 1 week ahead (2–3 weeks in peak season). Free entry on Mondays at 18:00–18:30 with online reservation.

**Î: What's the difference between authentic and tourist flamenco?**
R: The difference is significant. A tourist tablao (€50–80 with dinner) has skilled artists but a restaurant atmosphere. A peña flamenca (local flamenco club, €5–12) may have less famous artists but genuine emotion — the dancers aren't performing for tourists, they're living the music. Casa de la Memoria and Teatro Flamenco Triana are the ideal compromise: tablao quality at lower prices (€20–35). La Carbonería is free but overcrowded.

**Î: How much does a 3-day city break in Seville cost?**
R: Realistic budget per person for 3 days: flights round-trip €100–200, accommodation 3 nights €120–240 (3-star hotel), attractions €80–100 (Alcázar + Cathedral + flamenco), food €90–120 (tapas at local prices). Total: €390–660 per person. Seville is 30–40% cheaper than Barcelona or Madrid for the same level of experience.

**Î: Can I do Córdoba or Ronda as a day trip from Seville?**
R: Yes. Córdoba is 45 minutes by high-speed AVE train (€25–35 return) — the Mezquita and old town are comfortable in a day. Ronda is 2 hours by bus or car — the gorge views are unforgettable but a car adds flexibility to visit the White Villages nearby. Both day trips are worth it.

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/things-to-do-sofia

**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-08-05
**Actualizat:** 2026-08-05

**Descriere:** Complete Sofia 2026 guide — Alexander Nevsky Cathedral, Roman Serdica ruins, Boyana Church UNESCO, Rila Monastery day trip, Plovdiv, Bulgarian food, what's free. Bulgaria adopted the euro in 2026.

**Rezumat rapid:** Sofia deserves 3–4 days. Top priorities: Alexander Nevsky Cathedral (nave free, crypt €5), Roman Serdica ruins inside the metro station (free), Rila Monastery UNESCO day trip (€25–35 with guide), and Plovdiv — Europe's oldest continuously inhabited city (2h by bus). Sofia is Europe's most affordable capital — €35–60/day comfortable. Bulgaria adopted the euro on January 1, 2026.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Does Bulgaria still use the lev or has it switched to euros?**
R: Bulgaria officially adopted the euro on January 1, 2026. All prices are now in euros, cards work without currency conversion fees for EU citizens, and there is no longer any need to exchange currency. This is a major change from everything written before 2026 — always verify that the information you're reading is up to date.

**Î: Is the Rila Monastery day trip worth it from Sofia?**
R: Absolutely — it is one of the most important day trips in any Eastern European city break. 120 km from Sofia (2h by car), Rila Monastery is Bulgaria's largest Orthodox monastic complex, UNESCO since 1983, with Zahari Zograf's frescoes and Raphael's Cross with 140 biblical scenes carved at microscale. Guided tour with transport from Sofia: €25–35/person. Alternatively, a rental car takes about 2 hours.

**Î: What is special about the Roman Serdica ruins in Sofia?**
R: Serdica was the Roman name for Sofia — and the ruins are visible directly inside the central metro station. You can walk on a 2nd-century AD Roman street 3 meters below the current boulevard, for free, while waiting for the metro. It is one of the rare places in the world where modern and ancient infrastructure literally overlap.

**Î: How much does a 3-day city break in Sofia cost?**
R: Sofia is Europe's most affordable capital: 3-star hotel €35–60/night, local restaurant meal €6–12, attractions €3–8 each. Total per person for 3 days including flights: €200–350 (including the Rila day trip). Less expensive than any comparable European weekend at equivalent quality.

**Î: Is Plovdiv worth combining with Sofia?**
R: Yes. Plovdiv is 2 hours by bus or train, has an Old Town with Revival-era houses, an intact Roman amphitheatre, and the Kapana creative district with galleries and cafés. It is smaller and more relaxed than Sofia, with an atmosphere close to Prague or Kraków. With 4 days, combine: 2 days Sofia + Rila, 1 day Plovdiv.

**Descriere:** Complete Tallinn 2026 guide — UNESCO Old Town, Toompea viewpoints, III Draakon elk soup €5, Kalamaja district, Helsinki ferry day trip, Vana Tallinn liqueur. Europe's most intact medieval capital.

**Rezumat rapid:** Tallinn deserves 2–3 days. Top priorities: UNESCO Old Town (free to explore), Toompea with rooftop views (free), elk soup at III Draakon tavern (€5, no cutlery), Kalamaja creative district, and the Helsinki ferry day trip (2h, €20–45). Estonia is the world's most digital country and everyone speaks English. Comfortable daily budget: €50–70 — significantly cheaper than Scandinavian neighbours.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Why is Tallinn special compared to other Baltic capitals?**
R: Tallinn has the most intact medieval center in Northern Europe — towers, walls, and alleys from the 13th–15th centuries almost entirely undamaged. Estonia is the world's most digital country (e-residency, online voting since 2005, all government services digital-first). The proximity to Helsinki — 80 km across the Gulf — makes it ideal for a combined day trip. And it's the only place in Europe where you eat elk soup in a medieval cellar by candlelight for €5.

**Î: Is Tallinn expensive?**
R: Not compared to Scandinavian neighbours, but more than Eastern Europe. Realistic daily budget: €50–70/person (3-star hotel €60–90/night, local restaurant meal €12–20). Significantly cheaper than Helsinki or Stockholm (40–50% less), but more expensive than Riga or Vilnius. The trick: eat at the päevapraad (daily lunch special, €5–8) and avoid restaurants on Raekoja Plats.

**Î: Is the Helsinki day trip worth it from Tallinn?**
R: Yes, completely — it's one of the rare European one-day trips between two genuinely different countries. The Tallink/Viking Line ferry takes 2–2.5 hours, round trip €20–45 booked in advance. Helsinki has completely different architecture (Russian Neoclassical imperial), the Kauppatori fish market, a sea-view public sauna, and a unique Nordic design center. Plan at least 5–6 hours in Helsinki.

**Î: What is päevapraad and how do I find it?**
R: Päevapraad is the daily lunch special at Estonian restaurants — soup + main course + sometimes a drink at a fixed price, usually €5–8, available Monday–Friday at lunchtime. It is Tallinn's best deal and locals rely on it daily. Look for it on restaurant websites or the boards at the entrance. Even good restaurants outside the Old Town have excellent päevapraad at €7–9.

**Î: When is the best time to visit Tallinn?**
R: May–September: long days (in June the sun sets after 10:30 PM), festivals, Old Town at maximum life. July–August: most animated but also most crowded (cruise ships bring 5,000+ tourists daily). December: renowned Christmas markets, snow on medieval rooftops — the iconic image. Winter (Jan–Feb): extremely cold (−10 to −20°C possible) but minimum prices and zero tourists.

## Things to Do in Valletta & Malta: Complete 2026 Guide with Prices, Gozo & Insider Tips

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/things-to-do-valletta-malta

**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-08-05
**Actualizat:** 2026-08-05
**Traducere a:** [ce-sa-faci-in-valletta-malta](https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/ce-sa-faci-in-valletta-malta)

**Descriere:** Complete Valletta and Malta 2026 guide — St. John's Co-Cathedral with Caravaggio, Grand Harbour, Gozo, Blue Lagoon, Maltese food, what's free, and when to visit. Europe's smallest UNESCO capital.

**Rezumat rapid:** Valletta and Malta deserve 4–5 days. Top priorities: St. John's Co-Cathedral (€15, with Caravaggio), Upper Barrakka Gardens (free, harbour panorama), Blue Lagoon Comino day trip (€35–50), Gozo island for a day (ferry + tour €30–60). Maltese food is astonishingly affordable: pastizzi €0.50 each. Malta uses euros, is EU and Schengen. Direct Wizz Air flight from Bucharest ~2h30.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How many days do you need for Malta?**
R: 3 days: Valletta + Mdina + one excursion (Blue Lagoon or Gozo). 5 days: all of the above plus Marsaxlokk, Dingli Cliffs, more time in Gozo. 7 days: relaxed full-island exploration, possibly basing yourself in Gozo. Ideal first visit: 4–5 days.

**Î: Is Malta expensive?**
R: Mid-range compared to Western Europe. Local food is cheap (pastizzi €0.50, ftira €4–6, restaurant meal €12–18). Accommodation has risen significantly in recent years — good hotels in Valletta cost €80–180/night. Water excursions (Blue Lagoon, Gozo) are the main large expenses: €35–60 per person. Public transport: €2/ticket or daily pass ~€3.

**Î: When is the best time to visit Malta?**
R: April–June and September–November: 20–28°C, warm sea but not sweltering, fewer tourists than summer. July–August: 32–36°C, Blue Lagoon severely overcrowded, maximum prices. Winter (December–March): 14–18°C, perfect for Valletta cultural tourism, Blue Lagoon not worthwhile. Malta is a 12-month destination — winter is underrated.

**Î: Can you visit Malta without a car?**
R: Yes, completely. Valletta and Mdina are pedestrianised. The Tallinja bus network covers the whole island (€2/ticket, €3 daily pass). Bolt works well for short trips. A car makes sense only for Gozo (rent there after the ferry) or independent touring of inland villages.

**Î: Who were the Knights of Malta?**
R: The Order of Saint John (Knights Hospitaller) received Malta from Charles V in 1530 after losing Rhodes. They built Valletta and the Three Cities around the Grand Harbour, successfully repelled the Great Ottoman Siege of 1565 (one of history's most celebrated sieges), and governed the island until 1798 when Napoleon took it without a fight. Today the Order survives as a humanitarian organisation with UN observer status.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How many days do you need in Vienna?**

## Tirana 2026: The Complete City Break Guide to the Balkans' Most Surprising Capital

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/tirana-complete-guide
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-08-08
**Actualizat:** 2026-08-08
**Traducere a:** [tirana-ghid-complet](https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/tirana-ghid-complet)

**Descriere:** Complete Tirana guide: Skanderbeg Square, Bunk'Art 1 and 2, Enver Hoxha's Pyramid, the Blloku district, Pazari i Ri market and the evening xhiro. Albanian lek, real prices and why Tirana is Europe'...

**Rezumat rapid:** Tirana is the capital of Albania and one of Europe's most surprising and dynamic capitals — a city that has transformed radically in 30 years from complete communist isolation to a colourful metropolis with a thriving café scene and nightlife. It has Enver Hoxha's underground bunkers turned museum (Bunk'Art), the dictator's Pyramid turned youth centre, the Blloku district (former forbidden zone of the communist elite) and remarkable gastronomy at incredible prices. Direct flights from Bucharest with Wizz Air.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: How do I get from Bucharest to Tirana?**
R: Wizz Air operates direct flights Bucharest (OTP) → Tirana (TIA). Duration: ~1h45. Prices: 35–90 EUR return. Nënë Tereza Airport is 17 km from the centre — the Airport Shuttle takes 30 minutes (400 ALL/~4 EUR), private taxi 25–35 EUR. Note: airport taxis negotiate — use Bolt or agree the price before getting in.

**Î: What currency does Albania use?**
R: Albania uses the Albanian Lek (ALL). 1 EUR ≈ 100 ALL — an extremely simple calculation: divide the ALL amount by 100 to get the EUR price. Euros are accepted in many places in Tirana but at a less favourable rate. Pay in ALL for the best value. Critical note: Albanian ATMs charge a fixed fee of 700–800 ALL (~7–8 EUR) per withdrawal — withdraw large amounts in one go. City centre exchange offices (not the airport) offer the best rates.

**Î: What is Bunk'Art and which Bunk'Art is more worth visiting?**
R: Bunk'Art 1 is a huge nuclear bunker carved into Mount Dajti, built in 1978 for the communist elite, now a museum with 100+ rooms. Bunk'Art 2 is a smaller bunker in the city centre, focused on the communist Ministry of Internal Affairs and the secret police (Sigurimi). Both cost ~500 ALL (~5 EUR). Bunk'Art 2 is easier to reach (city centre, 5 minutes from Skanderbeg Square) and just as impressive as an experience.

**Î: What is the xhiro and how do I participate?**
R: Xhiro (pronounced 'dziro') is the Albanian evening promenade — a tradition where entire families go out on the boulevard to walk, see and be seen. In Tirana, xhiro happens on Dëshmorët e Kombit Boulevard and in the Blloku district every evening from sunset. You don't need to 'participate' — just walk at the same slow social pace as everyone else. It is one of the most authentic and pleasant customs to witness in the Balkans.

**Î: How much does a 3-day city break in Tirana cost?**
R: A 3-day/2-night city break costs 150–280 EUR per person (mid-range), including flights, accommodation and food. Tirana is one of Europe's most affordable capitals: a local restaurant lunch 3–8 EUR, a beer 1.50–2.50 EUR, mid-range accommodation 30–60 EUR per night. Albania is 40–60% cheaper than Greece or Croatia for comparable experiences.

**Î: Is Tirana safe for tourists?**
R: Yes, Tirana is a safe capital for tourists. The city centre (Skanderbeg Square, Blloku) is safe day and night. Watch out for: airport taxis without meters (use Bolt), pickpockets in Pazari i Ri and Euronet ATMs (high fees). Albania has a deeply rooted culture of hospitality (besa) — tourists are generally treated with warmth.

**Î: What is the story of the Pyramid in Tirana?**
R: The Pyramid was built in 1988 as a mausoleum for dictator Enver Hoxha (died 1985), the most isolated and most repressive communist dictator in Europe. It stood abandoned for decades. In 2022 it was renovated as a cultural space and youth centre, with slides on its sides for children and a belvedere terrace at the top. Its transformation symbolises Albania's reinterpretation of its communist past.

**Î: Are the day trips to Berat or Gjirokastër from Tirana worth it?**
R: Absolutely. Berat is 2 hours from Tirana (bus ~5–6 EUR) and is a UNESCO site with distinctive Ottoman architecture — nicknamed 'the City of a Thousand Windows'. Gjirokastër is 3 hours away (bus ~10 EUR) and is another UNESCO site with an impressive fortress and stone tower houses. Both can be done as day trips from Tirana or with an overnight stay.

## Transnistria 2026: The Complete Guide to Visiting Europe's Last Soviet State

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/transnistria-complete-guide
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-08-08
**Actualizat:** 2026-08-08
**Traducere a:** [transnistria-ghid-complet](https://plecari.com/ro/experiente/transnistria-ghid-complet)

**Descriere:** Complete Transnistria guide: how to enter, what to visit in Tiraspol and Bender Fortress, the Transnistrian ruble, Kvint cognac and the political context of this unrecognised state. Everything you...

**Rezumat rapid:** Transnistria (the Pridnestrovian Moldavian Republic) is a UN-unrecognised breakaway state from Moldova, with its own currency, border, government and Russian troops on its territory. It is the only place in the world where the hammer and sickle flag still officially flies. Its capital Tiraspol functions as a living Soviet museum — intact Lenin statues, Stalinist architecture, vintage trolleybuses. One-day excursion from Chișinău: 2 hours by minibus, free entry for EU citizens.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Do I need a visa for Transnistria as a Romanian/EU citizen?**
R: No. EU citizens (including Romanians) enter Transnistria without a visa. At the border you receive a migration card (no passport stamp). If you stay longer than 10–12 hours, you must inform the border and register with the Transnistrian Ministry of Interior. For a day trip, the process is simple — show your passport and receive the card.

**Î: Is Transnistria safe for tourists?**
R: Yes, Transnistria is generally safe for tourists. Tiraspol is a quiet city. Important rules: don't photograph military installations, border posts or government buildings (Presidential Palace, Parliament) — police can confiscate your phone. Avoid making public political comments. Don't lose your migration card — it must be presented on exit.

**Î: What currency does Transnistria use?**
R: Transnistria uses the Transnistrian Ruble (PRB). It is a closed currency — it cannot be exchanged outside Transnistria and has no value anywhere else in the world. Approximate rate: 1 EUR ≈ 20–22 Transnistrian rubles. Exchange at money changers in Tiraspol or local ATMs. Don't exchange more than you plan to spend — leftover rubles cannot be converted back.

**Î: How do I get from Chișinău to Tiraspol?**
R: Minibus (marshrutka) from Chișinău Central Bus Station to Tiraspol: ~2 hours, 80 Moldovan lei (~4 EUR). Departures every 30 minutes between 7:00 and 18:00. At the border, everyone gets off, presents their passport, receives a migration card, and reboads. Alternative: organised guided tour from Chișinău with transport included (15–40 EUR).

**Î: What is Kvint and is it worth visiting?**
R: Kvint is Transnistria's cognac and vodka factory, founded in 1897, with 10 million litres in storage. There is a daily guided tour at 12:00 (60 Transnistrian rubles, ~3 EUR) with a tasting of 5 types of cognac. The factory shop on Lenin Street sells cognac for 10–30 USD per bottle. It is a must-visit.

**Î: What is the political context of Transnistria and should I have ethical reservations?**
R: Transnistria broke away from Moldova in 1992 in a brief civil war with Russian support. International consensus considers it part of Moldova under Russian military occupation (~1,500 Russian troops are stationed there). Your visit provides indirect economic support to structures maintaining the separation. This is a personal decision — many tourists visit to understand, not to legitimise. Research before going.

**Î: Can I pay by card in Transnistria?**
R: Rarely. Cards are accepted in some larger hotels and restaurants, but the vast majority of transactions are cash in Transnistrian rubles. Bring sufficient EUR or MDL to exchange at the border or in the city.

**Î: Is there a risk of being arrested or detained in Transnistria?**
R: The risk exists if you violate the rules — photographing military installations, being suspected of espionage, or conducting unauthorised journalism. For the ordinary tourist who follows the rules (don't photograph forbidden buildings, don't make political comments in public, keep your migration card), the visit proceeds normally. Hundreds of thousands of tourists visit annually without incidents.

## 3 Best Day Trips from Bucharest to Transylvania 2026: Castles, Mountains & Medieval Towns

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/experiente/transylvania-day-trips-bucharest
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** experiente
**Publicat:** 2026-07-12
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-12

**Descriere:** Best day trips from Bucharest to Transylvania: Peleș Castle, Brașov, Bran Castle. Train times, costs, and whether to go solo or join a guided tour.

**Rezumat rapid:** The three best day trips from Bucharest to Transylvania are: Sinaia + Peleș Castle (1.5 hours by train, €8, often called the most beautiful castle in Europe), Brașov + Black Church + Tâmpa Mountain (2.5 hours by train, €10, stunning medieval city), and Bran Castle ('Dracula's Castle', 30 minutes from Brașov). You can combine Brașov + Bran in a single long day trip. Guided day tours from Bucharest start at €45 on GetYourGuide and include transport, entrance fees, and an English-speaking guide.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Can you visit Transylvania as a day trip from Bucharest?**
R: Yes. Sinaia (Peleș Castle) is 1.5 hours by train, and Brașov is 2.5 hours. Both have regular train connections. You can comfortably visit either one as a day trip. Combining Brașov + Bran Castle in one day is possible but makes for a long day (leave Bucharest by 7:00 AM, return by 9:00 PM). Guided tours handle the logistics and typically include Peleș, Brașov, and Bran in a single 12-hour day.

**Î: Is Bran Castle actually Dracula's Castle?**
R: Not really. Bran Castle's connection to Vlad the Impaler (the historical Dracula) is tenuous — he may have been imprisoned there briefly. Bram Stoker never visited Romania and his description of Dracula's castle doesn't match Bran. However, the castle is atmospheric, well-preserved, and genuinely interesting as a medieval fortress and royal residence. The Dracula marketing is a bonus, not the reason to go.

**Î: Tour or solo — which is better?**
R: Solo by train is cheaper and more flexible (€8-10 each way, go at your own pace). Guided tours (€45-75 via GetYourGuide) are better if you want to see multiple sites in one day (they combine Peleș + Brașov + Bran), include English-speaking guides who add historical context, and handle all transport. For first-time visitors with limited time, a guided tour is the pragmatic choice.

**Î: What's the best castle in Transylvania?**
R: Peleș Castle in Sinaia is almost universally considered the most beautiful. It's a Neo-Renaissance masterpiece with 160 rooms, Murano glass, hand-painted ceilings, and weapons collections. If you can only visit one castle, make it Peleș. Bran is more famous (Dracula marketing) but architecturally less impressive.

**Î: Is it safe to travel by train in Romania?**
R: Yes. Romanian trains (CFR) are safe, affordable, and reliable on main routes. Buy tickets at the station or online at cfrcalatori.ro. First class (€12-15 to Brașov) is recommended — it's still cheap and significantly more comfortable. Trains can run late by 15-30 minutes, so build buffer time for your return.

## Travel Insurance for Children 2026: Complete Parent's Guide

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/asigurari/travel-insurance-children
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** asigurari
**Publicat:** 2026-08-23
**Traducere a:** [asigurare-calatorie-copii](https://plecari.com/ro/asigurari/asigurare-calatorie-copii)

**Descriere:** Everything parents need to know: real prices, pediatric emergency costs by destination, family vs individual policies, activity coverage, and common mistakes.

**Rezumat rapid:** Children need their own travel insurance — they're not automatically covered by a parent's policy. A child's policy costs €6-14 per week in Europe (20-30% less than adults), and family packages save an additional 15-25%. Pediatric emergencies abroad cost €500-15,000 without insurance, and medical repatriation €5,000-80,000. For Schengen visas, children also need minimum €30,000 medical coverage. The policy must explicitly include: pediatric care, repatriation, companion accommodation, and any planned activities (skiing, swimming pools).

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Does a child under 2 need travel insurance?**
R: Yes. There's no minimum age for travel insurance — babies can have medical emergencies on holiday (fever, dehydration, allergic reactions). EKTA covers from age 0 (2 months). Children aged 0-2 may have a 5-10% premium surcharge due to higher medical vulnerability, but the policy remains very affordable (under €10/week).

**Î: Does the EHIC cover children too?**
R: Yes, each child can have their own European Health Insurance Card (EHIC), free of charge. But like adults, the EHIC only covers emergencies in PUBLIC hospitals within the EU and does NOT cover repatriation, private clinics, or adventure activities. The child's card is separate from the parent's — children are not automatically included on an adult's card.

**Î: How much does travel insurance cost for a child?**
R: €6-14 for 7 days in Europe (Schengen). €12-28 for 8-15 days. Children pay 20-30% less than adults. Family packages (2 adults + 2 children) offer an additional 15-25% discount vs individual policies. With EKTA, the price starts at $0.99/day/person (Start plan), regardless of age.

**Î: What documents does a child need when travelling with one parent?**
R: Requirements vary by country, but many destinations require a notarised consent letter from the absent parent, specifying the destination and travel dates. Some airlines also require this. Check the requirements for your destination well in advance — especially for non-EU travel.

**Î: Does summer camp or school trip insurance cover my child?**
R: Check with the organiser. Many camps and school trips include group insurance, but coverage may be limited (lower medical caps, no adventure sports rider). If the camp includes skiing, horse riding, or water sports, verify explicitly that the group policy covers those activities. If not, buy a supplementary individual policy.

**Î: What happens if my child gets sick and we have to cancel the holiday?**
R: A policy with trip cancellation coverage reimburses prepaid costs (flights, hotels, excursions) if your child falls ill before departure and a doctor certifies they can't travel. Children get sick more frequently than adults — cancellation cover is more important for families than any other traveller type.

**Î: Does insurance cover activities like swimming pools, water parks, or skiing?**
R: It depends on the policy. Swimming pools and beaches are considered 'calm' activities and are covered as standard. Water parks with slides, skiing, horse riding, and water sports may require an 'active sport' or 'winter sport' rider. Check the policy BEFORE departure — a skiing accident without a winter sports rider means a rejected claim.

**Î: Can a child under 14 be insured separately from their parents?**
R: Yes — a child can have their own travel insurance policy regardless of age. The insurer doesn't require parents to be insured with the same provider. But family packages are usually cheaper than separate policies. With EKTA, you add the child as an 'additional traveller' on the same policy.

**Î: What's the difference between travel insurance and trip cancellation insurance?**
R: Standard travel insurance covers what happens DURING the trip: medical emergencies, lost baggage, delays, repatriation. ## Travel Scams in Europe 2026: The 15 Most Common Tricks and How to Protect Yourself

**Rezumat rapid:** The most common travel scams in Europe in 2026: ATM skimming (use indoor bank ATMs only), taxi meter tricks (use Bolt/Uber instead), restaurants without prices on the menu (always ask before ordering), forced friendship bracelets in Paris and Rome, fake petitions that cover pickpocketing, and Dynamic Currency Conversion at ATMs (always choose local currency, never your home currency). Travel insurance covering theft costs €15-25/week and is essential.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: What are the most common tourist scams in Europe?**
R: Top 5: rigged taxi meters (or 'broken' meters with inflated flat rates), ATM skimming devices that clone your card, restaurants without prices that present inflated bills, street sellers forcing bracelets/roses then demanding payment, and the 'helpful stranger' who distracts you while an accomplice picks your pocket.

**Î: How do I avoid ATM skimming in Europe?**
R: Use ATMs inside bank branches only — never street ATMs in tourist areas. Wiggle the card slot before inserting (skimmers are loosely attached). Cover the keypad when entering your PIN. Enable instant transaction notifications on your banking app. Use Revolut or Wise for travel spending — they have instant freeze if compromised.

**Î: Is Uber/Bolt safe to use in Europe?**
R: Yes, and it's the single best defence against taxi scams. Price is fixed before the ride, route is GPS-tracked, payment is on card (no cash disputes), and you have a direct complaint channel in the app. Bolt and Uber work in most major European cities.

## Trip Cancellation Insurance 2026: What It Covers, When It Is Worth It and How to Claim

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/asigurari/trip-cancellation-insurance
**Limbă:** English
**Verticală:** asigurari
**Publicat:** 2026-07-30
**Actualizat:** 2026-07-30
**Traducere a:** [asigurare-anulare-calatorie](https://plecari.com/ro/asigurari/asigurare-anulare-calatorie)

**Descriere:** Trip cancellation insurance: what is covered and excluded, how much it costs, difference from standard travel insurance, Cancel For Any Reason (CFAR), claims process and common mistakes.

**Rezumat rapid:** Trip cancellation insurance covers non-refundable travel costs (flights, hotels, cruises, excursions) if you are forced to cancel due to a covered reason: sudden illness documented by a doctor, death or serious illness of a close family member, a home emergency requiring your presence, or a legal summons. It does NOT cover changing your mind, fear of travelling, or events already known when you bought the policy. It is worth buying whenever your total non-refundable bookings exceed €500–600 — the policy typically costs 5–8% of that amount.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: What is the difference between trip cancellation insurance and standard travel insurance?**
R: Standard travel insurance covers what happens DURING your trip: medical emergencies, lost luggage, flight delays, repatriation. Trip cancellation insurance covers what happens BEFORE departure: you cannot travel and want to recover the money you have already paid. Comprehensive policies combine both — medical cover, cancellation, baggage, and delays — in a single product. This is usually the better option for most travellers.

**Î: Can I buy trip cancellation insurance after booking?**
R: Yes, any time before departure — but with important caveats. There is typically a 24–72 hour waiting period after purchase before the policy activates. If you fall ill on the day you buy, you are not covered. For Cancel For Any Reason (CFAR) options, you must buy within 14–21 days of your first booking. The rule: buy immediately after your first non-refundable reservation.

**Î: Does trip cancellation insurance cover pre-existing medical conditions?**
R: Partially, depending on the policy. If you have a stable chronic condition and suffer an unexpected acute worsening documented by a doctor, many policies cover this. If you choose not to travel due to a pre-existing condition without a specific acute medical event, it is typically not covered. Always declare existing conditions at purchase — non-disclosure can invalidate the entire claim.

**Î: Is trip cancellation different from when an airline cancels my flight?**
R: Completely different scenarios. If the airline cancels your flight, it is legally required to refund you or reroute you under EU261/2004 — your insurance is not involved. Trip cancellation insurance activates when YOU cancel for a personal reason (illness, family emergency). These are separate entitlements. See: flight delay and cancellation rights EU261.

**Î: How much does trip cancellation insurance cost?**
R: Standard trip cancellation insurance costs approximately 5–8% of the total non-refundable booking value. For €1,000 of non-refundable bookings: €50–80. For €3,000: €150–240. A comprehensive policy covering medical emergencies, cancellation, and baggage costs €15–30/week for European travel — less than a restaurant meal.

**Î: What is Cancel For Any Reason (CFAR) insurance?**
R: CFAR allows you to cancel for any reason — no medical certificate, no documentation — and recover 50–75% of your non-refundable costs. It must be purchased within 14–21 days of your first booking (after this window, it is not available). It costs 2–3 times more than standard cancellation insurance. Worth it for large non-refundable bookings (cruises, expensive packages) where you want complete flexibility.

**Î: Do cruise passengers need trip cancellation insurance?**
R: Yes — cruise lines have the most severe cancellation penalties in the travel industry: typically 100% forfeiture with less than 15 days before sailing. On a €2,000/person cruise, an unexpected illness 10 days before departure means losing the entire amount. Trip cancellation insurance is practically mandatory for cruise bookings.

**Î: Does the insurance from my credit card cover trip cancellation?**
R: Premium credit cards (Visa Infinite, Mastercard Platinum, Amex Gold) sometimes include trip cancellation benefits — typically covering €1,000–5,000 per claim with specific conditions (the trip must be paid with that card). Read your cardholder agreement carefully before buying a separate policy. If your non-refundable bookings exceed the card's limit, supplement with a dedicated policy.

## Is Turkey Safe to Visit in 2026? Antalya, Istanbul and the Coast — Honest Guide

**URL:** https://plecari.com/en/asigurari/turkey-2026-safety-guide

**Descriere:** Current safety situation in Turkey for tourists in 2026, which regions to avoid, what travel advisories say, and essential practical advice for Antalya, Istanbul and the Aegean coast.

**Rezumat rapid:** Turkey's tourist areas — Antalya, Istanbul, the Aegean coast (Bodrum, Marmaris, Fethiye) — are considered safe for visitors in 2026 by UK, EU, and US government travel advisories. The regions to avoid are in southeastern Turkey, near the borders with Syria, Iraq, and Iran — approximately 1,200–1,700 km from the main tourist destinations. An eSIM is essential (buy before arrival — provider websites are blocked inside Turkey). Travel insurance is mandatory — the EHIC does not apply in Turkey.

**Întrebări frecvente:**

**Î: Is Antalya safe in 2026?**
R: Yes. Antalya is on Turkey's Mediterranean coast, approximately 1,200 km from the Syrian and Iraqi borders. UK, EU, and US travel advisories do not advise against travel to Antalya, Kemer, Side, Alanya, or Belek. The resort areas operate normally with full international tourist flows.

**Î: Which regions of Turkey should I avoid?**
R: All major government advisories (UK FCDO, US State Department, EU member state foreign ministries) advise against all travel or all but essential travel to southeastern Turkey: the provinces bordering Syria (Hatay, Gaziantep, Kilis), Iraq (Sirnak, Hakkari, Şırnak), and Iran (Van, Ağrı, Kars). These areas are 800–1,700 km from the main tourist destinations.

**Î: Is Istanbul safe in 2026?**
R: Yes, with normal urban precautions. Istanbul operates normally as a major global city and tourism hub. Hagia Sophia, Topkapi Palace, the Grand Bazaar, and the Bosphorus are all open and fully functioning. Standard advice: use Uber or Bolt rather than unlicensed taxis, watch for the 'friendly bar' scam (a 'local' invites you for drinks, bill arrives at €200+), and be alert to pickpockets in crowded tourist areas.

**Î: Do I need an e-Visa for Turkey?**
R: Most Western nationalities need an e-Visa. UK, US, Australian, and most EU citizens need to apply at evisa.gov.tr before departure. Cost: typically $50–60 USD, valid for 180 days with a maximum 90-day stay. EU citizens from some countries may enter without a visa — check your specific nationality. The e-Visa application takes 5–10 minutes and is processed within minutes to hours.

**Î: Do I need an eSIM for Turkey?**
R: Yes, strongly recommended — and it must be purchased BEFORE you arrive. Turkey is outside the EU, so your EU roaming allowance does not apply; carrier roaming typically costs €10–15/GB. A 5 GB / 30-day Turkey eSIM costs approximately $10–15 on Airalo. Critically: since 2025, Turkish authorities block access to major eSIM provider websites (Airalo, Saily, Holafly) from within Turkey. You cannot purchase after arrival.

**Î: Does the European Health Insurance Card (EHIC) work in Turkey?**
R: No. Turkey is not an EU member and has no bilateral healthcare agreement with the EU. The EHIC is completely invalid in Turkey. Private travel insurance is your only medical protection. A single night in a private Turkish hospital can cost €500–2,000+. Travel insurance for Turkey costs €15–25 for a week.

**Î: What currency should I use in Turkey?**
R: Turkish lira (TRY) is the official currency. In major tourist areas (Antalya, Istanbul, resort hotels), euros and US dollars are widely accepted, often at competitive rates. In bazaars and local shops, Turkish lira is preferred and you will get better prices. Withdraw TRY from local ATMs (not at the airport — rates there are poor). Use Revolut or Wise for card payments to avoid foreign transaction fees.
